title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Scribes in the Scriptorium keep notebooks, and every page is stuffed with outputs and images. Your Astral changed one line, and reviewing it means wading through all of it. Find out why, then find the single line that mattered.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster cannot review a notebook, and asks for a clean summary.


The Diviner’s notebooks are her lab books, and she guards them.


The Artificer strips the outputs before committing.


The Archivist keeps the outputs as a record, and the code apart.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: A notebook is a JSON file
text:
A notebook is a JSON file
You need this before an agent edits a notebook for you: if you cannot see what changed, you cannot review it. A .ipynb file is a JSON document with metadata, nbformat, nbformat_minor (the notebook file-format version numbers) and a list of cells. A code cell stores its source, and also an execution_count and its outputs. A plot is stored inside the file as a base64 string (the image bytes written out as plain text). Source and outputs share one file, so any run rewrites lines next to the code.
This is what git sees, with or without an agent. The two mock notebooks differ by one real change: the cutoff 30 became 40. Compare them:
diff before.ipynb after.ipynb
5c5
<    "execution_count": 3,
---
>    "execution_count": 7,
8c8
<     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 30]))"
---
>     "print(len([r for r in reads if r >= 40]))"
15c15
<       "3\n"
---
>       "2\n"
21c21
<       "image/png": "AAECAwQFBgcICQoLDA0ODxAREhMUFRYXGBkaGx...
---
>       "image/png": "AAMGCQwPEhUYGx4hJCcqLTAzNjk8P0JFSEtOUV...
Four spots changed, and one of them is the code. The rest is the run counter, the printed result and an image blob. A real notebook has more cells and bigger images, so the code change is harder still to find; git diff --stat shows how large a notebook diff is.
The risk is the same with a coding agent as with a human: a reviewer who cannot find the code change may approve without reading it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
section: Four ways to make changes reviewable
text:
Four ways to make changes reviewable
Each option moves the noise somewhere else. Pick by what your team can adopt.

nbstripout: strips outputs and some metadata when git stores the notebook. Outputs stay in your working file. A filter is a program git runs on a file as it stores it. Cost: each collaborator runs nbstripout --install themselves, because git does not copy filter settings when someone clones the repository.
jupytext: pairs the .ipynb with a .py (the py:percent format suits code). You review the .py and outputs stay in the .ipynb. Cost: two files to keep in sync.
nbdime: a notebook-aware diff, with nbdiff in the terminal, nbdiff-web in the browser, git integration and a merge driver. Cost: everyone reviewing needs it installed.
marimo: stores notebooks as pure Python, so ordinary git diffs work. Cost: a different notebook tool from Jupyter. marimo convert your_notebook.ipynb > your_notebook.py converts an existing notebook.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
Review the code cells
Whatever you choose, the review habit is the same:

Look at the source cells. Treat outputs as something to regenerate.
Run git diff --stat before committing and look for a notebook that grew by megabytes.
An output in a diff shows that something ran once; a re-run shows whether the code produces it.

title: Why Notebooks Diff Badly
text:
With an agent

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code reads a .ipynb with all its cells and outputs, and an output-heavy notebook fills the context window (the text the agent can hold at once). When an agent edits a code cell, expect that cell’s saved outputs and execution count to be cleared, so the diff shows lost outputs as well as new source.
nbstripout is a git filter, so outputs stay in the working file and the agent still reads them. To keep the agent on the code, strip outputs from the working copy (nbstripout’s pre-commit mode does this) or point the agent at the paired .py. Check the docs for your version.


The idea is the same: review the source cells. Check OpenCode’s docs for how it handles notebook files.

title: Review Agent-Written Work
text:
Sooner or later the work comes back across the reef to you, and it is your turn to be the reviewer. A good reviewer is kind and exact, and neither tires nor hurries, even when an Astral wrote the work and sounds sure of it. Learn the code that keeps both the work and the author in good shape.
You need this because you will also receive LLM-assisted work to review. This quest covers what to ask for and how to say it. Reviewing it is the same craft as any review, with a few shifts in attention.

title: Review Agent-Written Work
text:
Formats that review well
When you ask an agent to produce analysis, choose a format your reviewer can diff. A marimo notebook is stored as a plain .py file, so a diff shows what changed. A Jupyter .ipynb is JSON that also stores outputs, so its diffs are noisy unless you strip outputs with a tool such as nbstripout.

title: Send Small Changes, Say What You Checked
text:
A reef thrives on many hands, and a Review-leech clings to it, feeding on work passed along unchecked. An Astral’s vast haul of changes lands on one reviewer’s desk, and the leech grows fat. Four small habits starve it, and you can practise them on your next hand-off.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster wants small, reviewable pieces and a named reviewer.


The Diviner attaches the check to every change.


The Artificer’s changes fit on one screen.


The Archivist’s changes arrive with an audit note.
Checking an agent’s output takes time. When the output reaches the next person without a word, that cost moves to them. You are about to hand work to a collaborator, so four habits keep the cost with the sender.
A colleague who does not use LLMs can review work sent this way without learning a tool.

title: Send Small Changes, Say What You Checked
section: When you worry about looking lazy
text:
When you worry about looking lazy
A common worry is that people will think you are lazy or unoriginal for using an agent. Make the facts easy to see.

Say plainly what the agent did and what you checked. “The agent drafted the plotting code. I read it and compared the output with a hand calculation.”
Follow the local norm. Some groups want a note in the commit message, some in the methods. A journal or conference may have a disclosure policy, so read its own page before you submit. A lead or an editor can tell you what they expect.
Let the evidence speak. Tests, checks and your ability to explain every line show the work is yours.

title: Boss: Review Large Output
text:
At the maze’s heart rises a wall of text, thousands of lines high, and your Astral is already reading aloud from the bottom. The wall cannot be read in one sitting, and everything you have learned so far is needed to get past it.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster sets a review budget before the wall rises.


The Diviner samples the wall and checks each sample against ground truth.


The Artificer asks for smaller pieces.


The Archivist checks the wall’s totals against the ledger.

title: Boss: Review Large Output
text:
Too much output to review
An agent can produce thousands of lines of diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) faster than anyone can review them. If you merge them unread, unchecked errors enter your work. If you try to read all of them, your attention thins and you approve things you did not understand. Both routes fail.
Instead, accept only what you can check:

Keep a review budget: ask for no more than you can honestly review today. Bulk low-quality output is called slop.
Ask for smaller pieces.
Ground each piece in a check.
Pass on only work you have read yourself.

A human check can fail in two ways. Automation bias is trusting the machine’s output too readily. Rubber-stamping is approving without reading. An “approve each item” step at hundreds of items an hour turns into clicking through. A check that works:

shows what changed, at a volume a person can read;
offers approve, edit, veto and stop;
keeps a real decision point wherever results or other people are affected;
records the human step as part of the work’s provenance (the record of where a result came from).

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
A door in the maze swings shut behind your Astral. Its account of what it did is plausible, and the walls have changed shape anyway. You cannot follow the path without a record, so ask it to write one, then walk it yourself to see whether it holds.
“I do not understand what it did” is a fair worry. A paper trail answers it: short documents that say what changed, why and how to run it. The habit is to let the agent draft them, check each one against ground truth and own the why.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
The routine
Every document in this lesson follows the same four steps:

Ask. Request the draft, and say what it must cover.
Check against ground truth. Compare the draft with the real thing: the diff, a run on a clean copy, the code, the logs. Look for what the draft omits and for claims the real thing lacks.
Explain back. Say in your own words, one sentence per point, what the document records. A point you cannot put into a sentence is a point to question or leave out.
Keep, edit or revert. Decide after steps 2 and 3.

The agent drafts structure and wording well. Ground truth and the reasons come from you.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
1. Changelog
A changelog here is the agent’s short account of a change: files touched, behaviour change, what it left alone, and how to verify. The diff is the ground truth. A changelog can miss a change or overstate one, so use it as a guide to what to look for in the diff.
Ask for one after the agent finishes:
Write a changelog for the change you just made.
List the files you touched, what behaviour changed and why,
what you deliberately left alone, and one command I can run to verify it.
Mention every change in the diff, including defaults and thresholds.
Say which tests you added or ran, or say that you added none.
To check it, run git diff (changes to tracked files that you have not staged), git diff --staged (changes you have staged), or git diff --stat for a one-line-per-file summary. For a change the agent already committed, run git log -p. Run git status to list new files, which git diff does not show.

Try it on a small change
An agent was asked to fix a GC-content filter that crashed on empty sequences. This is the diff of the one file it changed (mock code):
--- a/gc_filter.py
+++ b/gc_filter.py
@@ -1,11 +1,11 @@
-MIN_GC = 40.0
+MIN_GC = 45.0
 
 
 def gc_content(seq):
-    seq = seq.strip()
+    seq = seq.strip().upper()
     gc = sum(1 for b in seq if b in "GC")
     return 100.0 * gc / len(seq)
 
 
 def keep(records):
-    return [r for r in records if gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
+    return [r for r in records if len(r[1].strip()) > 0 and gc_content(r[1]) >= MIN_GC]
This is the agent’s changelog:
Changelog
- Files: gc_filter.py only.
- Lowercase bases now count towards GC (gc_content uppercases the sequence).
- keep() skips empty sequences instead of dividing by zero.
- Added tests for both fixes.
- Left alone: the FASTA reading code and the output format.
- Verify: python -c "from gc_filter import keep; print(keep([('a', ''), ('b', 'ggcc')]))"
Read the diff against the changelog, line by line. Two things do not match, and one of them changes which records survive the filter. Find both before you read on.
You should have found:

Omitted: MIN_GC moved from 40.0 to 45.0. Fewer records pass the filter now, and the changelog never says so.
Overstated: “Added tests for both fixes”. The diff touches one file and adds no test.

Your explain-back could be three sentences: “Lowercase bases now count. Empty sequences are skipped. The cut-off rose from 40 to 45, which I have to decide whether to keep.” Then ask the agent about the threshold, and either revert that line or keep it on purpose.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
2. ADR: the decision record
An ADR (architecture decision record) is a short note about one decision. A common layout has four parts (Nygard’s original post adds a title and a status such as proposed or accepted):

Context: the forces at play, in neutral words.
Decision: what you will do, in full sentences.
Alternatives considered: the options you weighed.
Consequences: what follows, the good and the bad.

The agent does not know your constraints: your cluster’s rules, your team’s skills, your deadline. So the decision and the reasons are yours. The agent can structure the note and draft the options. Check that every alternative is real and every consequence is listed, including the costs.
A mock example:
ADR 3: Keep the FASTA filter as a script
Status: accepted
Context: we filter reads by GC content once per project. The pipeline
  has no other Python step. Two people maintain it, both new to Nextflow.
Decision: we will keep filter_gc.py as a plain script and call it from
  the run script. We will not add a workflow step.
Alternatives considered: a workflow process (reproducible, but new machinery for
  two maintainers); a one-off notebook (no record of parameters).
Consequences: simple to read and run. Resume and containers do not
  cover this step. We revisit if a second filter appears.
Only you can say whether “two maintainers new to Nextflow” is true. Only you can confirm that line, so an agent’s draft of it is a guess to check.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
3. Commit message
Your explain-back from step 3 of the routine makes a good commit message. Use one sentence per change as the body, and the reason for a change travels with the code.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
4. README and how-to-run notes
A README records how to set up and run the project. The agent drafts it well from the files. The ground truth is a run: copy the project into an empty folder (or clone it) and type the commands exactly as written. A step that fails, or that relies on a file only your machine has, is a gap in the document.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
5. Comments and docstrings
A comment records the why that the code cannot show. Ask the agent to draft docstrings, then read each one against the code. A docstring that says “returns the GC percentage” while the function returns a fraction is wrong, and a reader will trust it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
6. Analysis log and methods note
For science work, the log records what was run: the tools and their versions, the model and version that helped, the parameters, the input files, and what the agent did. The agent can draft it from the session. Check it against the real logs, the outputs and the output of each tool’s version command (often --version; run --help to see yours). Whatever you publish carries your name, so each line has to be right.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
section: The same habit for the next session
text:
The same habit for the next session
A handoff note records where the work stands for whoever starts next, including a fresh agent session. The routine is the same: let the agent draft it, check it against the files and git state, and edit it before you rely on it.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
When to use the habit

Small diffs: always. It costs a minute.
Large diffs: ask for a changelog per commit, so each one covers a piece you can read.
Better still: ask for work in small steps, so every diff stays small.

title: Keep a Paper Trail
text:
Battle: the paper trail




After the next real change an agent makes for you, ask for a changelog and check it against git diff. Write down one thing it missed or overstated, or note that it matched.


Run your project’s README commands in an empty folder, exactly as written. Fix the first step that fails.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
In the beastmasters’ college a trainer offers to raise a familiar for one trick. It takes many examples, a record of the lessons and a test of the result, and every trick costs a season. You ask whether a better command would do the same job. Weigh the offer before you pay for it.
A model out of the box is general. Fine-tuning trains it further on your own examples so that it handles one kind of task better. It is a heavy step with its own upkeep. You will meet the idea when someone offers it as the fix for a model that does a job badly. Check whether you need it before you collect training data. Using it is optional.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
1. What fine-tuning and LoRA are
To fine-tune a model is to continue training it on examples from your task. Its weights (the numbers it learned) change, so the result is a model of its own.
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) is one way to fine-tune. The base model is the model you start from. LoRA works in three steps:

Freeze: the base model’s original weights stay as they are.
Train a small adapter: you train a small set of extra number tables (matrices, called the “adapter”) on your examples.
Merge later: the adapter can be merged into the base model afterwards.

Training only the adapter needs far less memory than retraining everything.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
2. Four conditions
Consider LoRA when all of these hold:

You have the model weights. An open-weight model (its weights can be downloaded) qualifies; a hosted model reached through an API usually does not.
The task is narrow and repeatable. The same kind of input and output every time, such as tagging text with a fixed label set.
You have examples with known answers. You need enough to train on (hundreds to thousands for a narrow task, as in the worked decision below), and some held back for testing.
You have an eval (a repeatable test with a score). It shows that the tuned model beats the untuned one on that task.

If one condition fails, try something else first.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
section: 3. What to try first for agent work
text:
3. What to try first for agent work
Try these in order: first a working eval, because it shows whether anything helps; then a clearer prompt, which is the cheapest thing to change; then better tools. Fine-tune last, when you can show that those fall short on a narrow task.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
4. What fine-tuning adds to track

The training data: which examples went in, and which were held back.
The adapter version: each training run gives a new one.
The base model: the model you started from (defined above). An adapter belongs to the base model it was trained on.

The result is a trained model that does one task, so you check it the way you check any trained model: against held-back examples on that task.

title: Should You Fine-Tune?
text:
5. Worked decision: two mock tasks
A lab keeps free-text sequencing notes. Two jobs come up.









Task A
Task B




Job
Replace sample IDs in notes with [ID]
Summarise the methods section of papers


Input
Short free-text notes
Long papers of every kind


Right answer
Clear: an ID is masked or it is not
Many acceptable summaries


Examples with known answers
2,000 notes marked by hand
A few summaries



Task A is the LoRA candidate:

It is narrow and repeatable.
It has hand-marked examples, each with a clear answer, so some can be held back.
An eval is easy to write: count IDs left in the output.

Task B has no single right answer and few examples, so a clear prompt and a check by a reader come first. If the ID pattern is fixed and known, a script handles Task A without any training.
Now pick a task from your own work and write the four conditions beside it. Mark each one yes, no or unknown. Any “no” or “unknown” is where you start.

text:

title: Pick Your Model
text:
In the sages’ college the academics keep Astrals of every size on a long shelf. A great one speaks well, answers slowly and costs the most to feed, and a small one is quick and cheap and loses the thread. The academic says you must choose for each job, and decide how hard each should think. Learn to choose, then check that you chose well.
Every session starts with a model and an effort level, and the defaults do not suit every job. A model that is too small skips checks and loses the thread. One that is too large costs more and runs slower, and you may not notice because the answer looks fine. This page covers how to choose both, so you can run later quests without overspending or under-powering them and how to check the choice. Model names, aliases and defaults change often, so check your own tool for the current ones.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
Words to know

Model tier: a size class of model. A smaller one is faster and cheaper; a larger one is more capable and costs more. Anthropic names its tiers Haiku, Sonnet, Opus and Fable, from smallest and fastest (Haiku) to largest and slowest (Fable).
Alias: a short nickname (such as sonnet) that the tool maps to a concrete model version.
Effort: how much the model thinks before each step.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts with its own fresh context. It does a side task and returns only a summary. To delegate is to hand it a task.
Frontmatter: the small settings block at the top of a Markdown file.
Pin: name one exact model version so it never silently changes.
Inherit: use whatever the parent is using.
Prompt cache: a short-term store that makes re-reading an unchanged conversation cheaper.
Compacting: replacing the conversation history with a short summary.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
1. Two settings

Model: what the model knows and can do.
Effort: how much it thinks per step. Lower effort means fewer and terser tool calls (the actions the agent takes, such as reading a file or running a command); higher effort means more thoroughness.

Changing effort is often cheaper to try than switching models.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
2. How to set them

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Model. You choose a model by alias, and you pin a full name when results must be reproducible (shown below the table). The aliases are default (clears an override and names no model), best (same as opus), fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] (the [1m] forms ask for a longer context window), and opusplan (opus in plan mode, then sonnet for the execution). Plan mode is a mode in which the agent proposes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it. On the Anthropic API, opus, sonnet and haiku map to the current 5.5 versions; other providers can resolve the same alias to older versions.









Way
How
Note




In a session
/model <alias or name>
alone, it opens a picker; Enter saves it as your default, s keeps it for this session only


Per launch
claude --model <alias or name>



Environment
ANTHROPIC_MODEL



Settings file
model field




For results that must be reproducible (a lab pipeline, course material), pin a full model name such as claude-opus-5-5, because an alias moves when a new version ships. The variables ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL pin what each alias means.

Effort. Set it with /effort, claude --effort, the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, or the effortLevel setting. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh (between high and max) and max, and which ones exist depends on the model. The default differs by model and by surface: for Sonnet 5.5 it is medium in Claude Code and high on the API. Run /effort in your own tool to read yours.
Per skill and per subagent. Skill files and subagent files both take model and effort in their frontmatter.
Skill: model takes the same values as /model, or inherit. A skill’s model and effort apply for the rest of that one turn and are not saved. Its effort overrides the session level but not CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL.
Subagent: model takes sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit. effort takes low to max. If the subagent’s model differs from the main one and you give no effort, the session level does not apply to it, so set it.
Which model a subagent gets, first match wins: the per-call model parameter, then the definition’s model, then the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, then the main conversation’s model.

A subagent is a Markdown file with frontmatter in .claude/agents/ (project) or ~/.claude/agents/ (yours):
---
name: log-reader
description: Reads long pipeline logs and reports only failed tasks with their error lines.
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Read the logs you are given. Return: task name, exit status, the first error line.
Quote lines exactly. If something is unclear, say so.
A tools field can also limit what the helper may use. The sub-agents page in Lore has the exact syntax.
This sketch uses medium because Haiku 5.5 at low is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check. For reading logs, catching every failure is the point.



/models picks a model for the current session only; the config file is unchanged.
opencode run --model provider/model-id sets it for one run. The format is provider/model-id, with an optional #variant such as #high. IDs are case-sensitive.
The model key in opencode.json (or opencode.jsonc) sets your default.
An agent can have its own model key. A subagent with no model inherits the parent session’s model. The frontmatter example is mode: subagent plus model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5#high.
A local Ollama model is selectable like any other, for example ollama/gemma3:4b.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
3. Starting points
Start from the tiers and the table below, and test each row on your own jobs. The four tiers, in order of capability:

Haiku: fastest replies and lowest cost; suited to subagent tasks.
Sonnet: everyday coding and agent work.
Opus: complex agentic coding; most workloads start here.
Fable: the hardest, long-running work.










Job
Start with
Effort
Why




Most everyday work, no better information
Sonnet or Opus
the tool’s default
both suit everyday work; compare them on one of your own jobs


Bulk reading, classifying or extracting with output you can check
Haiku, often as a subagent
medium, or low if you re-run failures
cheap per item; a checker catches errors


Exploratory reading (“where is X handled?”)
a subagent
low or medium
the main context stays clean; only a summary returns


Planning a change
consider Opus or Fable
medium to high
a bad plan makes every later step wrong


Mechanical edits with tests that fail loudly
Sonnet
medium
the tests do the judging


Hardest multi-file change, or unfamiliar science
Opus or Fable
high, then up only if a check shows a gain
a stronger model may know more

title: Pick Your Model
section: 4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
text:
4. When the output is not good enough: the upgrade ladder
Climb one rung at a time and re-check after each.

Add a way to verify. A test, a script, a count against an independent tool, a second look that does not share the first one’s blind spot. Without it you cannot tell whether the next rungs helped.
Raise effort one level.
Change the model to the next tier up.


Cheap-then-retry: if outcomes are checkable (tests, or a verifier, which is a separate check that tests the output), run at low effort and re-run only the failures at higher effort. A checker that passes bad work lets failures through, and a failure costs two runs of waiting time.

Compare cost per finished task, because failed tasks still cost money and a few hard tasks can carry much of the bill.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
5. Delegation hygiene

Keep the expensive model’s context lean. Sending bulk reading to a subagent keeps that reading out of the main conversation.
Spot-check summaries. A subagent returns only a summary, and summaries omit and distort. Ask for exact quotes or file paths and open two yourself. Many subagents returning long answers can also fill the main context again.
State your rules in the delegation prompt. The built-in Explore subagent (a read-only search helper) and Plan subagent (a read-only research helper used in plan mode) skip CLAUDE.md, the instructions file the tool loads at session start. A rule like “never touch raw/” must be written into the task you hand them. Custom subagents load CLAUDE.md unless set to skip it.
Switch models at a quiet moment. Switching model mid-conversation can change prompt-cache behaviour, and the tool may ask you to confirm.
Change effort only between sessions when you compare, so one session never mixes two settings. On older models, and on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, changing effort mid-session invalidates the cache. On Fable 5.1 and later, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 with an API key or subscription, it keeps the cache.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
6. Measure on your own task
Pick one small real task that has an outcome check (a test that passes, a count that matches).

Choose two settings to compare, for example the same model at medium and high. Change only one thing.
For each, start a fresh session, run the task three times, and record pass or fail from the outcome check.
After each run, open /usage (shows what the session cost) and note the “Usage by model” block. The dollar figure is an estimate computed locally at list price, and on a subscription you may see plan usage bars instead. /usage resets on /clear.
Compare cost per passing run. Three runs is a small sample: it can expose a big difference, and a small one needs more runs.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
7. Other model families
The ideas above carry over to other families; the names do not. Mistral is one example:

Models: Ministral 3 comes in 3B, 8B and 14B, and Mistral Small 4 is also open-weight; both are Apache 2.0. Check Mistral’s models page for current names and deprecation dates.
Harness: Mistral Vibe is an open-source terminal coding agent (Apache 2.0) with four modes that set how much it asks first. Its config file is ~/.vibe/config.toml.

ask: asks before any tool.
accept-edits: the default; applies file edits without asking, and still asks before shell commands.
smart-approve: see the Vibe docs for how it decides.
auto-approve: for trusted, sandboxed environments only.

Trusted folders: Vibe loads project config only from folders you have trusted. Start in ask until you trust the project.
Local models: Vibe works with any model served behind an OpenAI-compatible API, such as vLLM, llama.cpp, LM Studio or Ollama. Check the Vibe docs for the Ollama setup.

When you switch families, redo the worksheet below. A tier ladder built on one vendor’s models does not carry over name for name.

title: Pick Your Model
text:
Exercise: assign six jobs
No model needed. For each mock job, write down a model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus or Fable), an effort (low, medium, high) and whether you would use a subagent, then open the key.

Rename 200 sample IDs in a samplesheet to a new scheme, given a mapping table.
Summarise the methods section of one paper into five bullets for your lab notes.
Debug a Nextflow stage that fails on one sample and passes on the others.
Classify 5,000 free-text tissue labels into 12 categories, with 200 hand-tagged rows to check against.
Plan a refactor of a 600-line QC script that three other people depend on.
Explain an error message you have not seen before.



Answer key (several answers are defensible)


Probably no model at all. A mapping table and a script do this exactly, and a script cannot invent an ID. If you use a model, Haiku at low or medium, with a diff or count check; no subagent needed.
Sonnet, medium, no subagent. The text is short, so there is no context to protect. Check two claims against the paper yourself.
Sonnet at medium, raised to high or Opus if the first attempt fails and a test says so. Keep it in the main conversation, because the debugging needs the history. Add a failing test first (rung 1).
Haiku, a subagent or a batch script, medium. The 200 hand-tagged rows are your outcome check; re-run only the rows that disagree at a higher setting. Spot-check a sample of the rest.
Opus, high, in plan mode, main conversation. A weak plan is expensive downstream and other people depend on the script. Ask for a test plan too.
Sonnet, low or medium, no subagent. It is a short, checkable question: try the suggested fix. Escalate when the explanation does not hold up.



Check what model and effort your tool is using right now (/model, /effort) and write them down.


Run the same small task at two settings and compare the result and /usage.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text: A tower stands far above the Collegium, where the Claude Astral can work on a borrowed machine that vanishes when the job is done. It is a fine place to sketch and write, and the boasters make it sound fit for any task. Asked plainly, an academic lowers their voice: nothing precious should be carried to the tower. Learn what the tower is good for, and what you must leave at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
The rule for this page
You may be offered a way to run an agent on someone else’s computer. You need this lesson before you start one, because what you send is stored away from your machine. Decide what may go there first.






NoteCloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation. Data analysis stays on your machine or the cluster.



Use a cloud session for writing scripts, updating documentation and similar low-risk text work. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository. Analysis runs on your own machine or the cluster, under your data agreement.
Think of the cloud agent as a drafting helper that returns a branch (a named line of commits in git) which you review and then run yourself, where the data lives.


Cloud sessions are optional. If you use one, the rest of the page shows how to keep sensitive material at home.

title: Claude in the Cloud
Claude in the Cloud
text:
2. What leaves your machine
Read this part twice. When you start a cloud session:

Your repository contents are cloned onto Anthropic’s VM. Anthropic reads only the repository you start the session in.
Your prompts and everything the agent reads and writes go to the model.
The session transcript (the saved record of the whole conversation, including tool output) is stored by Anthropic so you can return to it later.
Retention (how long Anthropic keeps stored data) depends on your account type: from 30 days up to 5 years. Check your plan’s current terms on the Data usage page in Lore. Deleting a cloud session permanently removes its event data.
Network level None may still let data exit. A network access level is the setting that says which internet hosts the VM may reach (None, Limited or Full; see section 5). The Anthropic API stays reachable even at None, which may allow data to exit the VM.
Environment variables (named settings handed to programs, often used for keys) set in a cloud environment can be read by any command Claude runs, and anyone who uses that environment can read the values.

Some organisation settings block cloud sessions outright, and your administrator can switch them off. Ask whether yours are available.
Keep controlled data out of the cloud repository. Treat the clone, the transcript and anything you paste as held by Anthropic. Read your data agreement before you push anything to a remote that a cloud session can see (a remote is the copy of a repository hosted elsewhere, such as on GitHub).

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
3. Good uses and bad uses







Fine for a cloud session (code and mock data only)
Keep for your machine or the cluster




Write a samplesheet validator, tested on a three-row mock file
Run the analysis


Write a QC summary plotting script, developed on mock data
Load real counts, genotypes or results


Draft or update the README, changelog, docstrings
Debug with real sample IDs in the repository


Refactor non-data code that has tests
Anything under a data agreement


Review a pull request that holds no identifiers
Anything that needs a local database or the cluster


Triage issues that hold no identifiers
Anything that needs your institution’s network or files



A cloud machine has no GPU and no access to your institution’s network. Work that needs a GPU, a VPN (a private network link into your institution) or local databases stays on your side.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
4. How to start

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Push first. claude --cloud "your task" starts a cloud session from your terminal. It clones the GitHub remote at your current branch, and your local folder is not used. Commit and push (save snapshots, then upload them to the remote) before you start, so the session sees your latest work. If the branch is not on GitHub the CLI prints Branch <name> is not on GitHub, and the session starts from a pushed commit or the default branch. One repository per session. You can also start from claude.ai/code in the browser.
Write a ticket-style prompt. That is a self-contained note like a work ticket: the problem, the expected result, and a command that proves it (in the example, pytest, a Python test runner). Be specific, name files and paste errors. Example, with no data in it:

Problem: scripts/validate_samplesheet.py accepts duplicate sample IDs.
Expected: exit status 1 and a message naming the duplicated ID.
Check: pytest tests/test_validate_samplesheet.py (mock rows only).
Add a test for the duplicate case. Only change files under scripts/ and tests/.
A repository with no real data anywhere in it is the safe one. Removing the data/ and results/ folders is not enough if real files sit elsewhere. A prompt line such as “do not read data/” is a request to the model and gives no protection. If the folder is in the repository, the cloud session can read it.

If there is no remote. When the repository has no git remote, or a GitHub repository does not have the Claude GitHub App (an app you install on a repository to let Claude clone it) installed, Claude Code bundles it and uploads the full history of all branches plus uncommitted changes to tracked files. Keep data out of this route entirely. Your history may already hold a file you deleted, and the bundle takes all of it. Check what is tracked and what your .gitignore covers first.
Getting the session back. claude --teleport pulls a cloud session into your local terminal. It needs a clean git state, the same repository, the branch pushed and the same claude.ai account.
GitHub access. Cloud sessions reach your repositories through the Claude GitHub App or a token that /web-setup (a command you run in the terminal) sends to Anthropic; it sends your local gh (GitHub command-line tool) token. The proxy that holds your credential does not limit which branches a push can update. Use GitHub branch protection or rulesets (rules on which branches may be changed and by whom) for that.



To run an agent away from your laptop with OpenCode, run it yourself in your own container or virtual machine. That is your own infrastructure and your own responsibility.
A local Ollama model keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls the agent makes may leave it. If your data agreement rules out third-party processing, ask whether this local route is allowed.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
5. Environments
An environment is a saved configuration for cloud sessions: network access, environment variables, a setup script and network secrets. A first-time setup creates one called Default, with Limited access.
Network access levels:







Level
What the VM can reach




None
No internet (the Anthropic API, the GitHub proxy and enabled connectors still work)


Limited
A default allowlist (a list of the only hosts permitted) of package registries, GitHub and cloud SDKs, plus domains you add


Full
Any host



Pick the narrowest level that lets the task finish.

Setup scripts: a setup script is a Bash script that runs once before Claude starts, to install what the task needs. Installs need network access, so None blocks them.
Environment variables versus network secrets: environment variables are readable by any command Claude runs. Network secrets are the safer option where possible: the key stays outside the VM, and a proxy adds it to requests to hosts you list.
Preinstalled tools: common programming tools are present. No R, conda or bioinformatics tools are listed, so ask Claude to run check-tools (a shell command on the cloud machine that reports tool versions; you ask Claude to run it) to see what is there.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
6. Permission modes in the cloud
A permission mode says how much the agent may do before asking you. Cloud sessions offer Accept edits, Plan and Auto. There is no Manual or Bypass mode there. You pick the mode in the dropdown.
Use Plan for anything you do not already understand, and read the plan before it edits. You can also plan locally with claude --permission-mode plan, commit and push the plan, and then start claude --cloud.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
7. Limits and failure modes

A fresh machine every time. An idle session stops and its VM is taken back. Commit and push work you want to keep.
Size. A cloud machine has limited CPU, memory and disk. Heavy jobs may be stopped.
Shared usage. Cloud work counts against the same plan limits as all your other Claude Code use.
GitHub comments under your name. Claude can reply on pull requests under your GitHub name, marked as from Claude Code.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
8. Review what comes back
The result is a branch. Treat it like a stranger’s pull request: it may be fine and it may be wrong.

Read the diff (the list of changed lines) as you would any other.
Look for accidents in the diff: committed data files, absolute paths, sample IDs in a test or a comment, a .env, a notebook saved with outputs (a notebook is a Jupyter document mixing code and results; its saved outputs are the tables and plots stored inside the file).
Run the tests locally, on your machine.
Only then run the script on your data, locally or on the cluster, under your data agreement. The cloud agent never saw that data and never ran that step.

A green test in the cloud is a claim to verify. A test passing on mock data tells you the script runs; your real data is the next check, run locally.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Exercise: the safe-to-send checklist
No cloud account, GitHub account or model needed, and no repository to clone. The tree is a text file in this course’s exercises folder. Open tree.txt, a mock repository tree (every name is invented).

Mark each path that must not reach anything a cloud session can see. Say whether it needs removing from history (it is already committed) or only ignoring, and write one reason each.
Write the .gitignore lines that would have stopped it.
Draft a ticket-style prompt for one low-risk task: update docs/usage.md, or add a missing-column test to scripts/validate_samplesheet.py. Include the problem, the expected result and a check that uses only data/mock/.



Answer key (some entries depend on your data agreement)


Every path under “Paths to remove” is committed, so remove each one from history before you push anything a cloud session can see. The ignore lines further down only prevent a repeat.

Paths to remove:

.env: a secret. It was already committed, so remove it from history and replace the token; ignoring it helps only from now on.
samplesheet_real.csv: identifiers and genotype calls.
data/raw/ and data/processed/: real reads and real counts.
notebooks/01_qc.ipynb and notebooks/02_diffexp.ipynb: outputs saved inside them contain real sample IDs, tables and plots. Clear the outputs, or keep the notebooks out.
results/ (including de_genes.csv and pca_real_samples.png): results.
logs/slurm-482913.out: real sample IDs and cluster paths.
notebooks/.ipynb_checkpoints/: autosave copies of the notebooks, with the same saved outputs.
Fine to send (they hold no real data): README.md, environment.yml, samplesheet_template.csv, config/params.yaml (check it for real paths), data/mock/, docs/, scripts/, tests/.

Ignore lines that would help:
.env
.env.*
samplesheet_real.csv
*.fastq.gz
data/raw/
data/processed/
results/
logs/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
Add a rule for notebooks too (for example, a pre-commit hook, a script git runs automatically before each commit, that clears outputs), because .gitignore alone cannot strip outputs from a notebook you do want to commit. Likewise, .gitignore only stops files that are not yet tracked; anything already committed stays in history until you remove it properly, and rewriting history is its own careful job.
Sample prompt:
Problem: docs/usage.md does not mention the --strandedness option added in v0.3.
Expected: a short section with the option, its allowed values, and one example
command using data/mock/ only.
Check: the example command in the new section runs on data/mock/counts_mock.tsv. Only edit docs/usage.md.
A prompt line is a request to the model. The safe version of this repository has no real data folders to read.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
What to remember

Cloud sessions are for drafting scripts and documentation; analysis stays on your machine or the cluster. Real data, controlled data, sample sheets with identifiers, genotypes and results stay out of a cloud session and its repository.
Your repository contents, prompts and session transcript go to Anthropic, and network level None may still let data exit the VM.
Return is a branch: read the diff, look for stray data, run the tests locally, then run on your data where it lives, under your data agreement.

title: Claude in the Cloud
text:
Battle




Look up your data agreement and check whether it allows any third-party processing before you ever push to a cloud-connected remote.


Check whether your organisation’s plan allows cloud sessions at all.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
A watchman stands at the heavy door and checks every visitor against a list. The list is code, so no one can talk their way past, and your Astral tries every honeyed word it knows. Learn to write one line of that list.
Advice can be ignored, and a hook cannot. You need one when a rule must hold whatever the model decides. A hook is a user-defined handler that the harness (the program around the model that runs its tools) runs automatically at a set point, such as just before a tool runs. In Claude Code it can be a shell command, an HTTP endpoint and other kinds, and it receives JSON about the event. An instructions file asks the model to behave. A command hook is ordinary code that the harness runs, so what it decides does not depend on what the model wants.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
A hook that refuses

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Hooks go in a hooks block in a settings file. For this exercise use .claude/settings.local.json in your scratch folder (yours alone). .claude/settings.json is the committable, shared file, and ~/.claude/settings.json covers all projects.

Save the script below as .claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh in the project folder and make it executable.
Add the hooks block below to .claude/settings.local.json. $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR in it is the environment variable holding the project’s root folder.

A PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs, and the matcher (the pattern that selects which tool the hook fires for) Bash selects the shell tool:
{ "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash",
  "hooks": [ { "type": "command",
    "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh" } ] } ] } }
The script, from the Claude Code hooks guide. It needs jq (a command-line JSON reader) installed, and it must be executable (chmod +x .claude/hooks/block-drop-table.sh):
#!/bin/bash
INPUT=$(cat)
COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q "drop table"; then
  echo "Blocked: dropping tables is not allowed" >&2  # stderr becomes Claude's feedback
  exit 2                                               # exit 2 = block the action
fi
exit 0  # exit 0 = no decision; the normal permission flow applies
The hook gets the event as JSON on stdin (the input stream a program reads, here fed by Claude Code), including tool_name and, for Bash, tool_input.command. Exit code 2 on PreToolUse blocks the call, and Claude sees the stderr text (the program’s error output) as the reason. Exit 0 expresses no decision: the call goes through the normal permission flow.
Two behaviours matter for trust:

A broken guard fails open. If the script crashes or exits with some other code and prints no valid JSON, the action proceeds on most events. To block on failure, add "onFailure": "block" beside "type" and "command" in the hook’s handler (needs Claude Code v2.1.295 or later).
Exit 2 blocks on some events only. On PostToolUse the tool already ran and exit 2 shows stderr to Claude. On Notification the exit code is ignored.



OpenCode’s V2 docs describe plugins (files under .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/) that can register hooks. To refuse an action, use the permission hook, ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", ...): it runs for allow and ask decisions, may change the effect to allow, ask or deny, and event.message is the denial reason. An explicit configured deny is final and never invokes the hook.
Treat an OpenCode plugin as code running with your privileges. Before relying on it, check your installed version’s docs for shell-hook configuration and an exit-code equivalent, and test whether throwing from a tool hook blocks a call. Test the whole setup with your local Ollama model too.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
What a hook covers

A string match is easy to dodge. The example matches the literal string “drop table” in one command. A matcher selects by tool name only. If the model runs a script that contains the dangerous command, or spells it differently, a grep on the command text never sees it.
Hooks fire only on tool calls. PreToolUse fires when Claude calls a tool. A file added with an @ reference in your prompt is added to the conversation directly. A hook does not see it, and a Read deny rule may not stop it. Keep secrets out of the folder.
Hooks cannot override your deny and ask rules. A hook’s allow never overrides a deny or ask rule: those are still evaluated.
Hooks run with your full permissions. Command hooks “execute shell commands with your full user permissions”, so review and test them before adding them.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
text:
One checkpoint for high-stakes actions
If an agent can reach something with real-world consequences, such as ordering DNA synthesis or commanding physical equipment, put a screening checkpoint in the path that refuses dual-use requests (requests where the same capability can help or harm). Do not connect an agent to such a capability without one. Test the checkpoint with requests you know it should refuse. A hook is one possible checkpoint for local actions, with the limits listed above.

title: Block Actions with a Hook
section: A hook in a repository is code you did not write
text:
A hook in a repository is code you did not write
If a repository commits hooks in .claude/settings.json, they are code from its authors, running as you. Interactive Claude Code holds hooks back until you accept the workspace trust dialog.
In -p and SDK runs (headless: non-interactive, no one to answer a dialog) there is no dialog, and hooks committed in a repository’s .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted. Read .claude/ before running headless in a clone. --bare and disableAllHooks switch hooks off.

In a throwaway folder with mock files, add the Bash-blocking hook above and ask for a harmless command that contains “drop table” in an echo. Expect the agent to report that the command was blocked, with your stderr text as the reason. Then change the script to exit 1 and see what happens.

title: Write the Brief
text:
The first branch of the great tree is bare. You told your Astral “tidy this up” and came back to find it had cut down something you loved. The old foresters say every good cut starts with a few plain words about where, why and how you will know it worked. Learn to write them before you swing anything.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster’s brief names the deadline, the budget and the proof of done.


The Diviner’s brief names the controls and the reference to check against.


The Artificer’s brief names the test that must pass.


The Archivist’s brief names the fields that must never change.
The brief is what you tell the agent. A vague brief invites a plausible guess. A good brief names the file and the symptom (what you see going wrong), says what “done” looks like, and gives the agent a check it can run.
Two habits make the rest of this safer:

title: Write the Brief
text:
Put effort into the brief
A common habit is to open with “You are a world-class bioinformatician.” Expert personas help with tone, format, safety and preference tasks. They can hurt tasks that rely on what the model already knows, such as factual questions. A role line is not a substitute for a brief.
So:

Brief first: put your effort into the file, the symptom, what “done” looks like, and a check. Those are testable. A role line is not.
Role for style: use a role or tone line when you want a style, such as “explain this for a first-year student”.
Test a persona: if you use one on a factual task, compare the result against a version without one.

title: Write the Brief
section: The context window has a size limit
text:
The context window has a size limit
Everything in the conversation takes up room in the context window, and the room is limited. Old conversation can crowd out the files you need next.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


/context shows what is filling the window. /compact summarises the conversation (you can say what to keep). /clear starts fresh, which is right when you switch to an unrelated task. Claude Code also compacts automatically near the limit.


/compact (alias /summarize, meaning another name for the same command) summarises the session and /new (alias /clear) starts a new one. In the TUI (the text user interface, OpenCode’s terminal screen), run /help to see whether your version has a command that shows what fills the window.

title: Test the Skill
text:
The smith holds the skill up against an empty hand and asks the forest one question: does it do anything the bare hand cannot? Only if the two differ does the skill stay, however fine it looks on the wall. Each test costs something, so the smith counts the cost before the first swing.
You have a Skill and need to know that the agent actually uses it. A Skill that never fires does nothing, and an eval case is how you find out. Running an eval costs money. Every eval run and every judge-model grader is a real model call on your account. Reading this page and writing the files costs nothing. Running the eval is optional here and gives bonus XP only. Check what your institution allows before you spend.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Set up the plugin folder
claude plugin eval is the Claude Code command that runs eval cases against a plugin. It needs Claude Code v2.1.269 or later. It evaluates a plugin directory: a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json. To evaluate your own Skill, put it in a folder of this shape. The example exercises/forge/fasta-tools already has it. It is a folder in the course repository (clone or download the repository to get it):
fasta-tools/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md
└── evals/skill-triggers/
    ├── prompt.md
    └── graders/skill-fired.md

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The case is a prompt plus one or more graders. The prompt is written the way a user would ask, and leaves the Skill unnamed:
---
runs: 1
---
I just got a new FASTA file called reads.fa from a collaborator. Can you check it is OK before I start the analysis?
The grader is a free check on the transcript, with no model call. It passes if the Skill tool was invoked for check-fasta:
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?check-fasta"'
---
The check-fasta skill should be used when the user asks to check a new FASTA file, without naming the skill.
Run it cheaply while you iterate: one case, one run, and --ablation none, which skips the without-plugin run (an ablation removes a part to see what it adds):
claude plugin eval . --case skill-triggers --runs 1 --ablation none --max-cost-usd 1
The full comparison runs each case three times by default, with the plugin (WITH) and without it (W/OUT), and reports the difference (Δ). The cost ceiling is --max-cost-usd, in US dollars:
claude plugin eval . --max-cost-usd 2
The run stops at the ceiling. Results land in evals/results/<timestamp>/ with a report.html. When you are signed in with a claude.ai subscription, Claude Code also uploads the report as a private artifact and prints Published: <url>. The report holds your prompts and outputs, so add --no-publish for data that must stay local.


Run opencode --help and read the OpenCode docs for your version to see whether it has an eval command. You can do the same comparison by hand: run one prompt several times with the Skill folder present, several times with it moved away, and compare using a script that checks the output. A small local model is cheap to run this way, but it follows Skills less reliably, so expect noisier results.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Reading the result
Open report.html and look at three things:

Δ (two-arm runs only; with --ablation none there is no Δ, so check that the grader passed). If WITH and W/OUT are about the same and the Skill did not fire, the description does not trigger on that phrasing, so edit the description.
The failed grader. The report expands it with an explanation.
Isolation. Each run happens in a child session (a separate Claude Code session started just for that run) with only the plugin loaded, so your own settings and other plugins are absent.

Graders that suit a first case: one on the result and one on the process (such as tool_used). In a two-arm run, tool_used: Skill is shown only as an indicator (a pass or fail chip that does not count towards the score), because it can never pass without the plugin. Set arm: both on the grader to score it in both arms. claude plugin validate <folder> checks that the plugin’s files are well formed. Four grader types are free (regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists) and two call a judge model (llm, baseline).
Running an eval is the same trust decision as loading the plugin yourself (--plugin-dir loads a local plugin folder for one session): hooks you did not write still run code. Review the plugin for safety, since a passing eval does not cover that.

title: Test the Skill
text:
Who checks the work

Use a separate verifier, a check done by something other than the agent that did the work. An agent that marks its own work gives a self-check. For a QC skill that edits a samplesheet, have a script or a person diff the changed file against the original, and make the verifier cite the lines it relied on.
Check the Skill in each client you use (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode). Passing in one tool says little about another. After installing, confirm that the client triggers the Skill for the right task, loads its files, uses the tools it needs and returns the evidence you expect.
Instructions guide; tests and people verify. A line in a Skill saying “check your work” steers the agent. Tests, CI checks (continuous integration: automatic checks that run when code is pushed) and human review verify.


Run the cheap one-case command above on exercises/forge/fasta-tools with a cost ceiling, and open the report.html. Note whether the Skill fired.

title: Write a Skill
text:
In a hollow of the forest the smith keeps procedures in folders, tired of watching Astrals ask the same question twice. A long recipe hung on every branch would crowd the clearing, so the smith hangs only a label and fetches the rest on demand. Now the smith shows you how to forge one.
An instructions file is read every session. A Skill is a procedure loaded only when it is relevant, so it can be long without filling the context (the limited amount of text, counted in tokens, the chunks of text a model reads, that the agent holds at once). You need this now because a repeated chore belongs in a Skill, so you stop retyping it each session.

title: Write a Skill
text:
What a Skill is
A Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file, in an open format called Agent Skills, so other tools that follow the format can load the same folder. A Skill loads in three steps, which keeps the context window (the text the model can see at once) small:

At session start the agent sees only each Skill’s name and short description. The format’s specification puts this at about 100 tokens per Skill.
When a task matches, the agent reads the body of SKILL.md. The specification recommends keeping it under 5,000 tokens.
Bundled scripts and reference files are read only when the body points to them.

In Claude Code, both you (by name, such as /check-fasta) and the agent (by matching the description) can start one.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Place it at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (project) or ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (all projects). All frontmatter fields are optional, but write a clear description so it triggers at the right time. Keep the body under about 500 lines. The older .claude/commands/ format still works and is merged into Skills.


OpenCode reads skills from .opencode/skills, .claude/skills and .agents/skills, so the same SKILL.md can serve both tools. Custom agents live in .opencode/agents/*.md.



An example you can write by hand in a scratch folder:
---
name: check-fasta
description: Count the records in a FASTA file and find duplicate IDs. Use before running any analysis on a new FASTA.
---

1. Run `grep -c '>' FILE` to count records.
2. Run `grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d` to find duplicate IDs.
3. Report what you ran and its output. Leave FILE unchanged.

title: Write a Skill
section: Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
text:
Do it: install it, then confirm it loaded
Writing the file is half the job. A Skill whose frontmatter has broken YAML loads silently with no fields set, and a misspelt field name is ignored, so always check.

Make a scratch folder (never a real project) and move into it: mkdir skill-scratch && cd skill-scratch. Save the example above as .claude/skills/check-fasta/SKILL.md. The --- must be the very first line of the file.
In the same folder, make a tiny test file: printf '>a\nACGT\n>a\nGGCC\n' > reads.fa (two records, one duplicated ID).
Confirm the agent can see it:


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start claude in the scratch folder. Type / and look for check-fasta in the menu, or run /skills, which lists the skills the agent can see. If the Skill does not appear, run /reload-skills (it re-reads the skill folders) and look again. Then ask in plain words, leaving the Skill unnamed: “I just got reads.fa from a collaborator. Is it OK to analyse?” The agent should say it is using the check-fasta Skill, run the two grep commands, and report two records and the duplicated ID a.


Start opencode in the scratch folder. OpenCode finds .claude/skills too. The model loads a Skill through its skill tool, and you can load one yourself by writing @check-fasta in a prompt. Then ask the same question and check whether the Skill was used.




If it did not trigger, check in this order:

The file starts with --- on line 1.
The YAML (the key: value text format used in that block) parses.
Field names are spelled right.
The description says when to use it, with the key use case first (long descriptions are cut off in the listing).


A Skill that is listed but never picked up points to the description or the prompt.
Two slash commands help you look:

/skills lists the skills the agent can see, and t sorts them by token count.
/skill-doctor shows each skill’s context cost (how much of the context its text takes up) and how often it is used, and flags skills that sit in the listing but are never invoked. It excludes bundled and enterprise skills.

In Claude Code, allowed-tools in a Skill pre-approves tools for that turn (one prompt and its reply). It restricts nothing: other tools still ask as usual. A Skill offers no sandbox, and a Skill you download is code you choose to trust, so read it before installing it, as you would read a script.

title: Write a Skill
section: Design the Skill like a small job
text:
Design the Skill like a small job

One Skill, one job. Give it a defined input (what it is handed, such as a FASTA path) and a defined output (what it must return, such as a count and a list of duplicate IDs). If the description needs “and also”, split it into two Skills.
Say when to use it and what evidence to report (the commands run and their output), so a reviewer can see what happened.
Write only what the agent would get wrong without you. For each line, ask whether the agent would make a mistake if the line were missing. If not, cut the line. A short list of gotchas (for example “a FASTA header may contain spaces”) earns its place.
Start from a task you keep explaining, such as confirming a FASTQ file has no truncated records.
A Skill describes the method. The tool that runs it supplies the tools, credentials and permissions. “Submit this to the cluster” brings no cluster account with it.
Use an application when you need more. Work that needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail or permissions enforced from outside, such as a lab’s shared sample-tracking service, suits an application (a separate program with its own tests and access rules).

For portability: both Claude Code and OpenCode read .claude/skills, so one SKILL.md can serve both. The open format requires a name and a description, while Claude Code treats both as optional. Write both. Make the name match the folder name (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, up to 64 characters), and keep the description under 1,024 characters. After installing, verify in each client (the tool that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or OpenCode) you use:

Does it trigger on the right request?
Does it load the files the Skill refers to?
Does it use the tools it needs?
Does it return the evidence you asked for?

Clients differ in models, tools and permissions, so a Skill that works in one can fail in another.

Write a SKILL.md for one chore you repeat (checking an input, summarising a log). Make the description say when to use it.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
At the forest’s edge a satchel waits to be packed with the smith’s finest skills and their tests. Whatever you carry, others will unpack, and whatever you unpack from another traveller’s satchel runs with your own authority. A pack that looked fine on the table once split open on a stranger’s back. Pack with care, and open with more.
A single Skill in your folder helps you. You need a plugin when a group should install the same set and get updates. A plugin is a folder that bundles Skills and, optionally, agents (helper assistants with their own instructions), hooks (scripts the harness runs at set points) and MCP servers.

title: Bundle a Plugin
section: Installing one is a trust decision
text:
Installing one is a trust decision
A plugin you install can run arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges. Hooks, monitors (background watchers that feed output to the agent), and local MCP and language servers (programs that give editor-style code checks) run outside the sandbox and the permission rules. A plugin’s bin/ folder holds executables that go on Claude’s shell PATH (the list of places commands are found), so Claude can run them, and each call follows your permission rules. Skills and agents enter the context as instructions, and instructions can steer the agent too.
Before installing or updating a plugin:

Check where it comes from. A marketplace name says who publishes it. Reading the plugin shows what it does.
Read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and anything in bin/. These are where code lives.
In a session, /plugin shows what will be installed. claude --plugin-dir <dir> plugin details <name> prints a list of the plugin’s components without starting a session.
Remember that auto-update can change files you reviewed, so re-read a plugin after each update. Pin a version for plugins you publish.

title: Bundle a Plugin
text:
When a team shares Skills

Keep project names and conventions in one file. Put the reference genome build, the sample-ID pattern and the results folder names in a project-facts file (a plain file that lists them) that every Skill reads. Another lab can then reuse your Skills with its own file.
Keep discovered details apart from team standards. A pattern the agent finds in your code is an observation. A person confirms it before it becomes a standard.
Check generated copies. If you generate copies of a SKILL.md, run a check in CI (automated checks that run on every change) that fails when a copy differs from its source.
Merge blocking is a repository setting. Whether a bad change is stopped depends on repository rules and required checks. A review step written in a Skill is advice unless a required check backs it.


Turn the Skill you wrote into a plugin folder with a plugin.json, then run claude plugin validate on it and read the output.

When you review a rule, ask where each input comes from, where each output goes, and what would change if you re-ran it.
