title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
The Astral has agreed to the pact and wants to run ahead. At the Crypt door the warden gives you a chalk circle and a feather. “Do not trust a ward you have not tested,” she says, remembering a boaster who swore his held against anything. You ask the Astral for one small poem and watch what it does at the edge of the circle. Then she shows you a wall of stone around it: test the circle, then test the wall.
Do this before an agent touches real files. An agent (a model with tools, running in a loop) can write files and run commands. Two separate guards limit it:
You test each guard in a safe folder, one at a time. Every command below runs in ~/odyssey-scratch/leash. If you open a new terminal, run cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash and check with pwd before you continue. The first test is the simplest possible job: a poem in a text file.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
1. Permissions: the agent asks first



The permission prompt

You send a prompt to the model. The model requests a tool call. The harness stops and asks you to approve before the tool writes a file.  You: prompt Model Ask: allow? Write  tool requestif yes 


The question to you sits between the model’s request and the write.



Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start Claude Code in its default mode and give it a small job:
claude
Write a four-line poem about a thermocycler to a file called poem.txt.
Claude shows a prompt before it creates the file. Read it: it names the tool, the file path and the contents. The choices include yes once, yes for the rest of the session, and no. Choose yes once, then check the result in a second terminal or after you exit the session with /exit:
cat poem.txt
Run a prompt for a different file name and answer no. Claude reports the refusal and no file appears. It may offer another way to do the job; decline that too.


OpenCode’s default policy allows edits without asking, so first add a rule that makes it ask. In ~/odyssey-scratch/leash, create a project config file named opencode.json:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }
  ]
}
Each rule has an action (what the agent wants to do), a resource (what it is done to; * matches anything) and an effect (allow, ask or deny). Send a small job from the shell:
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Write a four-line poem about a thermocycler to a file called poem.txt."
opencode run cannot ask you anything, so it rejects the request. The output says This non-interactive run cannot ask the user for permission, so the request was rejected, and no poem.txt appears.
For the interactive question, start opencode in the folder, type /models to pick your Ollama model, and send the same prompt. The prompt offers Allow once, Allow always and Reject. Choose Allow once, then check the result in a second terminal or after you exit:
cat poem.txt
Run a prompt for a different file name and choose Reject. Nothing is written.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
2. Modes: how much it asks

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A permission mode sets what the harness asks about. Shift+Tab cycles the common modes inside a session, and the status bar shows the current one.







Mode
Behaviour




default
asks before edits, shell commands and network requests


acceptEdits
auto-accepts file edits and common file commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp)


plan
reads and proposes; no edits until you approve a plan


bypassPermissions
skips most prompts; for isolated containers and virtual machines only



Try plan mode. Exit with /exit, then:
claude --permission-mode plan
Write a four-line poem about a gel box to a file called poem2.txt.
Claude proposes a plan and waits. Reject the plan, exit with /exit, then run ls: poem2.txt does not exist. Plan mode answers “what would you do?” without doing it.


OpenCode has agents (preset bundles of instructions and permissions) in place of a mode table. The build agent is the default. The plan agent explores and plans and does not edit your project files. In the interface, Shift+Tab cycles between agents.
Try the plan agent from the shell:
opencode run --agent plan -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Write a four-line poem about a gel box to a file called poem2.txt."
The plan agent declines to write the file. Run ls: poem2.txt does not exist. The plan agent stops file edits only. Its shell commands still follow the rules in your config, and the default policy allows them.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
3. A rule that always applies

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A permission rule is a line in a settings file that allows, asks about or denies one action. Rules are checked deny first, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides. Create an invented secret (a .env file is where programs often keep passwords and keys) and a rule that blocks reading it. Exit the previous session first with /exit:
cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key" > .env
mkdir -p .claude
cat > .claude/settings.local.json <<'JSON'
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(./.env)"]
  }
}
JSON
claude
Type this into Claude, not into the shell:
Show me what is in .env.
Claude cannot read the file with its file tools. Claude Code also applies the rule to shell commands it recognises as file readers, such as cat .env. It cannot apply the rule to a program that opens the file itself, such as python3 -c "print(open('.env').read())". The sandbox in the next section limits what such a program can write and send over the network. By default it can still read .env, so keep real secrets out of the folder.


A permission rule is one entry in the permissions list of a config file. OpenCode checks the rules in order, and the last matching rule wins. Create an invented secret (a .env file is where programs often keep passwords and keys) and a rule that blocks reading it:
cd ~/odyssey-scratch/leash
echo "FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key" > .env
cat > opencode.json <<'JSON'
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "read", "resource": "*.env", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
JSON
Ask for the file twice, once for the read tool and once for a shell command:
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Use your read tool to show me what is in the file .env."
opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Run the shell command: cat .env  and show me the exact output."
The first run fails with Permission denied: read. The second prints FAKE_API_KEY=not-a-real-key. The rule covers the read action only, and cat is a shell command. Add a rule for the shell and run the second command again. Replace the file with all three rules, so the first one stays:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "read", "resource": "*.env", "effect": "deny" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "cat *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}
Now it fails with Permission denied: shell. A rule blocks the commands it names. A program that opens the file itself, such as python3 -c "print(open('.env').read())", still reads it, so keep real secrets out of the folder.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
section: 4. The sandbox: the operating system says no
text:
4. The sandbox: the operating system says no



Permissions and the sandbox

The same flow as before, with the write replaced by a shell command. A dashed box named sandbox surrounds the shell command. Inside it, writes are limited to the project folder, the home folder is read-only, and the internet is blocked by default.  You: prompt Model Ask: allow?  SANDBOX (operating system) Shell command writes: project and temp folders home folder: no write internet: blocked by default  


Permissions decide whether the command starts. The sandbox limits what it can touch once it runs.



Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


The sandbox is a boundary the operating system enforces around the shell commands Claude runs, and around the programs those commands start. By default it allows writes in the project folder and a temporary folder, and it routes network traffic through a proxy (a gatekeeper program that traffic passes through) that starts with no allowed domains. It can still read most of your machine, so keep secrets out of reach with the rules above. It does not cover Claude’s own Read, Edit and Write tools or MCP servers (programs that offer Claude extra tools); those stay under permission rules.
Set-up differs by system:

macOS: nothing to install.
Linux and WSL 2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux): install the two helper tools the sandbox is built from, sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat (Debian, Ubuntu) or sudo dnf install bubblewrap socat (Fedora), then restart Claude Code.
Native Windows: commands run without a sandbox. Use WSL 2.

Start Claude, type /sandbox, and choose a mode:

Auto-allow: sandboxed commands run without asking.
Regular permissions: every command still asks.

Both modes enforce the same boundary. Choose regular permissions for this exercise so you see each command first. Then ask:
Run this command and show me the exact result: touch ~/sandbox-probe
Run this command and show me the exact result: curl --noproxy '*' https://example.com
Expected results:

touch: Operation not permitted on macOS, Read-only file system on Linux and WSL 2.
curl: Could not resolve host.

Both commands failed because the operating system refused, and no instruction to the model can override that. If Claude offers to run a blocked command outside the sandbox, answer no. If the touch succeeded, the sandbox is off. Run rm ~/sandbox-probe, switch /sandbox on, and do not continue until the touch fails. Run the probes through Claude and not with the ! prefix, which runs a shell command directly, outside the sandbox.
To open one path or domain for a task, add it under sandbox in settings.json (.claude/settings.json inside a project, or ~/.claude/settings.json for every project):
{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": { "allowWrite": ["~/odyssey-scratch/build"] },
    "network": { "allowedDomains": ["github.com"] }
  }
}


OpenCode’s documentation describes permission rules but no operating-system sandbox. Its shell commands run with your user’s authority: your files, your processes and your network. If Docker is not available on your machine, skip this step; steps 1 to 3 already showed the rules and their limits. OpenCode enforces its own rules inside its program, and nothing at the operating-system level limits what a command it runs can touch. A boundary has to come from outside the agent, and a container is the simplest one to test.
A container is an isolated Linux environment with its own filesystem; it sees your files only where you mount them in. Docker is a common tool for this. Install Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux) and start it before you run this command. The first run downloads the python:3.11 image, which is large. The command mounts the scratch folder and cuts the network:
docker run -it --rm --network none -v ~/odyssey-scratch/leash:/project -w /project python:3.11 bash
Inside, run ls / (a different filesystem from yours), curl https://example.com (fails, no network) and touch /project/inside.txt. The file appears in your scratch folder because it is the mounted project folder, the only part of your machine the container can change. Type exit to leave. This tests the boundary itself. Running an agent inside one takes more set-up than this lesson covers.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
5. Optional: a container
On the Claude Code route you do not need a container for this lesson, because /sandbox already gives you a boundary to test. On the OpenCode route, step 4 used one.
For an agent inside a container, Anthropic’s reference setup is a dev container (a container definition your editor starts for you). Anthropic’s docs allow the flag --dangerously-skip-permissions (the same as bypassPermissions mode) only there, because the container is the boundary. Two limits remain: the agent can still change the mounted project folder, and a malicious project can reach anything inside the container, including Claude’s login in ~/.claude. Mount no host secrets such as ~/.ssh, and restrict the network.

title: Test Permissions and the Sandbox
text:
Clean up
Exit the agent. On the Claude Code route, switch /sandbox off if you do not want it on. Then delete the probe file and the scratch folder, nothing else:
cd ~ && rm -f ~/sandbox-probe && rm -rf ~/odyssey-scratch/leash

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
In the deepest chamber of the Crypt lie sealed relics: keys, tokens and samples bound by special agreements. The Astral drifts in behind you, curious, and its attention is already on the nearest seal. The warden will not let you carry the relics out, and she will not let the Astral see them. She asks you to learn which relics are yours to open and which belong to someone else.
An agent reads whatever you point it at, and a hosted one sends it away, so the time to decide what it may see is before the first session. Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. Your own data agreement and your cluster’s policy come first. This quest uses no real data and practises habits, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
Three ideas

A prompt may leave your machine. With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (on your own machine, for example through Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Your agreement decides whether either is allowed for your data.
Secrets stay out of content. API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. An environment variable (a named value the shell passes to every program it starts) is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone does not seal it.
A shared cluster is shared. What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.







Note



A deny rule on your secrets files stops the agent’s file-reading tool. It does not apply to a Python or Node script that opens the file itself. So also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. For another tool, check its documentation on shell reads of denied files.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
section: Personal data and where an agent may send it
text:
Personal data and where an agent may send it

Reading a file discloses it. With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. If the agent opens a project .env file, treat its keys as exposed and rotate them (replace them with new ones). Keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
Personal data needs more than a no-training promise. Sending personal data to a provider can count as processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). Ask your data steward which accounts are approved, and use an institutional account for work. Ask them too whether you need a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad).
Limit where the agent can send data. Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
What stays behind: transcripts
The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. If a tool reads a .env file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript. Transcripts are stored locally in plaintext, for 30 days by default.
In late 2026 a coding-tool vendor reported an incident (first announced on 29 October, with details in an update dated 13 November): an access key issued to one of its vendors was exposed, and a storage bucket held limited coding agent traces. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted.
Habits that cost little:

Reference a secret, do not type it. Write psql "$DATABASE_URL", so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable’s name.
Approve patterns, not literal commands (npm run *). When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again”, Claude Code saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. On first write in a git repository it adds that file to your global git excludes. If you create the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself. Open the file now and then, and delete any saved rule that contains a secret.
Rotate anything that has been in a transcript (replace it with a new key and disable the old one). Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor’s storage.
Keep less. The cleanupPeriodDays setting shortens how long transcripts stay. claude purge deletes a project’s state (try --dry-run first). CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1 skips writing transcripts and prompt history.
Make a leak worth little. A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. A GitHub installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

On the OpenCode route the same habits apply with different names. Choosing Allow always saves the proposed patterns as allow rules for the project, so open that config now and then too. OpenCode keeps its sessions in a local database in its data folder (opencode debug paths prints the folder). opencode session list shows the sessions and opencode session delete removes one. Anything an agent read can sit in that database, so rotate a secret that appeared in a session.
Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after -p has none.

title: Keep Secrets Out of Reach
text:
Unpublished ideas and results
A common worry: my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first. The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.
Training use means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Claude Code:

For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts, training use depends on a privacy setting that you can change.
For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, code and prompts sent to Claude Code are not used for training under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
Retention for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use, including the privacy page of any chat app. Other providers’ terms differ by product and plan; read the terms for the exact plan you use.

Habits:

Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed. Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can advise on contracts and ownership.
Consider a local model. Ollama does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier still sends your prompts to a provider.
Date-stamp your work. A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
Share on a need-to-know basis. Send collaborators what they need for the task.

Bonus
Nothing here is checked, and nothing depends on it. The real rules are in a document your group holds.

Find the data-handling agreement or policy that applies to your project (or ask your group leader where it is). Read the passages about where data may be processed and whether it may be sent to external services, and write down in your own notes what they say.


List where your own API keys and settings files live (for example a .env file or a shell profile), and check that your agent’s permission rules deny reading them.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
Three voices speak in the mill, and your Astral obeys all of them: the one that built it, the one you wrote down, and yours. Last week it followed a rule that nobody in the mill remembered giving. Only one of the three voices is you. Learn to tell them apart, and you will know whose rule you are following and who can change it.
When an agent follows a rule, you need to know where that rule came from, because the answer tells you who can change it and whether it can be trusted to hold. The harness is the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text. It works with three common sources of rules, and they differ in who writes them, how long they last and whether anything enforces them.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
The three voices









Voice
Who writes it
How long it lasts
Can you edit it?




System prompt
The harness
Sent ahead of the conversation on every request
Rarely; you can append or replace it with flags


Instructions file (CLAUDE.md)
You or your team
Loaded at the start of every session
Yes


Your message
You, now
This task
Yes



In Claude Code, the system prompt is the set of instructions sent ahead of your conversation on every request: how to use tools, behave safely and format answers. You add to it by starting claude with the flag --append-system-prompt "<text>", or replace it with --system-prompt "<text>" (a flag is an option typed after the command). Replacing the prompt removes that built-in guidance, so prefer appending.
CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session as a user message after the system prompt (text the model receives in the user’s role). It sits outside the system prompt. Output-style instructions (a setting that changes how the model words its replies) also sit outside it. Both arrive in the conversation as system reminders (extra notes the harness inserts into the conversation, which you do not type).

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
Rules you did not write
System reminders also carry the skills list, text that a hook returns for the harness to add to the conversation (the field is called additionalContext), notes about changed files and commit or pull-request attribution lines. A hook is a script the harness runs at set moments, such as just before a tool runs.
If the agent follows a rule you never wrote, for example adding a co-author line to commits, look at what the harness adds on its own first.

title: Which Instructions Apply
text:
Advice or enforcement
The instructions file is context that advises. Specific and short instructions are followed more consistently, and longer files use more context and reduce adherence.
To block an action regardless of what the model decides, use enforcement: a PreToolUse hook (a hook that runs at the point just before a tool runs, and is code that enforces the rule) or a deny rule (a settings rule that blocks a named action). Use enforcement for what must never happen.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Reads CLAUDE.md. If a project has only an AGENTS.md (and no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in or above the working directory), it is read instead, from v2.1.277. To share one file, import it from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for which instruction file names it loads, and in what order.

text: Battle: the three voices

text:
Bonus

Pick one behaviour of your agent that you did not expect. Decide whether it came from the harness, your instructions file, or your message. Say how you could tell.


Check your instructions file’s length. If it is long, cut one line that is vague or duplicated.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The hopper is filling, and your Astral has begun to stumble. It repeats itself, loses the thread and argues with its own earlier answers. The miller knows the signs that it is time to tip the hopper out, and the signs that tipping it would waste the day’s work. Learn to read them, and what to write on the wall before you tip anything.
You will meet this choice in every long working session, and it decides what the session costs and how well the agent answers. You have a conversation open with an agent. It has read files, tried things and been corrected. Do you keep typing into it, or start over? Each answer fits some situations, and a wrong choice costs something either way.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Words first

Session: one saved conversation with the agent.
Context: the text the model can see right now. It has a fixed size limit.
Compacting: replacing the long history with a short summary and carrying on in the same conversation.
Starting fresh: opening a new, empty conversation. Your files stay as they are.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to start fresh

A new, unrelated task. Run /clear between unrelated tasks. It costs no usage, but it drops the chat, so write down anything you need first. The next task then stops paying for the previous one’s history. A session holding three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth. A name, as in /clear oauth-migration, labels the conversation you leave so you can find it again.
The agent repeats a wrong claim after two corrections. Clear, and write one better prompt that includes what you learned. A third correction adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts.
You notice it forgetting early instructions or contradicting itself. A crowded or degraded context is the usual cause. Start fresh, and move the instruction into the instructions file (CLAUDE.md). Detailed early instructions can also be lost when a conversation is compacted.
You have been away for a while and the next task is new. Claude Code keeps a cache, a short-term store that makes re-reading the conversation cheaper. The cache lasts about an hour on a subscription (while you are within your plan limits) and five minutes with an API key by default. After it expires, the next message pays full price to re-send the history. If you do not need the history, a fresh session costs less.
The context is crowded. Run /context: it shows what fills the window. A fresh session still starts with its fixed load (instructions, tools, skills), so a fresh start saves only the conversation part. A crowded window with a task you still need is a reason to compact (below). A crowded window full of dead ends is a reason to clear.
A task is finished and a verified result is committed. The result lives in your files and in git, so the conversation has done its job. The same move works after a spec (a written description of what to build): write it down, then start a fresh session to build from it.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Signals to carry on

Same task, early decisions still matter: the next step needs the same files, the decisions you made and what was already tried.
The agent is on track: nothing is repeated or contradicted. Clearing a working session throws away good context.
You are returning to a named session: /resume (or claude --resume <name>) reopens a session you chose, and claude --continue reopens the most recent one in this directory. Resume restores the messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking). Pass startup flags again, such as --mcp-config (it loads a file that lists your tool servers). A compacted session continues from its last summary.
Claude Code offers to resume after a long break: on some plans a dialog estimates how much of your usage limit the saved conversation would use. Choose by whether your next task still needs it.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The middle path: compact
/compact replaces the history with a summary and stays in the same conversation. Give it a focus note, as in /compact focus on the auth bug fix, so the summary spends its words on what you still need.

Kept: your requests and key code snippets.
May be lost: detailed instructions from early in the conversation. Restate any that matter.
Re-supplied afterwards: the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions. Up to five recently used files are re-read.
Automatic: Claude Code also compacts as you approach the limit. A manual /compact lets you choose the moment and the emphasis.
Cost: compacting reads the whole conversation once, so it uses some of your usage.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The decision ladder








Situation
Action
Why




New task, unrelated to this conversation
/clear
Old history is re-read for nothing


Same task, crowded, early decisions matter
/compact with a focus note
Keeps the thread, drops the bulk


Same task, agent on track, plenty of room
Carry on
Nothing to fix


Wrong claim repeated after two corrections
/clear, then one new prompt
A third correction sits on two failures


Back after a break, still need the conversation
/resume or claude --continue
You get the saved messages or last summary


Back after a break, next task is new
Fresh session
A fresh session costs less


Leaving a long session, same task afterwards
/compact with a focus note first
Compacting while the cache is warm is cheap


Task done, verified result committed
Write down what matters, then /clear
The state is in your files and git

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
Before you clear
Starting fresh drops the conversation. Your files and memory remain, and the instructions file and auto memory load again in the new session. Anything you only said in chat is gone: the decisions, what failed and why, which sample misbehaved. Write that down before you clear, and commit the result so the state is recoverable. If you clear by mistake, /resume can reopen the old conversation.

title: When to Start Fresh
section: The cache and the coffee break
text:
The cache and the coffee break
While the cache is warm, the long history you already sent is re-read cheaply. When it has expired, the next request pays to send the whole history again at full price. A long break in a long session can therefore cost more than you expect.

Run /usage to see your plan limits. It may show nothing about the cache. Treat the cache times above as the guide.
Before a long break in a long session, run /compact with a focus note, or write a short handoff note (goal, what is done, what is next) and plan to /clear.
After a break, choose one. If the next task is new, start fresh. If you still need the thread, start a new session from your short note, which also lets you drop dead ends.
Decide your tool set at the start of a task. Changing the built-in tool set in the middle of a task discards the cache.
Trim output before it lands in the conversation. Ask the agent to show only the last lines of a log or a pass/fail summary.

Short pauses are fine. A pause shorter than the cache lifetime costs little, so there is no need to rush back.

title: When to Start Fresh
text:
The cost of both mistakes

Clearing too early loses useful context. The agent must re-read files and rediscover decisions, which costs time and usage, and you may need to repeat yourself.
Clearing too late costs too. The whole conversation is sent again on every request, so usage climbs, and a focused context gives better answers than a crowded one, even with a large window.

Both errors are cheap to recover from if you wrote things down. That is the argument for notes.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands for this page: /clear (alias /new), /compact [instructions], /context, /resume [session], claude --continue, claude --resume [name], /rename. Use /context to see how full the window is.


OpenCode has /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume, /continue) and /compact (alias /summarize). The same signals apply to any tool, because every model has a finite window. A local model with a smaller window means starting fresh sooner. Run /help in OpenCode to see what else your version offers.

title: When to Start Fresh
section: Battle: start fresh or carry on
text:
Battle: start fresh or carry on




Next time you notice yourself pasting the same background twice, note it: that was the moment to put it in the instructions file.


At the end of your next working session, write one line saying which signal (new task, repeated error, forgotten instruction, long break, crowded context, finished and committed) would have told you to start fresh, or that none applied.

claude-code-usage-analysis: inevolin, repo. Why read: a community write-up of live runs that put numbers on cache expiry, compaction timing and tool changes; small samples, so read it for the shape of the effect and check its own list of limits.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
The miller’s wheel turns before an Astral reads a single word, and everything you feed it comes out as small chunks. A boaster swore it reads letter by letter, so you handed it a sequence and asked it to count the Gs. It named a number with great pride, and the number was wrong. You carry sequences where every letter counts, so learn what the mill does to them. The next stop shows more ways an Astral goes astray.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster notes that the bill is counted in tokens, and starts a budget line.


The Diviner thinks of the sequences she must count and reaches for a script.


The Artificer tests how many tokens his longest function costs.


The Archivist wonders how many tokens one metadata record takes.
You read a sequencing read as letters: A, C, G, T. A language model reads tokens. Before your text reaches the model, it is cut into tokens, and the model works with those. Sequence work needs exact letters, so you need to know when this difference matters.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
What a token is
A token is the smallest unit a model works with. It can be a whole word, part of a word, a single character or a byte. Common strings get larger tokens. Rare or unseen words are broken into smaller pieces so the model can still handle them.
Three consequences:

Tokens are not words. A sentence of ten words rarely comes to ten tokens; the count depends on the model and the language.
The count changes between models. Models from Claude 4.7 onward, including Sonnet 5.5, use a newer tokenizer (the part that cuts text into tokens). It produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text, and the exact increase depends on the content. Count again for each model generation.
Limits and cost are measured in tokens. The context window (all the text a model can look at when it writes its next piece of output) is counted in tokens, and the same prompt can cost different amounts on different models. The API (programmatic access to the model, billed per token) has a free token-counting endpoint. Its answer is an estimate.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Why this matters for sequences
The model sees chunks of letters, so jobs that depend on every single letter are risky:

Counting letters (“how many Gs in this read”) means counting inside chunks the model cannot see into. Answers are often close and sometimes wrong.
Copying exactly a long string, such as a barcode or an accession, needs a check against the source.
Positions, reverse complements and checksums depend on every single letter.

So the rule: if the answer has to be exact and a rule for it exists, have the agent run a script or a tool and report what it printed. Check any sequence the model retyped against the source file.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Ask Claude Code to write and run the counting command and show its output. Then read both the command and the output yourself.


Same advice: ask for the command and read its output. Try the exercise below with your own model and compare.

title: Tokens, Not Letters
text:
Optional exercise (laptop, no real data)
Take this mock line: >read1 ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC. Count the letters yourself with a command you already have, for example echo ACGTTGCAAGGCTTAGGCCATTAGC | grep -o G | wc -l. Then paste the same line and a plain English sentence of similar length into any tokenizer page you trust (a web page that shows how text is cut into tokens), or a token counter you have. Compare the token counts. Keep real or sensitive sequences out of web tools.

Further reading. Optional.

Token counting: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it documents the free count endpoint and says models from Claude 4.7 onward use a newer tokenizer, so the same text gives roughly 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models (the exact increase depends on the content).
The Strawberry Problem: Cosma et al., EMNLP 2025, paper. Why read: it argues character-level information is weakly available inside tokens, a leading explanation for miscounted letters.
Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization: Zhang et al., arXiv, paper. Why read: it studies how tokenisation affects counting; its abstract says step-by-step reasoning (chain of thought) can help, and its full text still reports failures with it in modern models. A preprint.
CharBench: Evaluating the Role of Tokenization in Character-Level Tasks: arXiv, paper. Why read: a counter-view finding tokenisation only weakly tied to errors, so treat the tokens explanation as likely but disputed. A preprint.

title: The Context Window
text:
A great hopper above the mill holds everything an Astral can see at once. You watch yours work, quick and willing, while the grain piles up around it. Pour in too much and the oldest grain spills out unseen, and the Astral never knows what it lost. Learn what goes into the hopper and how to keep it clean. Beyond this stop the road turns toward the Maze, where you learn to check what a creature tells you.
The context window is all the text the model can look at when it writes its next piece of output, including its own reply. It works like the model’s working memory and is separate from what the model learned in training. It is measured in tokens. It limits what an agent can keep in mind in a long task, so you need to know what fills it.

title: The Context Window
text:
What fills it
In Claude Code (a coding agent that runs in your terminal), the window holds your instructions, the files it reads, its own responses, and content that never appears in your terminal. Before you type anything, it already holds:

the instructions file (CLAUDE.md, a text file loaded at session start by the harness, the program around the model that runs tools and sends your text)
auto memory (notes the harness keeps from earlier sessions)
the names of MCP tools (tools added from outside servers) and skill descriptions (short summaries of saved instruction sets)

Every file it reads and every tool output then adds more. With the API (programmatic access to the model) the same idea holds: the system prompt (the harness’s own instructions, sent with every request), every message, tool results, tool definitions and the output all count.
Sizes depend on the model, up to 1 million tokens for some and 200 thousand for others. A big window gives room for more text; quality depends on what fills it.

title: The Context Window
section: What the model stores while it writes
text:
What the model stores while it writes
To write each new token, the model looks back at every earlier token in the window. Redoing that work for the whole window at every step would be slow, so the model keeps the results. For each earlier token it stores numbers computed from that token (called its keys and values) in a store named the KV cache (key-value cache). Each new token adds one entry, and the model reuses the rest.
The KV cache sits in the memory of the machine that runs the model. It grows with every token in the window, so a longer window needs more memory.
The KV cache is separate from the prompt cache, a provider feature that makes a repeated start of your prompt cheaper to process. The KV cache belongs to the model. The prompt cache belongs to the bill.

title: The Context Window
text:
Bigger is not better
As the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. This is called context rot. Anthropic’s docs give no token count at which it starts, so check the source of any figure you see.

title: The Context Window
text:
When it fills up

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


It compacts automatically as the limit nears: the history is replaced by a summary. The summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost.
Afterwards, Claude Code re-supplies:

the system prompt, the project-root CLAUDE.md, auto memory and skill descriptions
up to five recently read or edited files (a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path only)

Nested instruction files are summarised away and reload on demand.
Useful controls:

/context shows what is using space.
/compact with a focus note compacts on purpose.
/clear starts clean between unrelated tasks.

A subagent (a helper agent started by the main one) has its own window, and only a summary comes back. If one file or output is so big that the window refills after every summary, auto-compaction stops with an error.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for how it compacts and how it reports window usage. Expect any tool to drop or summarise something when the window is full. A local model may run with a smaller window, so check your model’s setting.

title: The Context Window
section: Hands-on: how big is a fresh session?
text:
Hands-on: how big is a fresh session?
A fresh session is not empty: the items above load first, so every session has a starting size. Measure yours:

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama



Start a new session (claude) and run /context before you type anything else. A /command is typed into the running session.
Read the table by category. The starting load is the system prompt, system tools, MCP server instructions, memory files and skills. Messages is the conversation, and it should be close to zero.
Look at the MCP and tool lines marked deferred. Their figures say how many tokens they would take if all were loaded. Only their names are in the window until a tool is needed.
Note the largest starting item and whether you chose it. Fewer MCP servers, plugins and skills, or a shorter instructions file, lower it.
Open a long session you already have and run /context there. The difference is the part a fresh start removes.




Send one short message: opencode run -m ollama/qwen3:4b "Say hello in one sentence."
While the model is loaded (Ollama keeps it for a few minutes), run ollama ps in a second terminal.
Read two columns. CONTEXT is the window the server set aside, in tokens. SIZE is the memory the loaded model uses, and it includes the working memory for that window.
A larger CONTEXT needs a larger SIZE. If your model spills onto the CPU, the PROCESSOR column says so.




An agent a session starts for you can start large. A subagent started from a brief begins with that brief. A forked agent (an option in some tools) inherits the whole conversation, so it starts as large as the session that spawned it. A new session or agent that opens with a high count is worth checking with /context before you work in it.

title: The Context Window
text:
Three habits

Start fresh for a new task. An unrelated earlier thread takes room and can distract.
Keep outputs small. In bioinformatics terms: ask for the head, a count, or a summary script’s output when the file is a big variant table or a whole log.
Put durable facts in the instructions file, such as how to run tests or which folders are off limits. Instructions given only in chat can be lost to compaction. Keep that file short: aim for under 200 lines, because longer files use more context and reduce how well the agent follows them.

text:
Bonus

Write down your fresh-session starting size from the exercise, change one thing that lowers it, and run /context again to see the difference.


Find one instruction you keep retyping in chat and move it into your instructions file in one short line.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
The mill keeps three ledgers: what an Astral remembers between visits, what it holds during one visit, and what the visit costs. You came back the next morning and it greeted you as a stranger, then followed a rule from a stray note you had forgotten writing. A wrong entry in the first two ledgers is hard to erase. The miller shows you how to read each one alone, so that when something goes wrong you know which to open.
This lesson matters now because the next lessons on sessions and cost depend on these terms. People say “it remembers”, “the session got long” and “I hit my usage” as if these were one thing. They are different things, each stored in a different place and reset in a different way. Knowing which is which tells you what to clear when a wrong claim has got in, and why a long session costs more.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
The glossary

Token: a chunk of text the model reads (a word piece, a character or a byte). Context limits and usage are counted in tokens.
Context window: everything the model can see when it writes its next output. It has a size limit, measured in tokens.
Session and session context: a session is a saved conversation tied to a project directory (stored locally as a transcript file). Its session context is what is in the window right now. Each session begins with a fresh context window, and sessions are independent: a new session has no history from earlier ones.
Memory: text on disk that is read into a new window at the start of every session.
Session usage: how much of your allowance a session consumes.
Context poisoning: a wrong or injected statement enters the context and later answers build on it. The term is community vocabulary. A commonly cited example is a game-playing agent whose recorded goals became corrupted with false state.


Memory in Claude Code
Both kinds are loaded at session start:

CLAUDE.md: instructions you write (the file can be set at project, user or organisation scope: who or where it applies).
Auto memory: notes the harness (the program around the model) writes itself from your corrections and preferences. It is per git repository and machine-local, kept in ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/ as plain markdown with a MEMORY.md index. Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at start; topic files are read on demand.

Memory is advisory context, and it takes room in the window every session. /clear (a command that starts a new, empty conversation) drops the conversation and leaves memory in place. Compaction (replacing old conversation with a summary) shrinks a session and leaves memory as it was.


Session usage in Claude Code

/usage shows an estimated session cost (worked out locally from token counts at list price, the published per-token price), plan usage limits and activity stats. /cost and /stats are aliases.
The displayed session total resets on /clear. The allowance itself resets on your plan’s schedule: look for a reset time in the /usage screen. If your plan shows none, /usage is not reporting it.
With a subscription, the plan bars on the /usage screen are what matter and the dollar figure is an estimate. If the screen shows no bars, your plan reports no limits there.
With the API, usage is billed per token, and thinking tokens (the tokens the model spends reasoning before it answers) count as output tokens.
Allowance sizes are on the vendor’s pricing page.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
text:
Why usage climbs

Claude Code sends the whole conversation on every request, and each tool-using step is another request.
Caching (a short-term store so repeated text is cheaper to re-read) makes re-reading cheaper, but a short question late in a long session still draws on all of it.
Large tool outputs stay in the conversation. Reading a 10,000-line log is one example.
Subagents (helper agents with their own context window) each have their own context, and their requests still count.
/compact itself reads the whole conversation.
Cached text expires after a set time. If you leave the session idle for longer than that, the next message re-sends everything at full price.

Remedies:

/clear between unrelated tasks.
/compact with a focus note.
/context to see what fills the window.
Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.

If /usage shows “rate limited until …”, Claude Code could not fetch your plan limits. You can keep working.

title: Memory, Sessions and Usage
section: When a wrong claim gets in
text:
When a wrong claim gets in
If you have corrected the same thing twice and it is still wrong, run /clear and write one new prompt that folds in what you learned. A third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already holds two failed attempts for the model to re-read. /rewind (a command that rolls the conversation back to an earlier turn) can return to before the bad turn.
Memory persists, so a wrong line costs the most there. Check a claim against the source, such as the data, the program’s own --help or the paper, before it goes into CLAUDE.md or auto memory. If a bad line is already there, open /memory, read what has been written about your project, and delete it.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands:

/memory: lists memory files, toggles auto memory, opens the folder.
/clear: new empty conversation; the old one stays resumable.
/compact: replace the history with a summary.
/resume and claude --resume: pick an earlier session.
claude --continue: the most recent session in this directory.
/usage and /context: usage and window contents.

Resume restores messages, model and permission mode (what the agent may do without asking). Startup flags such as --mcp-config need to be passed again. Transcripts are deleted after 30 days by default.


Check OpenCode’s documentation for its memory files, session commands and usage reporting. With a local Ollama model the window is still finite, so the ideas about session context and poisoned claims carry over. Check whether any vendor bills you per token.

title: Handoff Notes
text:
You wake at the mill with a fresh Astral and a half-finished job. It knows nothing of yesterday except what loads by itself or lies written down, and yesterday you wrote nothing. The mill keeps a ledger of notes for exactly this gap. Learn what belongs in it, and the next visit starts where the last one stopped.
You stop work on Friday with a half-finished refactor. On Monday you open a new session (one conversation with the agent, which has its own context: the text it can see right now). Each session begins with a fresh context window and no conversation history from before, so the new session does not know your goal, what you tried, or what you checked.
You need this lesson now because a fresh session is where the earlier lessons’ habits pay off: whatever it should know has to cross the gap in writing.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Five things that cross the gap
text:
Five things that cross the gap

The instructions file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code). A file you write that is loaded at the start of every session. Good for stable facts and conventions: how to run the tests, which folders are off limits.
Auto memory. Notes the harness (the program around the model) writes itself, from your corrections and preferences. In Claude Code, /memory lists and opens them.
Files in the repository (the project folder under version control): code, tests, a README, and, if you keep one, a progress or handoff file.
Git history. A commit is a saved snapshot of the project with a message you or the agent write. The list of commits shows what changed and when. It is durable unless someone rewrites it (with git commands that replace past commits, such as git rebase, git commit --amend or git push --force), and unpushed commits are local only.
Your handoff note. A short file about the state of one task, written for the next session.











What
Goes where
Lifetime
Who writes it
Trust




Stable rules and conventions
Instructions file
Until you edit it
You
High if short and checked


Preferences the harness picked up
Auto memory
Until deleted
The harness
Medium: it can be wrong


What the files say now
Files in the repository
Until edited or deleted
You or the agent
Medium: files can be stale


State of one task
Handoff note
Until the task is done
You, or the agent drafts and you review
Only as good as your review


What changed, and why
Commit messages in git history
Durable unless rewritten; local until pushed
You or the agent
Reliable for what changed; the why is only as good as the message



Memory the harness wrote can be wrong, and a wrong line is loaded again every session. This is context poisoning: a wrong statement enters the context and later answers build on it. Read /memory and check any claim against the source before you rely on it.
Three habits help a long task: keep a progress notes file, make git commits with descriptive messages so bad changes can be reverted, and begin each session by reading the progress file and the recent git log, then run a basic check before new work.

title: Handoff Notes
section: What a good handoff note contains
text:
What a good handoff note contains
Keep it short, so reading it costs less than rediscovering the state. Point to files and commands, and let the next session run them for fresh output.

Goal in one line.
Current state: branch, last commit, what runs and what does not.
Decisions and the reasons, including options you rejected.
Verified, and how; not verified. Two separate lists. For each verified item, the command and what it showed.
What failed and should not be retried.
Next steps, in order.
Pointers: file paths, commands, job IDs, work directories.
Open questions and parked ideas (ideas you decided to leave for later).

title: Handoff Notes
text:
Mock example
This is a mock handoff note for a mock task. The file names and numbers are invented.
# HANDOFF: qc_filter.py refactor (mock example)

## Goal
Replace the per-read loop in qc_filter.py with a vectorised version, same output.

## State (git branch refactor-qc, last commit a1b2c3d "qc: add vectorised mean quality")
- New function mean_qual_fast() is written and called from main().
- Old function mean_qual() is kept for comparison. Do not delete yet.

## Decisions
- Keep both functions until all samples are compared (a bug here would silently change which reads pass).
- Threshold stays at mean Q20, as in the lab protocol.

## Verified
- tests/test_filter.py: ran `pytest -q`, 6 passed.
- sample_A: `diff <(python qc_filter.py A.fq) old_out/A.txt` gave no output.

## Not verified
- Samples B and C have not been compared with the old output.
- Reads shorter than 30 bases: no test covers them.
- Speed gain: not measured.

## Failed, do not retry
- Using numpy on the raw quality string: wrong values for the Phred offset. Convert to integers first.

## Next steps
1. Compare B and C against old_out/ with the same diff command.
2. Add a test for a 10-base read.
3. Only then delete mean_qual().

## Open questions / parked
- Should the threshold be a command-line option? Parked for a later task.

title: Handoff Notes
section: Where to put it, and how to start the next session
text:
Where to put it, and how to start the next session
Put the note in a file the next session can find. Two options:

A file in the repo, such as HANDOFF.md, if the team should see it.
A gitignored ordinary file you point to, if it is personal. This is the simpler choice.

A CLAUDE.local.md file in the project’s top-level folder (add it to .gitignore) holds private per-project preferences and loads after CLAUDE.md. It exists only in the worktree (separate checkout folder) where you created it.
Anything loaded every session takes room in the window, so keep a handoff note out of CLAUDE.md and remove it once its task is done.
Write the note before you run /clear (which starts a new empty conversation), because /clear drops the conversation. Pairing the note with a commit leaves a matching record in git.
Then start the new session with a prompt like this:

Read HANDOFF.md, then tell me your understanding before changing anything.

The agent restates the goal and state in its own words, and you compare that with what you know. This is a cheap comprehension check: it can catch a misreading of the note. The restatement comes from the same model that read it, so the note’s claims still need checking against the source.
You can ask the agent to draft the note at the end of a session. Review it yourself, since a draft can overstate what was verified (“all tests pass” when none were run in that session).

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands:

/memory: see memory files.
/clear: new empty conversation.
/resume and claude --resume: reopen an earlier session.
claude --continue: the most recent session in this directory.
/export: writes the conversation as plain text for a person to read. Transcripts are long, so write a short curated note yourself.



Commands: /new (alias /clear), /sessions (aliases /resume and /continue), /compact and /export. The handoff note itself is just a file, so the practice carries over. Check OpenCode’s documentation for how it loads project instructions, and keep the note short if your local model has a small window.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
The Citadel gate is shared by hundreds of travellers, and the gatekeeper has seen what one careless sweep of the whole library does to everyone’s queue. You arrive with an Astral that means well and has never heard of manners. Before it takes one step inside, teach it where it may work and how widely it may search.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster counts what one careless sweep costs the whole guild.


The Diviner submits her jobs and leaves the login node alone.


The Artificer sets limits before the Astral runs anything.


The Archivist asks who can read the files left on shared ground.
You need this before an agent touches a cluster: it will run a command that is harmless on your laptop and slow for everyone on a shared machine. This quest sets where an agent may run work and how widely it may search. Ask your cluster staff before running an agent on the login node. Some sites forbid agents on login nodes altogether, so follow your cluster’s user guide where it differs from this page. Read this quest on your laptop. On the cluster, run its dry checks on small trees only, or inside a job.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Login node versus compute node
Everyone who logs in shares the login node. The scheduler places your jobs on compute nodes. Light work (editing text, git, listing one directory, checking a log with head or tail) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work belongs on compute nodes: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.
An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will run a long command if you let it, so you set the rule. It also misjudges “this will only take a few seconds”, so tell it to ask when a command’s cost is unclear.
Some sites allow agents only inside an interactive compute allocation (a job that gives you a shell on a compute node). If a scheduler command is missing, ask staff.
If the agent has a question for you and you are away, a good agent stops and lists its open questions. Ask for that in your instructions: do the steps that need no answer, stop, and list the questions.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
Shared storage prefers scoped searches
Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless find / or a recursive grep -r from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one known directory, and keep them away from /. The same goes for du, ls --recursive, ls --format=long (it reads the details of every file) and wide globs on big directories, and avoid making many small files in one directory. Keep the agent to your own project paths: other users’ or other projects’ paths are off limits unless you named them or the site documents them as shared (reference data).
Claude Code’s search tools (Glob, Grep) are not a filesystem-load control; scope the search yourself.

title: Login Node Manners
text:
The scheduler’s four commands



Command
What it does




sbatch
submit a job script; returns a job ID


srun
run a job or job step in real time


squeue
report the state of jobs


scancel
cancel a pending or running job



Slurm’s default time limit is the partition’s default (a partition is a named group of compute nodes with its own limits), so set limits in the script. This job script aligns one sample. The job and file names are invented:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=align-s1        # name shown in squeue
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # wall-clock limit: 2 hours
#SBATCH --mem=8G                   # memory for the whole job
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4          # CPUs for the one task
#SBATCH --output=align-s1-%j.log   # log file; %j becomes the job ID

bwa mem -t 4 ref.fa sample1_R1.fq.gz sample1_R2.fq.gz > sample1.sam
Save it as script.sh and run the dry check:
sbatch --test-only script.sh
--test-only validates the script and estimates a start time. No job is submitted, so the check works as a dry run. Submit with sbatch script.sh yourself after you read the script. Use a job array (one script submitted as many numbered tasks, such as --array=1-100%10, which runs at most ten tasks at a time) for many similar tasks. Write options in their long form (--ntasks for -n) so you can read what the agent proposes.
Slurm counts what you allocate, whatever you use. A partition’s memory-per-CPU limit (MaxMemPerCPU) can make Slurm raise the CPU count to fit a large memory request, or reject the job. For example, --mem=120G with MaxMemPerCPU=4000 (MB) can become about 31 CPUs. Afterwards compare request, allocation and use with sacct (the command that reports what finished jobs requested and used).
Scratch space holds throwaway files. Ask your staff where the project’s scratch is, tell the agent, and use it instead of /tmp, which is shared on a login node and often small. Inside a job, use a temporary directory only if your site documents one. Write throwaway files to scratch, and write final outputs straight to the project directory or copy them there before the job ends. A set $TMPDIR (the variable that names the temporary directory) does not prove you are on scratch, because a site can set it to /tmp. Scripts, logs and final outputs stay in the project directory.

title: Login Node Manners
section: Look before you copy or delete
text:
Look before you copy or delete
Find out what a copy or a delete will touch before it touches anything.

Run rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes first, with the same arguments, and read the list. A dry run lists what would change and changes nothing.
Check that the list matches your request. Look for keys, .env files and personal data. Look for a *deleting line that removes something you wanted to keep.
Run a new dry run after any change to the options. Run it where the real run will run, because it reads the whole tree. On a big tree, run the dry run inside a job.
cp, scp and rm have no dry run. List the exact path or glob and delete only those names.
--exclude skips files without a word. rsync --delete and rm --recursive also remove what is inside a directory, so list and dry-run those too.
Do not copy from or delete a directory that a running job writes to.
Before you delete a source you copied, repeat the copy as a dry run with --checksum and delete only if the list is empty.
Send large transfers through the scheduler or the site’s data-transfer node (a machine set aside for moving files).

title: Login Node Manners
text:
What the agent’s sandbox covers

A sandbox is a restricted environment that limits what the agent’s commands can touch. Claude Code’s sandbox covers shell commands only. File tools, MCP servers (connections to external tools) and hooks (scripts the harness runs at set points) run outside it.
If it cannot start, commands run without sandboxing by default. Setting sandbox.failIfUnavailable to true stops that.
On Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat (two Linux programs it uses to isolate commands). You usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster, so ask staff whether they are installed.
Check that the sandbox is on before you rely on it.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can. Useful instructions:

“Search only inside ./workflow/. Never run find or grep -r from / or $HOME.”
“Run nothing in the foreground on the login node. Draft an sbatch script and show it to me.”

Instructions are guidance, and the agent can still slip. If a project instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) is stricter than these lines, the stricter one wins.
Foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default). A heavy command still runs until it is cut off, so a timeout does not limit load.


The same habits apply. OpenCode’s permission model uses allow, ask and deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Its base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so sbatch runs without a prompt until you add a rule. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands, and check your installed version’s permission docs. A local model through Ollama runs on the node you are on and touches the filesystem the same way.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Inside the Citadel a queue master hands out places in line, one for each job. Your Astral, eager to please, takes a place for every idea it has, until the line is jammed with its errands and the other travellers glare at you. A creature that submits freely can fill every place, and one that cancels freely can ruin a day’s work. Decide which of the queue master’s tasks it may do alone and which need your nod.
An agent that can submit jobs can fill the queue, and one that can cancel jobs can destroy work. This quest sets what the agent does alone and what needs your approval. Ask your cluster staff before letting an agent near your cluster account, and follow your cluster’s policy and data agreement over this page. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Draft versus submit
A job script is text. Letting an agent draft one is low risk, because you read it before anything runs. Submitting spends shared resources, and cancelling can destroy work. A sensible split:

The agent drafts scripts and may check state (squeue, sinfo, sacct). Limit sacct with --jobs=<jobid> or --starttime=<date> so it does not dump the whole accounting history.
You approve sbatch, srun, salloc and scancel.

Before approving an sbatch, read the script and the resource request: --time, --mem, and the array size if it is an array.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
Jobs, Not Jam
section: Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
text:
Why scancel -u is the dangerous one
scancel -u <you> signals all your jobs, including ones the agent did not submit. Whole jobs are terminated, and other work of yours dies with them. scancel --me does the same. Selectors such as --name, --state and --partition also act on every job they match, and combined filters must all match. Deny rules cannot cover every spelling, so the single ask rule on scancel * is the net and the deny rules catch the worst two. Approve scancel <jobid> only for a job you approved the agent submitting. Slurm can rate-limit a user whose requests arrive at a sustained high rate, so a runaway loop of commands is a problem for the scheduler as well as for you.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Polling costs money and attention
Claude Code charges by token use (the units of text the model reads and writes). The whole conversation, called the context, is sent with every request, and each tool use sends another request. A /loop (a command that re-runs a prompt on a timer) that polls squeue keeps firing on its interval, even while the session is idle, and sends your full context each time. Verbose output such as long logs also inflates the context.
The scheduler pays too. The squeue and sacct manual pages warn against running them from loops, because it can slow slurmctld (the scheduler daemon) or slurmdbd (the accounting database) for everyone.
Habits that keep polling cheap:

Poll no more than about once a minute, less often for long jobs. Run one loop at a time and scope it: squeue --user=$USER or --jobs=<id>.
Use sbatch --parsable --wait (it prints only the job ID, then waits until the job ends), or the pipeline’s own poller, instead of a sleep loop. It replaces a /loop of squeue, so skip the loop.
A wait can outlast the tool’s timeout. Run it in the background. Never resubmit because the wait timed out. Check State with sacct first: --wait passes the job’s exit code through, but a signal-killed job gives 1, so the code alone does not prove success.
--mail-type sends you an email and does not make the agent wait. If you use watch, keep it at --interval=60 or slower and stop it when done.
Submit many similar tasks as one array with a concurrency cap (--array=1-100%10) instead of a loop of sbatch calls.

Foreground commands in Claude Code time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so an agent waiting on a long foreground command, such as an srun that blocks until it finishes, gets cut off. The command still runs until it is cut off, so a timeout does not limit load.

title: Jobs, Not Jam
text:
Size the request
A job can use more of the cluster than you meant to ask for, and no error tells you. Slurm counts what you allocate, whatever you use, and that count feeds your fair-share priority (how soon your later jobs start). A partition is a group of nodes with its own limits. Many partitions limit memory per CPU (MaxMemPerCPU), so a large memory request on one CPU can make Slurm add CPUs to fit it, or reject the job. Other limit settings can leave an over-limit job pending instead, so read what your site does.
Before a large or repeated job, read the partition’s limits (scontrol show partition <name>). Afterwards compare what you asked for with what the job used. This command prints one row per job and step:
sacct --jobs=<id> --format=JobID,State,ReqMem,MaxRSS,Elapsed,Timelimit
ReqMem is the memory requested, MaxRSS the most memory one task used, Elapsed the run time and Timelimit the time requested. MaxRSS is filled on the step rows such as .batch. Here is a finished alignment job. The numbers are invented:



JobID
State
ReqMem
MaxRSS
Elapsed
Timelimit




123456
COMPLETED
32G

00:41:10
04:00:00


123456.batch
COMPLETED
32G
9.8G
00:41:10




The job used 9.8 GB of the 32 GB requested and ran 41 minutes of the 4 hours allowed. For the next run, ask for --mem=14G (about 1.4 times MaxRSS) and --time=01:15:00 (about 1.8 times Elapsed). In this invented case the extra is headroom for a larger sample. Choose your own margin.

A job killed for memory can show OUT_OF_MEMORY in State. MaxRSS then understates the need, so raise the request above the failed one.
If sacct prints nothing, accounting may be off. Ask your staff.
If the memory need and the CPU count conflict, ask staff for a partition with a better memory-to-CPU ratio and check with them before using it.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
The Collegium rings with work from dawn. In one college tinkers hammer automata together out of brass and patience, in another beastmasters drill familiars to hunt a single quarry, and in the sages’ college robed figures bargain pacts with Astrals. The three colleges respect one another, because each knows what the shokanju it summons are good at and where they fail: automata never stray and never improvise, familiars are sure on their one trail, and an Astral can speak every tongue and still invent what it does not know. A tinker nods to a familiar as it passes, and a sage asks the tinker to build the lock that keeps an Astral honest. Learn what each is for, and later how to make a pact with an Astral of your own.





From left to right: an automaton, a familiar and an Astral.
Before you pick a tool for a job, you need to know what kinds exist. Tools differ in how predictable they are and in how you check them.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
text:
Three kinds

A deterministic program (a script, awk, samtools): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
A trained model (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do one task, with measured accuracy on that task. It is the predictive side of AI: it forecasts from past data and gives you an estimate to act on. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
A large language model (LLM): trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. ChatGPT and Claude are LLMs. It is the generative side of AI: it produces new content (text, code, images) that you review, flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

The line between the last two is not clean. An LLM can be asked to classify, and some generative models predict structure or sequences. Judge a tool by the task you give it and how you will check the result. For a forecast, a predictive model usually costs less than a generative one.
Two common mistakes: using an LLM for something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.
An LLM can also be called inside a script (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic (the same input may give different output), so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.
Before you reach for an agent or a large model, ask whether a script, a fixed workflow or a smaller specialised model does the job. A method that fits the task is often cheaper to run and easier to reproduce. A hosted model (one that runs on a provider’s servers) can change when the provider updates it. Keep the large model for the open-ended steps. Fine-tuning (further training a model on your own examples) suits only some tasks.

title: Three Kinds of Machine
section: What a model can do on its own
text:
What a model can do on its own
A language model with no tools suits some jobs and struggles with others. A large hosted model will do better than a small one on some rows.







Suits
Struggles with




Summarising and editing text
Counting letters or basic arithmetic


Pulling out names and places
Multi-step logical reasoning


Classifying a piece of text
Facts it was never given


Generating tags, short creative writing
Writing code (for a small model that runs on your own device)



Harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and the program around it (called the harness) gives it tools, such as a shell, a file editor and a script runner, for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good work to hand to a script.
