title: Know Your Tools
text:
An old wanderer spreads the tools of the trade across the long table: the Astral you will summon, the binding circle that holds it, and a pile of fittings nobody has labelled. The boasters swear a good pact needs nothing more than a name. The wanderer picks the pieces up one at a time and says what each is for. Start with the Astral alone, then watch the circle go down around it.
People mix these words up, and the mix-ups cause real mistakes, such as blaming “the model” for something a setting did. The pictures below start with one part and add one more each time.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
1. The model



A model with an effort setting

One box named model, which reads text and writes text. A dashed box inside it, named effort, shows how much it thinks per step.   MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step 


The model reads text and writes text. Effort is a setting on it.



Model. The large language model (LLM) that reads and writes text (for example Claude Sonnet 5.5, a Mistral model, or a local model through Ollama, a program that runs models on your own computer). Aliases such as sonnet move to newer versions over time, so use the full model name when a result must be reproducible.
Effort. A setting for how much the model reasons before it answers, from low to max in Claude Code (/effort, --effort; a /command is typed inside the running tool, a --flag when you start it). Low is faster and cheaper; high thinks longer and checks more. It steers how much the model reasons per step. max can show diminishing returns and overthink, so raise it only where you measure a gain.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
2. The harness



A model inside a harness

A large box named harness contains the model with its effort setting, and three boxes: tools, permissions, and the loop with context.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context 


The harness surrounds the model. It supplies tools, applies permissions and runs the loop.



Harness. The program around the model. The product you type into is the harness. It provides the tools, manages the context the model sees, runs the loop (gather context, act, check, repeat) and enforces permissions. Claude Code, OpenCode (an open-source harness) and Mistral Vibe (Mistral’s open-source terminal coding agent) are harnesses.
Tool. An action the model can request and the harness runs, such as reading a file or running a shell command. A tool call is one such request; tool output is what comes back.
Permissions. The harness’s rules for which tool calls it runs, asks about or refuses.
Agent. A model inside a harness that picks and runs tools in a loop toward a goal.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
3. Extensions



Extensions plugged into the harness

The harness from the previous picture, with a row of extensions: skill, MCP, hook, and an instructions file. A line under skill, MCP and hook marks a plugin as a bundle of them.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK INSTRUCTIONS FILE  PLUGIN: a bundle of skills, hooks, MCP 


Extensions change what the harness offers. A plugin installs several as one unit.



Instructions file. A text file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode where read) that the harness loads at session start. It advises and does not enforce.
Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md. Only its short description is preloaded; the body loads when it is used. It advises.
MCP (Model Context Protocol). An open standard for connecting the harness to outside tools and data, such as a database or a literature search. A server you connect can act on your behalf, so treat it like software you install.
Hook. Your own command, request or prompt that the harness runs automatically at a set point, such as before a tool call. A command hook that exits with code 2 before a tool runs stops that action whatever the model wants (an exit code is the number a script returns; 0 means success, and a hook uses 2 to mean block). A rule in an instructions file can only ask, so hooks are the stronger guard.
Plugin. A folder that bundles skills, hooks, MCP servers and more, installed as one unit. It can run code, so install only plugins you trust.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
4. Evals



An eval measuring from outside

The harness with its extensions, and below it, outside the harness, a box named eval that runs with and without an extension and compares the results.   HARNESS  MODEL reads text, writes text  EFFORT: how much it thinks per step Tools: read, edit, run Permissions Loop, context EXTENSIONS you plug in SKILL MCP HOOK INSTRUCTIONS FILE  PLUGIN: a bundle of skills, hooks, MCP  EVAL: run with and without, compare 


An eval sits outside the harness and compares runs.



Eval. A repeatable test of agent behaviour: a prompt plus checks on the result. Comparing runs with and without something (a skill, a rule) shows what it contributed. A score of 100% both ways means the test cannot tell the difference, so make it harder.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
5. One model, different harnesses



The same model in two harnesses

Two harness boxes side by side, each holding the same model X, each with its own tools, permission rules and loop.   HARNESS A Model X its own tools, rules, loop  HARNESS B Model X its own tools, rules, loop 


Claude Code and OpenCode are two harnesses.


The same model can behave differently in each harness, because tools, permission rules and the loop differ. Naming differs between tools too. Check another tool’s docs for how its hooks, plugins and effort settings work.

title: Know Your Tools
text:
Other words you will meet
These are not in the pictures.

Prompt. The text you send to the model.
Turn. One prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Subagent. A helper agent with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Sandbox. An operating-system layer that limits what commands can touch.
Hallucination. A plausible-looking statement that is false, such as an invented DOI (a paper’s permanent identifier).
Prompt injection. Text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.


Words about what the model can see
These get mixed up more than any others.

Token. The chunk of text a model actually reads and writes. Somewhere between a letter and a word. Limits and costs are counted in tokens.
Context window. Everything the model can see at once right now: instructions, files it has read, tool output and the conversation so far. It has a size limit, and a fuller window is not automatically a better one.
Session (session context). One running conversation, and the context window it has built up. A new session starts with an empty conversation. Two sessions do not share their context.
Memory. Notes that the harness loads at the start of every session, such as your instructions file and, in Claude Code, notes the harness writes itself. Memory outlives a session; session context does not.
Compaction. The harness replaces old conversation with a summary to free room.
Session usage. How much of your allowance or bill a session spends. It climbs with the size of the context, because the whole conversation is sent again with each request.
Context poisoning. A community term: a wrong statement gets into the context, and later answers build on it. Start a fresh session and keep unverified claims out of memory files.


Redraw the picture from memory for the tool you actually use: which model, which harness, which extensions are loaded right now?

Define success criteria and build evaluations: 5 quests
Manage sessions: 5 quests

title: Lore library
text:
Gaia’s Rest

Reduce hallucinations: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 7 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Name the Fears: it lists concrete habits such as allowing “I don’t know” and checking claims against quotes, and says plainly that none of them remove errors.
Where Machines Fail: it gives habits such as allowing “I don’t know” and checking claims against quotes, the kind of fix for the confident-but-wrong rows in this quest; it says none removes errors.
Spot Hallucinations: it lists ways to make a model show its support (quote first, allow “I don’t know”), the opposite of a confident mirage.
Ground Truth: it lists model-side habits (quote first, retract unsupported claims); read it to see why a check the model did not write is still needed.
Send Small Changes, Say What You Checked: it suggests asking for quotes and allowing “I don’t know”, habits you can request from a collaborator who sends you LLM-assisted work.
Same Every Time: it suggests comparing repeated runs, a cheap way to see whether an LLM step gives the same answer each time, and admits such habits reduce but do not remove errors.
Boss: Review a Messy Session: it lists ways to ask for support and to allow “I don’t know”, useful when a summary states a flag or default with confidence.

Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models: Sharma et al. (Anthropic authors), ICLR 2024, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Name the Fears: it shows assistants often agree with a user’s stated view, so you can see why asking for the case against your idea helps.
Spot Hallucinations: it shows assistants often agree with a user’s stated view, which is why asking an agent “are you sure?” proves little.

Mitigating prompt injections in browser use: Anthropic, article. Why read: a vendor’s own account that injection is not solved and what defences exist; the attack figures are Anthropic’s own tests. Cited in: Name the Fears.
Security: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 7 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Name the Fears: it describes the built-in protections and advice on untrusted content, a practical start for the fear of prompt injection.
Claude in the Cloud: its cloud execution section lists the isolation, credential and audit controls.
Write Permission Rules: it summarises the built-in protections and the advice for untrusted content and sensitive code.
Keep Secrets Out of Reach: it covers prompt injection, credential storage and advice for sensitive code.
Send Small Changes, Say What You Checked: it says you are responsible for reviewing proposed commands and changes, a duty you cannot hand to a collaborator unseen.
Keys on Shared Ground: it covers credential storage and advice for sensitive code, relevant to where keys sit on shared storage.
Boss: Review a Messy Session: it says you review the commands and changes an agent proposes, which is the job in this fight.

Building effective agents: Anthropic, article. Why read: it separates fixed workflows from agents and argues for the simplest option, which is the choice this quest asks you to make. Cited in: Three Kinds of Machine, Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents.
AI for Science, practice 1: match the method to the task: AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it argues for the cheapest method that fits, with a script or small model before an agent. It is a draft with no endorsements yet. Cited in: Three Kinds of Machine.
Understand model capabilities: Apple, docs. Why read: it is a short table of what a small on-device model suits and what it does not, a useful reminder of what a model can do before you give it tools. Cited in: Three Kinds of Machine.
Generative AI vs. predictive AI: What’s the difference?: IBM, article. Why read: a short vendor explainer of the two terms, with business examples; it is secondary and written for enterprise readers, so use it for the vocabulary. Cited in: Three Kinds of Machine.
Define success criteria and build evaluations: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 5 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Three Kinds of Machine: it shows how to turn “it seems fine” into a measurable check, which is how you test an LLM step.
Know Your Tools: it gives the guidance on specific, measurable criteria that evals need.
Should You Fine-Tune?: it shows how to turn “it seems fine” into a measurable check, which is how you compare a tuned model with an untuned one.
Turn Mistakes into Tests: general guidance on specific, measurable criteria and on automating the grading.
Test the Skill: how to write criteria and graders that discriminate.

Claude Code overview: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the front page of the docs, a good place to see how much more there is than this course covers. Cited in: Know Your Tools, Set Up Your Agent.
How Claude Code works: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Know Your Tools: it is the page that defines the agentic harness and the gather, act, check loop used in this quest.
Which Instructions Apply: it describes what the harness adds to the conversation, useful for tracing where a behaviour came from.

Model configuration: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Know Your Tools: it covers model aliases and the effort setting, so you can pin a model and see what /effort changes.
Pick Your Model: it covers model aliases, the effort setting and how to pin a model in Claude Code.

Skills: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Know Your Tools: it shows the SKILL.md format and how only descriptions load at startup.
Write a Skill: the reference for SKILL.md fields, where skills live and how to confirm one loaded.

Introduction to the Model Context Protocol: Model Context Protocol, docs. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Know Your Tools: it explains what MCP is as an open standard before you connect a server.
Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents: it explains what MCP is before you decide which servers to connect.
Connect an MCP Server: it explains MCP as an open standard, so you know what a server is before you plug one in.

Is my data used for model training? (consumer): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the page that says the training setting exists for Free, Pro and Max chats, which decides your first account question. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.
How long do you store my data?: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it gives the 5-year and 30-day figures for consumer chats and what happens after you delete one. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.
How long do you store my organization’s data?: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the commercial-account counterpart: the API’s 30-day default, how saved chats are kept and deleted, and the cases that keep data longer. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.
Use incognito chats: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows what incognito does and does not change, so you do not over-trust the name. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.
Data usage (Claude Code): Anthropic, docs. Cited by 4 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Choose What to Hand Over: it states that the agent sends prompts and outputs over the network, which is what makes steps 4 and 5 different from running a query yourself.
Set Up Your Agent: it states what /feedback sends and how long it is kept, which matters before you paste a bug report.
Claude in the Cloud: it states what Anthropic stores from a cloud session and how retention differs by plan.
Keep Secrets Out of Reach: it says what is sent to the provider, how training and retention differ by plan, and what telemetry can be turned off. It does not replace your own data agreement.

Ollama FAQ: Ollama, docs. Why read: it says local runs do not send prompts to Ollama and separates its cloud models, which matters if you choose a local model for sensitive data. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.
AI for Science: the short version: AI for Science, article. Why read: a one-page European summary of research practices, useful for a conversation with your data steward. It describes itself as a living record and shows no endorsements. Cited in: Choose What to Hand Over.

title: Lore library
text:
The Collegium

Advanced setup: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it holds the install commands for every platform, WSL notes and how updates work. Cited in: Set Up Your Agent.
Authentication: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it explains login methods and which credential wins when a subscription and an API key are both present. Cited in: Set Up Your Agent.
Troubleshooting: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it maps symptoms to the right fix page and says when to use /doctor or claude doctor. Cited in: Set Up Your Agent.
OpenCode docs: OpenCode, docs. Why read: it lists the install methods, the plan and build agents, and how OpenCode finds Ollama models. Cited in: Set Up Your Agent.
Ollama quickstart: Ollama, docs. Why read: it covers installing Ollama and running a first model, and links to the context-length page that agents need. Cited in: Set Up Your Agent.
awesome-free-models: GitHub, repo. Why read: a large, regularly corrected list of free models, tiers and tools; check its banner for what changed lately. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
OpenRouter FAQ: OpenRouter, docs. Why read: it explains free model variants, daily allowances and how prompt logging and provider retention differ. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Google AI Studio terms: Google, docs. Why read: it spells out how unpaid and paid services treat your prompts differently. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Groq: your data: Groq, docs. Why read: it states the default retention and log period for inference requests. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
OpenCode Zen: OpenCode, docs. Why read: it lists free models together with their data-retention line, model by model. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Cloudflare Workers AI pricing: Cloudflare, docs. Why read: it shows a daily free allowance and what happens when you pass it. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Do you use my user data to train your models?: Mistral, docs. Why read: it lists, plan by plan, which Mistral products train on your data by default and where the opt-out lives. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Providers: OpenCode, docs. Why read: it shows how to connect an OpenAI-compatible gateway to a coding agent. Cited in: Free Is Not Free.
Safety, approvals and permissions: Mistral, docs. Why read: it describes Vibe’s four approval modes, trusted folders and per-tool rules, for comparison with other harnesses. Cited in: Pick Your Model.
Models overview: Mistral, docs. Why read: it lists which Mistral models are open-weight, which carry a deprecation date and what licence each shows. Cited in: Pick Your Model.
Choosing the right model: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it gives the official way to pick a starting model and to test the choice on your own evaluations. Cited in: Pick Your Model.
Effort: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it defines each effort level and gives per-model starting advice, with the advice to test on your own tasks; its API defaults can differ from the Claude Code defaults on the model-configuration page. Cited in: Pick Your Model.
Sub-agents: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Pick Your Model: it gives the exact frontmatter fields for a subagent (model, effort, tools), the order in which a subagent’s model is chosen, and how the built-in Explore and Plan helpers behave.
Capture Ideas Mid-Task: it shows how a subagent keeps noisy work in its own context and returns only a summary.
Teach and Share the Load: it shows how side tasks run in their own context, a way to share work between agents whose output you still review.

Manage costs effectively: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Pick Your Model: it shows how /usage is computed and where model choice, effort and subagents change the bill.
Memory, Sessions and Usage: it explains why a long session keeps costing more and which habits (clear, compact, model choice) cut usage.
When to Start Fresh: it explains why a long session keeps costing more and which habits (clear, compact, model choice) cut usage.

Fine-tuning LLMs Guide: Unsloth, docs. Why read: a beginner-friendly walk through LoRA, QLoRA, dataset shape and training settings; it is a vendor guide for its own tool, so treat its speed and hardware claims as the vendor’s. Cited in: Should You Fine-Tune?.
LoRA: Hugging Face, docs. Why read: the PEFT library’s explanation of how LoRA works, what rank and alpha control, and how to merge an adapter back into the base model. Cited in: Should You Fine-Tune?.
Use Claude Code in the cloud: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the main page on cloud sessions, including what gets uploaded when a repository has no GitHub remote. Cited in: Claude in the Cloud.
Configure cloud environments: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it covers network access levels, environment variables and setup scripts for a session. Cited in: Claude in the Cloud.
Claude Code in the cloud article: claude.dev blog, article. Why read: a community field guide to cloud sessions; use it for ideas and rely on the official pages above for facts. Cited in: Claude in the Cloud.

title: Lore library
text:
Ancient DNA Crypt

Checkpointing: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Save Point: it explains /rewind and its limits, including that Bash-made changes need version control, so you see why git is the real save point.
Boss: Review a Messy Session: it says Bash-made changes need version control, which is why the rm -rf in the summary had no way back.

Manage sessions: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 5 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Save Point: it lists the commands for naming, resuming and clearing sessions, including claude --resume, a companion when work is interrupted.
Memory, Sessions and Usage: it covers naming and resuming sessions, which is what makes a session’s context something you carry forward on purpose.
When to Start Fresh: it lists the exact commands to name, resume, branch and clear sessions.
Capture Ideas Mid-Task: it shows how to branch a session, the command to reach for when a side thought deserves its own line of work.
Handoff Notes: it lists the exact commands to name, resume, branch and clear sessions.

Sandboxing: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 5 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Test Permissions and the Sandbox: it lists what the sandbox covers, the settings keys and the two probe commands used here.
Write Permission Rules: it states what the sandbox covers and what it does not, so you do not over-trust it.
Connect an MCP Server: it states what the sandbox limits and where that limit ends, so you can judge it as one layer.
Advice or Enforcement: it shows an operating-system limit on shell commands and where that limit ends.
Keys on Shared Ground: it states the sandbox reads most of the machine, including ~/.ssh, unless you deny it, and it fails open by default.

Choose a permission mode: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Test Permissions and the Sandbox: it defines each mode and how to switch between them.
Plan Before You Edit: it is the source for how plan mode is entered, approved and (not always) enforced.

Configure permissions: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 10 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Test Permissions and the Sandbox: it gives the rule syntax and the deny, ask, allow order.
Write Permission Rules: it documents allow, ask and deny rules and how settings files combine, which is the core of this quest.
Keep Secrets Out of Reach: it shows the deny rules that keep the agent’s file tools away from files such as .env.
Connect an MCP Server: it shows how to allow or deny a server’s tools by name, the way to grant read-only access.
Block Actions with a Hook: it covers deny and ask rules, which still apply when a hook says allow.
Advice or Enforcement: it explains deny, ask and allow rules and permission modes, the built-in enforcement layer.
Login Node Manners: it shows allow, ask and deny rules by command pattern, the way to make heavy or sprawling commands ask first, and warns Bash rules are not a security boundary.
Jobs, Not Jam: it shows how to make sbatch ask while read-only checks such as squeue are allowed, with the warning that Bash rules are not a security boundary.
Keys on Shared Ground: it explains how settings files apply and combine by scope, so you can see which level should hold deny rules for your keys; it warns Bash rules are not a security boundary.
Boss: Review a Messy Session: it shows deny rules that hold where a line in NOTES.md only asks.

OpenCode permissions: OpenCode, docs. Why read: it gives the rule fields, the allow, ask and deny effects, and says the last matching rule wins. Cited in: Test Permissions and the Sandbox.
Development containers: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it sets out when running without permission prompts is acceptable and what a dev container does not protect. Cited in: Test Permissions and the Sandbox.
Scenario III: full agentic code development: CodeRefinery, docs. Why read: a course lesson with a Docker demo and exercises on supervising an agent. Cited in: Test Permissions and the Sandbox.
AI for Science, practice 11: decide where research data may go: AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it ties the choice of service to the contract and legal basis for your data, and limits agent sends through the environment. A draft with no endorsements yet; it is not legal advice. Cited in: Keep Secrets Out of Reach.
The .claude directory: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what is written to transcripts on disk, how long it stays, and how claude purge clears it. Cited in: Keep Secrets Out of Reach.
Settings: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it explains where “don’t ask again” approvals are saved and how settings.local.json is kept out of git. Cited in: Keep Secrets Out of Reach.
An update on our recent security incident: Cursor, article. Why read: a first-hand account of agent traces with unredacted credentials. Cited in: Keep Secrets Out of Reach.
Authenticating as a GitHub App installation: GitHub, docs. Why read: it shows the one-hour token that keeps a leak small. Cited in: Keep Secrets Out of Reach.

title: Lore library
text:
The Codon Mill

Token counting: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it documents the free count endpoint and says models from Claude 4.7 onward use a newer tokenizer, so the same text gives roughly 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models (the exact increase depends on the content). Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
The Strawberry Problem: Cosma et al., EMNLP 2025, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it argues character-level information is weakly available inside tokens, a leading explanation for miscounted letters.
Ground Truth: it studies why models miscount letters and links it to tokens, which is the idea behind miscounted bases.

Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization: Zhang et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Tokens, Not Letters: it studies how tokenisation affects counting; its abstract says step-by-step reasoning (chain of thought) can help, and its full text still reports failures with it in modern models. A preprint.
Ground Truth: it shows how tokenisation changes counting accuracy in language models, which is why a script, not a model’s reading, should do exact counts (that last step is our general practice, not the paper’s claim). A preprint.

CharBench: Evaluating the Role of Tokenization in Character-Level Tasks: arXiv, paper. Why read: a counter-view finding tokenisation only weakly tied to errors, so treat the tokens explanation as likely but disputed. A preprint. Cited in: Tokens, Not Letters.
Lost in the Middle: Liu et al., arXiv, paper. Cited by 3 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Where Machines Fail: it shows recall is best for text at the start or end of a long input and weaker in the middle. A preprint.
RAG and Its Cousins: it shows why a long, stuffed prompt can hide the passage that matters.
Boss: Review Large Output: it measures how accuracy drops when the relevant fact sits in the middle of a long input.

On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization: Maynez et al., ACL 2020, paper. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Where Machines Fail: it found hallucinated content in neural summaries; older models, but it shows why summaries need a spot check.
Spot Hallucinations: it found invented content in every neural summary tested; the models are pre-chat-era, so read it for the direction, not current rates.

LLM The Genius Paradox: A Linguistic and Math Expert’s Struggle with Simple Word-based Counting Problems: arXiv, paper. Why read: its abstract says specialised math and coding models still struggle with simple counting and that reasoning before answering is the most reliable fix; its full text adds that explicitly asking coding models for Python code worked. A preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as we checked. Cited in: Where Machines Fail.
Explore the context window: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 4 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

The Context Window: a walk through what loads before you type, what a file read costs and what survives compaction.
Handoff Notes: a walk through what loads before you type, what a file read costs and what survives compaction.
Boss: Review Large Output: it shows what fills a Claude Code session and what survives compaction.
Write the Brief: an interactive timeline of what fills the window and what survives compaction.

Context windows: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it states what counts toward the window and names context rot, the page’s own warning that more context is not better. Cited in: The Context Window.
Effective context engineering for AI agents: Anthropic, article. Cited by 6 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

The Context Window: it explains why long contexts degrade and why curating what goes in matters; compaction trade-offs are discussed.
Handoff Notes: it explains why long contexts degrade and why curating what goes in matters; compaction trade-offs are discussed.
RAG and Its Cousins: it describes loading information just in time with search tools instead of pre-building an index.
Keep an LLM Wiki: it describes the opposite habit of loading information just in time with search tools, which helps you decide when a pre-built wiki is worth the upkeep.
Boss: Review Large Output: it explains why more text in context is not free and why stale material hurts.
Write the Brief: background on why more context is not always better and what compaction can lose.

How Claude remembers your project: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 6 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

The Context Window: it says CLAUDE.md and auto memory are context, which is why they take up room in the window.
Memory, Sessions and Usage: it defines CLAUDE.md and auto memory, the “memory” term this quest sets beside session context.
Handoff Notes: it separates CLAUDE.md from auto memory, two of the things that carry knowledge across to a fresh session.
Which Instructions Apply: it says CLAUDE.md is context that advises, which is why the instructions file sits at the “advises” end of this quest.
Write an Instructions File: it covers CLAUDE.md placement, AGENTS.md and auto memory, and describes these as context that guides the agent.
Teach and Share the Load: it covers CLAUDE.md files a team can share, and notes they advise rather than enforce, which matters when teaching a lab shared rules.

KV Caching Explained: Hafedh Hichri (Hugging Face), article. Why read: a step-by-step picture of what the model stores and reuses for each token. It shows one attention head and does not cover the prompt cache. Cited in: The Context Window.
Best practices for Claude Code: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 12 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

When to Start Fresh: it gives the check-to-run habit and the rule to clear after repeated failed corrections, the trigger for starting fresh.
Capture Ideas Mid-Task: it covers when to clear after repeated failed corrections, the point where a new idea belongs in a fresh session instead of this one.
Spot Hallucinations: it recommends giving the agent a way to verify its work, the habit this quest turns into a check you run yourself.
Ground Truth: it says to give the agent a way to check its work; this quest’s check is one the agent did not write.
Keep a Paper Trail: it covers giving the agent a way to check its work and reviewing what it produces, the same instinct as checking a draft against ground truth.
Boss: Review Large Output: it says to give the agent a check to run, so you can read one pass or fail line instead of the whole wall of output.
Write the Brief: it explains why a brief needs a check the agent can run, and how to keep context and cost down.
Plan Before You Edit: it says when planning pays off and describes the interview-then-spec pattern.
Write an Instructions File: it shows what belongs in an instructions file and what to enforce another way.
Block Actions with a Hook: it says when to reach for a PreToolUse hook instead of an instruction.
Advice or Enforcement: it describes instructions as context and not as enforced configuration, which is this quest’s core split.
Boss: Review a Messy Session: it asks you to give the agent a check to run, the habit this whole fight rests on.

How Long Contexts Fail: Drew Breunig, blog, article. Why read: it names context poisoning and distraction, the failure modes behind starting fresh; a personal blog, not vendor documentation. Cited in: When to Start Fresh.
claude-code-usage-analysis: inevolin, repo. Why read: a community write-up of live runs that put numbers on cache expiry, compaction timing and tool changes; small samples, so read it for the shape of the effect and check its own list of limits. Cited in: When to Start Fresh.
Hooks reference: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 5 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Which Instructions Apply: it is the reference for the one control here that enforces, while the others ask; skim it to see what hooks can act on.
Write an Instructions File: hooks are the way to enforce a rule that an instructions file can only request.
Bundle a Plugin: hooks are the plugin part that runs code, so read this before trusting one.
Block Actions with a Hook: it lists the hook events, handler types and the exit-code rules, including exit 2 to block.
Advice or Enforcement: it documents how a hook blocks a tool call, the code-level lock.

Tool search tool: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is where Anthropic states a roughly 55k-token example for tool definitions and says tool selection degrades past 30 to 50 tools; it gives no method for either figure, so read them as Anthropic’s own claims about the API, with no independent measurement. Cited in: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents.
Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP: Anthropic, docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents: it explains how MCP tools load and how to scale or limit them in Claude Code.
Connect an MCP Server: it is the reference for adding HTTP and stdio servers and for the local, project and user scopes.

Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems: Kim et al., arXiv (2025), paper. Why read: it measures when extra agents help and when they hurt; a preprint, and its figures changed between versions. Cited in: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: Lewis and colleagues, arXiv, paper. Why read: it is the 2020 paper that named RAG, so you can see how much the common recipe has been simplified since. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Introducing Contextual Retrieval: Anthropic, article. Why read: it walks through the improved-RAG add-ons and states the 200,000-token rule of thumb for skipping RAG. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization: Edge and colleagues (Microsoft), paper. Why read: it explains the entity graph, communities and summaries, and discusses the indexing cost. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Guo and colleagues, paper. Why read: it shows how keyword-based retrieval over an entity graph differs from community summaries. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights: Han and colleagues, paper. Why read: it is an independent comparison with costs and a warning about order effects in LLM judges. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?: Li and colleagues (Google), paper. Why read: it compares RAG with putting everything in the prompt and proposes a hybrid. Cited in: RAG and Its Cousins.
Embeddings: Ollama, docs. Why read: it documents the /api/embed call the scripts use and says to embed documents and questions with the same model. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Structured outputs: Ollama, docs. Why read: it explains the format field with a JSON schema that makes fact extraction return usable JSON. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Context length: Ollama, docs. Why read: it gives the default context by memory size and how to check what loaded with ollama ps. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
LightRAG: HKUDS, repo. Why read: the README and docs give the Ollama wiring, the context and model-size requirements, and the storage defaults. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Get started with GraphRAG: Microsoft, docs. Why read: it lists the init, index and query commands and the warning about LLM cost. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Language model selection: Microsoft, docs. Why read: it is where the docs describe the JSON requirement and the problems seen with Ollama. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
When to use Graphs in RAG: Xiang and colleagues, paper. Why read: it studies which kinds of questions benefit from graphs, with token costs per method. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
Advanced RAG Techniques: Nir Diamant and contributors, repo. Why read: its notebook list includes graph RAG with a local Ollama model and LightRAG, plus chunking and evaluation, though we did not open the notebooks and the repo carries sponsor and book promotions. Cited in: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama.
LLM Wiki: Andrej Karpathy, GitHub gist, article. Why read: it is the original idea file, short enough to read in ten minutes, with the three layers, the three jobs and the Obsidian tips in the author’s own words. Cited in: Keep an LLM Wiki.

title: Lore library
text:
Sequence Maze

AI for Science, practice 7: provenance and citation: AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Cited by 2 quests; each quest says what to read it for.
Cited in:

Ground Truth: it covers citing by identifier, generating references with a deterministic tool, and disclosing agent use. A draft; it calls one of its own cited papers self-audited.
Keep a Paper Trail: it covers recording what a person did and what an agent did, which an analysis log does.

Documenting Architecture Decisions: Michael Nygard, Cognitect blog, article. Why read: it is the short original post behind ADRs, with the title, status, context, decision and consequences layout. Cited in: Keep a Paper Trail.
Architectural Decision Records: ADR GitHub organisation, docs. Why read: it defines an ADR and links to templates for writing one. Cited in: Keep a Paper Trail.

title: Agent Odyssey
text:
Meet the party
Four travellers share the long table. Choose the one closest to your own work: the choice is remembered, and it adds a little extra to some of the stories. The lessons are the same for everyone.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist



Research or project manager. The Guildmaster keeps the ledgers, lights the milestone beacons and rations the budget. Their guild runs on deadlines, and a pact promises roadmaps and status reports without waiting on anyone. They have watched a flawless-looking demo turn out to be nothing of the kind, so they know the difference between “it ran” and “it is done”.
Where your discipline matters most: the Gatehouse, the Scriptorium and the Cluster Citadel.



Bioinformatics analyst. The Diviner reads the signal in noisy data with trained hounds and a lens for ground truth: reference databases and controls. A pact offers literature summaries and analysis scripts in minutes. The Diviner knows how a fluent, flattering explanation can lead a tired mind to a conclusion that the primary sources never supported.
Where your discipline matters most: the Ancient DNA Crypt, the Sequence Maze and the Phylogenetic Forest.



Bioinformatics engineer. The Artificer builds with automata: scripts, pipelines and containers that do exactly what they were built to do. A pact could draft a workflow and its tests before the kettle boils. The Artificer has inherited a pile of code that nobody could explain, and will not add to it.
Where your discipline matters most: the Codon Mill, the Sequence Maze and the Pipeline Factory.



Data steward. The Archivist guards the vaults: raw data, checksums, ontologies and the metadata that makes a dataset findable. A pact can tidy a messy sample sheet in a moment. The Archivist knows the danger of a tidy table whose missing values were quietly invented, and keeps a ledger of every change.
Where your discipline matters most: the Gatehouse, the Biodiversity Reef and the Scriptorium.

If something fails

If the shell cannot find claude, add its folder to PATH: export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal. If it cannot find opencode or ollama, open a new terminal and try again.

title: Start Here
text: Agent Odyssey is a short role-playing course on using coding agents (LLM tools that read and run code for you) safely in bioinformatics work. You need no LLM experience, and nothing here asks you to use these tools. It shows how to use them with care if you choose to.

title: Start Here
text:
Who is who

The story uses a few names. The lessons themselves use plain technical words.

Shokanju: the umbrella word for every creature you can summon, from scripts to language models.
Automata: clockwork creatures. Scripts and pipelines: obedient, the same every time, and brittle when the road changes.
Familiars: creatures trained for one task. Classical machine-learning models.
Astrals: spirits that speak every tongue. Language models and the coding agents built on them. Generous, fast and unbound from physical reality, so they invent when unchecked.
The pact: summoning and binding an Astral, which is installing and starting a coding agent. The binding circle is the harness, the wards are permission rules and the sandbox, and the terms of the pact are the instructions file.
The Blight: plausible but false output that spreads when nobody checks it.

Clear the Murk. The final boss opens after the whole trunk and any 3 of the 8 branches.
Save your progress. It lives in this browser. Save code in the top bar copies a code, and Load code restores it elsewhere.

title: Name the Fears
text:
The boasters have gone to bed, and the corner by the hearth has grown loud. Brannoch the tinker lost his workshop, Sefa the scholar published a tree built on phantom citations, Tam the steward pasted restricted records into a chat, and Oleander the clerk shipped a demo that “ran fine”. Each was warned by the academics, and each was sure it would not happen to them. Every worry in the room has a habit that answers it. Name yours here, then go and meet the creatures.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster hears Oleander’s tale and checks that nothing leaves the guild unreviewed.


The Diviner winces at Sefa’s story, having once trusted a citation that did not exist.


The Artificer thinks of Brannoch’s workshop and counts the backups at home.


The Archivist watches Tam and tightens a grip on the key ring.

title: Name the Fears
text:
Where people start
Before you learn any habit, it helps to name the worry it answers. People come to these tools from different places:

Some are keen and want to know how to begin well.
Some are curious and want to see what is involved before deciding.
Some hold back, often for good reasons: the environmental cost of AI, harm to people and their work, or the quality of what comes out.

Every one of these starting points is reasonable, and nothing here asks you to use these tools. This course leaves the larger questions to you. It covers the practical worries that come with using an agent and gives each one a habit that makes the risk smaller. Whether you go on to use agents or decide to leave them alone, you will have a clear picture of what they ask of you.
An agent is a language model running inside a program that picks and runs tools (such as reading a file or running a command) in a loop toward a goal. A prompt is the text you send to the model. The rest of the course trains the habits below, and each row links to the lesson that teaches it.

About the output



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It makes things up.”
Check against something the agent did not write.
Sequence Maze


“It produces slop in bulk.”
Take small steps, test before code, keep a review budget.
Sequence Maze: Wall of Output


“I do not understand what it did.”
Ask for a changelog and explain it back.
Sequence Maze: Keep a Paper Trail



Slop is low-quality bulk output. A review budget means you only produce as much as you can honestly review in a day.


About the work and your data



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It could delete or overwrite my work.”
Undo with git, set permission rules, work on a scratch copy.
Ancient DNA Crypt


“It could leak my data or my secrets.”
Keep secrets and private data out of prompts; use an approved account or a local model.
Ancient DNA Crypt


“Someone could see my unpublished results and publish first.”
Read your tool’s data terms; keep unpublished work out of consumer chat tools.
Ancient DNA Crypt



A sandbox is a layer of the operating system that limits what commands can touch; it is one way to protect your files. A scratch copy is a duplicate you let the agent work on, so the original stays safe. For unpublished work, prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed or a local model, and record the date you made each result.


About you and the people around you



The worry
The habit
Where you learn it




“It will stop me learning.”
Write it first, predict before you look, ask it to explain.
Biodiversity Reef


“Someone else has to review all this.”
Review it yourself first, say you used an LLM, send small changes.
Biodiversity Reef


“It will feel hollow, as if it was not my work.”
Make the decisions, explain each step, keep a decision log.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everyone will expect work faster now.”
Say where the time goes; agree timelines that include review.
Biodiversity Reef


“Everything I write will sound the same.”
Draft in your own words first, then edit.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will spend my days checking drafts.”
Keep the question and interpretation; count checking as work.
Biodiversity Reef


“People will think I am lazy or unoriginal.”
Say what the agent did and what you checked.
Biodiversity Reef


“I will stop trusting my own judgement.”
Decide first, then ask for a second opinion.
Biodiversity Reef



For voice and judgement, use the agent for structure and checks, and keep a few decisions agent-free. For credit and workload, follow your team’s norm, credit the agent’s part openly and share how long checking took.
Sometimes the right answer is to skip the LLM. The next lesson shows how to tell when.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text: In a corner of Gaia’s Rest, four travellers each picture what a pact with an Astral could do for them, and then the doubts arrive. The boasters at the bar say you cross the stream at the Astral’s side or you stay on the bank. Beside the water a stone shows, and another beyond it, each a little further out, and you may stop on any of them. Before you step, you ask what you would carry across with you.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
The scene
Four people want help from an LLM (a large language model, the kind of tool behind chat assistants). Each pictures what it could do, and then the same two worries arrive: where their data would go, and whether using an LLM means giving a program the run of their computer.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


“I keep twelve projects in one spreadsheet. If an LLM could read it, I would have a status report and a risk list for the board by lunch.”
“But where does my data go once I paste it? And a colleague said I would need Claude Code (a coding agent that can read and change files on my computer), which means giving it access to all my files. I cannot allow that, so I will keep writing the report by hand.”


“The sample counts fell in two cohorts. If an LLM could write the query and the first summary, I would have an explanation before the meeting.”
“But the samples database holds participant codes, and my data agreement is strict. Does using an LLM mean installing an agent that can reach the database? Then the answer has to be no LLM at all.”


“Our pipeline has a script nobody has tested. If an LLM could draft the tests and tidy the module, I would clear this week’s backlog by Friday.”
“But an agent that edits files and runs commands in my repository could overwrite something, or run something I never reviewed. It is all or nothing, and nothing feels safer.”


“A collaborator sent a sample sheet with mixed columns and units. If an LLM could clean it and map it to our schema, a week of tidying would take an afternoon.”
“But the sheet holds controlled health metadata. I cannot paste it anywhere, and I do not want an agent loose in the data store. So it is a no.”



All four treat the choice as all or nothing: either no LLM, or an agent with the run of the machine. They have not considered that there is a middle. Between those two ends are several steps, each handing over a little more, and many useful tasks sit on the lower ones. This lesson walks up those steps.
You decide how much to hand over before the first prompt. A wrong choice can send data you meant to keep, or let an agent change files you meant to leave alone.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Two questions

What leaves your machine? A hosted model runs on the provider’s servers, so anything you type, paste or upload is sent there, and so is anything an agent reads. A local model runs on your computer and keeps prompts there, though an agent’s web or tool calls can still reach out.
What may the agent do? Produce text, read files, edit files, or run commands.

Question 1 is about data leaving. Question 2 is about changes on your machine. They vary independently:

A chat window with a pasted table: it can only write text, so little can change on your machine, but the whole table is sent.
A local model in an agent with access to your files: nothing is sent to a provider, but it can edit files and run commands.

The more data leaves, the higher the first answer. The more the agent may change, the higher the second.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
The ladder
A ladder is six ordered steps of how much you hand over. Each step up raises one or both answers. Terms used in the table: a schema is the list of table and column names with no rows; an extract is a small slice of the data; an agent is a model that reads files and runs commands for you; a copy is a duplicate of the data, so the original cannot be edited.








Step
What you hand over
What leaves




0
Nothing: do the task yourself
nothing


1
A question in words, with no data in it
your words


2
Structure only: headings, a schema or invented rows. You apply the answer yourself
names and invented rows


3
A small extract you are allowed to share, or a local model
the extract; nothing if local


4
A read-only agent (plan mode: it reads and proposes, and does not edit) working on a copy
everything it reads


5
An agent that edits files and runs commands
everything it reads, plus whatever its commands send



Pasting the results of a step 2 task back into the chat sends those rows too, which makes it step 3. Plan mode (the agent reads and proposes, and does not edit) belongs to step 4: a copy protects the original from edits, and anything the agent reads is still sent.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Three questions before any step

What kind of data is it? The table gives a typical starting point. Your agreement and your data steward decide, and they can be stricter. A data steward is the person at your organisation who looks after data rules.
Which account will you use? Consumer and organisation accounts have different terms (next section).
What leaves at this step? Say it in one sentence before you press enter.








Kind of data
Typical starting point




Public or published
Any step


Internal, not personal
Steps 1 to 3; 4 to 5 on an approved account, on a copy


Personal, including pseudonymised codes (codes that replace names)
Steps 0 to 2, invented rows only


Health, genetic or otherwise controlled
Steps 0 to 2, unless your agreement says otherwise in writing



Under GDPR (the EU data-protection law), pseudonymised codes still count as personal data. Small counts can single people out, so check your policy before pasting results for rare groups.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
What a chat window keeps

Training: consumer accounts (Free, Pro, Max) have a setting that lets chats improve the models; with it on, data may be kept for up to 5 years. The setting is in your privacy settings.
Account type: commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise and the API, which is programmatic access billed per use) are not used for training unless the organisation opts in. The API deletes inputs and outputs within 30 days by default. Team and Enterprise keep saved chats until they are deleted, then remove them within 30 days. Ask your administrator which applies.
Deleted chats: they leave the provider’s storage within 30 days.
Incognito chats: not used for training, and still kept for 30 days by default. Flagged chats can be kept longer.
Screenshots, images and uploads: treat them as data you share, like pasted text.
Other providers: their chat tools have their own terms. Read them.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Hands-on: pick the step
For each task, decide three things before you open the answer: the lowest step that does the job, what leaves your machine at that step, and one thing you will check in the result. The tabs hold the same four people, and the tab you chose earlier stays selected.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


Task: a one-page status summary and risk list for twelve projects, from a spreadsheet of project names, milestone dates, owner names and status. The data is internal, and owner names are personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2. Paste only the column headings and three invented rows. Ask for an outline of the summary and a formula that counts open milestones per project. Apply both to the real sheet yourself. Only the headings and the invented rows leave. Step 3 would send real rows with owner names, which needs an approved account and your steward’s agreement.
To check: count the open milestones of one project by hand and compare.



Task: explain why the sample count per project fell between two cohorts, from a samples database that holds participant codes under a strict agreement. Pseudonymised codes still count as personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2. Share the schema only and ask for one read-only query. Run it yourself. The table and column names leave, so decide first whether even the names are fine to send, and drop to step 0 if your agreement says they are not. Pasting the results back into the chat would make it step 3.
To check: write a second, simpler count query yourself and compare the two numbers before you explain anything.



Task: write tests for a script that reads sample sheets in your pipeline repository. The code is internal and holds no personal data.


Check your answer

The answer is step 3. Paste the one function (a small allowed extract) and ask for tests. Apply them yourself. Only that function’s code leaves. If you later want an agent to run the tests inside the repository, that is step 5: work on a copy, keep a way to undo, and limit what the agent may do first.
To check: break the function on purpose and confirm that a test fails.



Task: clean and map a sample sheet with controlled health metadata to your schema, under an agreement that forbids sharing the values.


Check your answer

The answer is step 2 at most. Describe the mess in words, give headings and invented rows that copy it, and ask for a validation and mapping script. Run the script locally on the real sheet. Do not ask a model to fill or harmonise the values itself: it can invent plausible ones. Only the headings and the invented rows leave.
To check: compare row counts and a checksum before and after, and keep a log of every change.




Now take your own task. Write the three answers in a sentence each, then ask your data steward the question at the end of the next section if any of them is unclear.

title: Choose What to Hand Over
section: Climbing, if and when you want to
text:
Climbing, if and when you want to

Move up a step when the lower step cannot do the task and you can say what leaves.
Before steps 4 and 5, work on a copy, keep a way to undo, and limit what the agent may do.
For personal or controlled data, a local model (step 3) is allowed only where your agreement says so.
If you pasted something you should not have, stop and tell your data steward.
Ask your steward: “I want to use [tool, account type] at step [n]. What leaves is [what]. Is that allowed for [data kind]?”

title: Choose What to Hand Over
text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

Is my data used for model training? (consumer): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the page that says the training setting exists for Free, Pro and Max chats, which decides your first account question.
How long do you store my data?: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it gives the 5-year and 30-day figures for consumer chats and what happens after you delete one.
How long do you store my organization’s data?: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it is the commercial-account counterpart: the API’s 30-day default, how saved chats are kept and deleted, and the cases that keep data longer.
Use incognito chats: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows what incognito does and does not change, so you do not over-trust the name.
Data usage (Claude Code): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it states that the agent sends prompts and outputs over the network, which is what makes steps 4 and 5 different from running a query yourself.
Ollama FAQ: Ollama, docs. Why read: it says local runs do not send prompts to Ollama and separates its cloud models, which matters if you choose a local model for sensitive data.
AI for Science: the short version: AI for Science, article. Why read: a one-page European summary of research practices, useful for a conversation with your data steward. It describes itself as a living record and shows no endorsements.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Your home directory lies on ground that hundreds of others can reach. Keys, tokens and settings lie there too, in plain files, and your Astral trots through them as if the ground were its own. Shared ground has many passers-by. Before it works here, find out who can read what it leaves behind.
You need this before you run an agent under your cluster account: keys and agent settings live in ordinary files, and on a shared cluster other people may be able to read them. It covers Claude Code only, and keeping them private and keeping data within its agreement. Ask your cluster staff before sending any cluster data to an external model API, and follow your institution’s data agreement. Step 1 below checks your cluster home, so run it on the cluster. Steps 2 and 3 are safe to practise on your laptop.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
What lives where
Claude Code keeps sessions, settings and plugins in the folder ~/.claude. It also writes the file ~/.claude.json, which holds account details, MCP configuration (the list of external tool servers you connected) and trust decisions. The environment variable CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR moves the ~/.claude folder elsewhere.
If your home directory is shared across nodes, session history sits on shared storage and can contain pasted data or paths. Three commands check and fix this.

Check who can read the folder:
ls -ld ~/.claude
Safe looks like drwx------: only you can read, write or enter the folder. Any r or x in the last six characters lets a group or other users in. Fix it with chmod 700 ~/.claude.
Practise the key-file mode on a throwaway file. In a scratch folder, make a stand-in file and lock it to you:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch/keys-demo && cd ~/odyssey-scratch/keys-demo && touch demo_key && chmod 600 demo_key && ls -l demo_key
ls -l shows -rw------- at the start of the line: you can read and write the file and nobody else can.
Block the agent’s file-read tool from your SSH keys. Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json (merge it with any permissions block you already have):
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(~/.ssh/**)"]
  }
}
Read(...) is the rule for the file-read tool. ~/ anchors the path at your home directory, and ** matches everything below .ssh.

Two settings files are yours to control: user ~/.claude/settings.json (all your projects) and project .claude/settings.json (commit it for the team). Managed settings (settings an organisation sets for everyone) override both, so your site may already have decided some of this.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Keys

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, when set, overrides a subscription login. In -p mode (one prompt, no interactive session) it is always used, and interactive mode asks you once to approve it. If a key is exported in a shared profile, the key in use may not be the one you expect.
Never put a key in a script or in a committed .claude/settings.json. On a shared account, use a per-user key kept in a file readable only by you (mode 600, as in step 2), and keep a lab-wide key out of shared directories.
The sandbox’s default reads cover most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials. The sandbox is the restricted environment Claude Code runs shell commands in. To block key files, add the Read(...) deny rule from step 3 and the sandbox.filesystem.denyRead setting (a list of paths the sandbox hides from shell commands). The sandbox covers shell commands only, so you need both.

apiKeyHelper is a Claude Code setting that runs a shell script you provide and uses the key it returns, so the key need not sit in a file. For OpenCode, read your version’s docs on where it stores keys before you use it on a shared account.

title: Keys on Shared Ground
text:
Data and egress

Before any cluster data, paths, logs or code go to an external model API, check your institution’s policy. Human genomic, clinical or controlled-access data often has agreements that forbid third-party processing.
Reading files inside the working directory is approved without asking, so the agent can read a project folder that holds controlled data unless a Read(...) deny rule or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead covers it. Keep controlled data off every path the agent can reach: outside its working directory, or under a Read deny rule and sandbox.filesystem.denyRead. Give the agent synthetic or de-identified test data.
Some sites restrict internet access from compute nodes, so an agent there may not reach a model API. Ask staff what outbound access your jobs have. A common pattern is the agent on your laptop writing scripts, with jobs running offline.
The sandbox’s network.allowedDomains starts empty, so a shell command that reaches an unlisted host prompts you. The sandbox does not cover file tools, MCP servers or hooks.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


If your project has an instruction file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) stricter than these notes, the stricter one wins, and your cluster’s policy outranks both. Ask staff these before use: is an external model API allowed for my data, which tools are allowed on login nodes, what outbound access exists, and where are my home and scratch backed up and who can read them? For restricted networks, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 turns off auto-updates, telemetry, error reporting and feedback traffic.


The same questions apply. Ask staff whether a local model through Ollama changes what your data agreement requires, and whether running one on a login node is allowed, since models are heavy.

Bonus

Find your cluster’s AI or acceptable-use policy (or ask the staff whether one exists). Write down in your own notes what it says about external model APIs, local models, and which data classes are covered.

Configure the sandboxed Bash tool: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it states the sandbox reads most of the machine, including ~/.ssh, unless you deny it, and it fails open by default.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
In a back room the miller strings yarn between pegs: one peg for each name, one thread for each link. It takes a long time, and every knot is worth checking, because an Astral that follows one wrongly tied thread does so with confidence. A traveller asks whether the web finds answers that a plain search misses. You will build a small one and test that.
You need this exercise before you pay for a graph tool: it tests whether a graph answers a question that plain lookup misses, using notes small enough to check by hand. It runs on Ollama (a program that runs language models on your own machine). Three terms first:

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Set up
mini-rag holds ollama_min.py (two helpers), rag.py (simple RAG), graph.py (a hand-made graph RAG) and notes/ (twelve short mock notes, 233 words in all). Save the folder anywhere. It sits at exercises/codon-mill/mini-rag in the course repository, so a clone of the course already has it. If neither works, ask your agent to recreate it from the descriptions below.
Pull an embedding model (it turns text into vectors for search) and pick a chat model. ollama pull <name> downloads a model; wait for it to finish. The run below used the tag gemma4:12b-mlx. Any chat model on your machine works: run ollama list to see what you have, or pull another and use its name.
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
export CHAT_MODEL=gemma4:12b-mlx      # or any chat model from `ollama list`
cd mini-rag
The scripts read three environment variables: CHAT_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL (default nomic-embed-text) and OLLAMA_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:11434). Ollama’s default context window is small, so the scripts send each request with num_ctx (the context window size in tokens) set to 8192. You do not have to restart the server.
Open notes/ and read a few. They are fictional: two sequencers (Orion and Vega), two projects (Heron and Kelp), two pipeline releases, and some distractors such as the lunch rota. One question needs a chain of four hops: Project Heron studies samples S31 to S36, run R7 loaded those samples, run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, and release 2.3 has a known bug.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 1: simple RAG
rag.py is simple RAG in about thirty lines.
python3 rag.py "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
With the default -k 3 the run printed:
Retrieved:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt

Answer:
The notes do not contain the answer.
The notes that hold the answer were in the folder, but the run log that connects Heron’s samples to pipeline 2.3 ranked fourth. Try -k 5:
  0.668  pipeline-2-4.txt
  0.653  pipeline-2-3.txt
  0.644  project-heron.txt
  0.549  run-r7.txt
  0.528  run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because the primary analysis of run R7 used pipeline release 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.
Then try --all, which skips retrieval and pastes every note into the prompt. It also gave a correct answer. With twelve short notes, the window holds everything.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 2: build the graph
graph.py build sends each note to the chat model and asks for (subject, relation, object) facts. It uses Ollama’s structured outputs: the request carries a JSON schema (a description of the JSON shape wanted: JSON is a text format of keys and values) in the format field, so the reply has the shape the script expects. The helper also sets temperature to 0 (the model picks its most likely word each time, so output varies little).
python3 graph.py build
python3 graph.py show
The run printed saved 67 facts, and the build took 1 minute 20 seconds for twelve notes. A sample of what show printed:
Run R7 --loaded onto--> Orion    [run-r7.txt]
Run R7 --used--> Pipeline 2.3    [run-r7.txt]
Pipeline 2.3 --has bug--> double-counts duplicate reads    [pipeline-2-3.txt]
Project Heron --studies--> S31    [project-heron.txt]
Orion --looked after by--> Dana Okafor    [orion.txt]
You --bring--> own cup    [lunch.txt]
Read the whole list. Most facts match their notes. Two did not: the lunch note produced You --bring--> own cup, which is not a fact about anything in the lab, and one name came back with a stray leading space, which would split a single entity into two nodes (the script now strips names when it loads them). Extraction is a model’s reading of your text, so a graph is a second thing to check. Every fact carries the note it came from, so you can.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Step 3: ask the graph
graph.py ask does three things. It finds starting entities (names that appear in the question, plus the three closest by embedding). It walks outward two hops along the links. Then it hands the collected facts and their source notes to the model.
python3 graph.py ask "Does project Heron need to re-analyse its data because of a known pipeline bug?"
Starting entities: ['pipeline 2.3', 'pipeline 2.4', 'project heron']
Collected 40 facts from 8 notes: freezers.txt, meeting-march.txt, pipeline-2-3.txt, pipeline-2-4.txt, project-heron.txt, project-kelp.txt, run-r7.txt, run-r8.txt

Answer:
Yes, Project Heron needs to re-analyse its data because Run R7, which loaded the samples for Project Heron (S31 to S36), used Pipeline 2.3, which has a known bug that double-counts duplicate reads.

Notes used:
- [pipeline-2-3.txt]
- [project-heron.txt]
- [run-r7.txt]
The wording of the answer differs a little from run to run even at temperature 0, so yours will not match word for word.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
What we saw
With gemma4:12b-mlx for chat and nomic-embed-text for embeddings:

Simple RAG missed at k=3 and succeeded at k=5. The run log was not among the top three notes. Raising k fixed it, at the price of more text in the prompt.
Putting everything in the prompt also worked, because the collection is tiny.
The graph walk reached the run log without a bigger k, because the link from Heron’s samples to run R7 is an edge. It also pulled in 40 of the 67 facts and 8 of the 12 notes. A bigger collection needs a smaller hop count or a ranking step.
The graph took a minute and twenty seconds to build for 233 words and needs a model good enough to extract facts. Embedding twelve notes for simple RAG takes seconds. Build cost grows with the size of the collection, and Microsoft’s Graph RAG paper describes indexing a large corpus as slow.
A whole-collection question failed in all three setups. “Who works in this group, and what does each person do?” got “the notes do not contain the answer” from simple RAG, --all and the graph walk. No note lists a roster. Microsoft’s Graph RAG builds community summaries for such questions; this toy graph builds none.

One question, one model, one run: this shows the mechanics and does not rank the methods or the models.
Try your own questions and compare.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
A second model: Mistral’s Ministral 3
Swapping the chat model is a one-line change (export CHAT_MODEL=...). ministral-3:8b from Mistral is 6.0 GB on Ollama, supports tools and has an Apache 2.0 licence. Retrieval is the same, since the embedding model is the same. The graph is rebuilt by the new model, so its walk differs: 25 facts from 7 notes, against 40 facts from 8 notes with gemma4:12b-mlx.








Setup
gemma4:12b-mlx
ministral-3:8b




Simple RAG, -k 3
“The notes do not contain the answer.”
Not enough information in the notes.


Simple RAG, -k 5
Yes, re-analysis needed (correct).
No (wrong): says R7 used release 2.4.


--all (every note pasted)
Correct.
Lists the right facts, then No (wrong).


Graph walk
Yes (correct).
Collects the R7 and 2.3 facts, then No (wrong).


Whole-collection question
Not answered.
Not answered.



In the --all run, ministral-3:8b listed R7 using 2.3, which has the bug, then answered No because “no re-analysis was done”. In the -k 5 run it misread the release: the note says 2.3.
The graph build with ministral-3:8b took about a minute, saved 80 facts and returned valid JSON for all twelve notes. show printed a few odd entries: Pipeline 2.3 --has issue fix--> Dana Okafor, a node called Pipeline 2.3 issue, and a User node taken from the safety note. Read show against the notes yourself.
With this model, the right passages reached the prompt in three setups and the final answer was still wrong. Retrieval is one half of the job and the reader model is the other half. Read the notes the answer names and see whether they say what the answer says. Test a model on a few questions whose answers you know before you trust it on new ones.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
A note on model size
We did not run LightRAG or Microsoft GraphRAG here; this section summarises what their documentation asks of an Ollama setup. Extraction asks a model to produce well-formed JSON for every chunk. With Ollama, Microsoft GraphRAG users “frequently see issues with malformed responses (especially JSON)”. The LightRAG README calls Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct (a 30B-parameter model) “a reasonable minimum” for local use, and its programming guide says at least 32B. The 12B model here produced valid JSON for all twelve notes, and show lets you judge the facts. If you try a model under about 7B, read the triples before you trust the answers.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
section: Using a real tool with Ollama
text:
Using a real tool with Ollama
graph.py is a teaching toy. Two real projects do this at scale. Check their current docs before you rely on the details below.
LightRAG (github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG):

Install pip install "lightrag-hku[api]" (the README also shows uv), copy env.example to .env, and run lightrag-server.
For Ollama, the project’s guide wires ollama_model_complete for chat and ollama_embed for embeddings.
LightRAG requires at least 32k context tokens, and Ollama’s default is smaller. Set num_ctx to 32768 in code or in a Modelfile. For the server, set OLLAMA_LLM_NUM_CTX in .env. The default context is 4k on machines under 24 GiB of video memory, so check with ollama ps.
Use a non-thinking model for extraction. Models slower than about 50 tokens per second may time out on dense chunks.
Pick your embedding model before indexing and keep it. EMBEDDING_DIM must equal the model’s output size (the guide uses 768 for nomic-embed-text). Changing the model later means re-embedding everything.
The default storage is in-memory files meant for small tests.
Server safety: lightrag-server binds to all network interfaces with authentication off by default. On a laptop or shared machine, set HOST=127.0.0.1 before you start it.

Microsoft GraphRAG (microsoft.github.io/graphrag):

The commands are graphrag init, graphrag index and graphrag query "..." --method local (or global). Text files go in input/.
It can consume a lot of LLM resources. Start with the small tutorial dataset and cheaper models.
It calls models through LiteLLM and requires structured JSON output. Users put Ollama behind a proxy and report frequent malformed responses. Check the current docs for an Ollama setup.
Check that the embedding vector size in its settings matches your embedding model’s (nomic-embed-text gives 768).

If you later build a graph over your own notes, try a tiny folder of mock files first and read the facts it extracted before pointing it at anything real.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Verify the graph
A confident answer built on a wrong link is the failure to look for. A graph gives you a list of facts, each with its source note, to check.

Read the extracted facts for a few notes against the notes themselves. Count the wrong ones.
Ask the agent or the script to name the notes behind each answer, then open them.
Keep a short list of questions whose answers you know, and run it after you change the model, the prompt or the notes.
Keep real and controlled data out of this exercise. The same scripts pointed at a hosted model send every note to that provider.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Choose your setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Ask Claude Code to read graph.py and explain the walk in ask, then predict what changes if you set hops=1 before you run it. Running the scripts needs your approval for each shell command. These notes are mock data, so sending them to a hosted model is fine for this exercise. Check your data agreement before a hosted agent reads your own unpublished notes.


The scripts talk to Ollama directly, so any agent can run them. If you use OpenCode with the Pet, ask it to explain the code and change hops.

title: Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama
text:
Battle: the graph




Run python3 graph.py show and write down one fact that is wrong or odd, and the note it came from.


Change hops=2 to hops=1 in graph.py, predict what happens to the Heron answer, then run it and compare.
