title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text: A scribe in the mill keeps a ledger that tidies itself. Each new sack of papers is read once, and every page it touches is updated and cross-linked before the scribe sleeps. In the morning the ledger looks perfect, and you cannot tell which entries the scribe checked and which it merely smoothed over. Learn how it is built and where it can mislead you.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
section: The problem: understanding that does not accumulate
text:
The problem: understanding that does not accumulate
Think about the last time you read ten papers on a method, or went through six months of meeting notes. You understood it all at the time. A month later, the understanding lives in your head and in a pile of files, and the next question sends you back to the pile.
You need this lesson now to judge whether a wiki suits your material before you build one. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) answers that with a lookup: each question searches the pile again, pastes a few passages into the prompt, and starts from scratch. Nothing builds up between questions. If an answer needs five documents stitched together, the stitching is redone every time.
This quest follows Andrej Karpathy’s “LLM Wiki” gist (a short shared text page), which proposes another arrangement. An agent keeps a wiki: a folder of interlinked Markdown pages (plain text files with simple formatting) that it writes and updates as new sources arrive, so the stitching is done once and stays. The gist calls it a “persistent, compounding artifact”. People drop their notes because the bookkeeping is tedious (updating links, rewriting summaries, spotting that two pages now disagree), and an agent does that bookkeeping without getting bored. You keep the parts that need a person: choosing sources, asking questions, and deciding what the findings mean.
The gist is an “idea file”, meant to be handed to your agent so the two of you work out the details together. It describes a pattern and includes no program.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Three layers

Raw sources: you add files and nobody edits them afterwards. Papers, clipped web pages, meeting transcripts, run logs, data files. The agent reads them and never changes them, so they stay the source of truth.
The wiki: the agent writes it and you read it. Markdown pages: a summary per source, a page per entity (a tool, a dataset, a person, a gene) or concept, comparisons, an overview. The agent owns this folder.
The schema: here, “schema” means the rules for the wiki, written as plain instructions. You and the agent write it over time. It is one instruction file (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code, AGENTS.md in OpenCode) that the agent reads at the start of every session. It describes how the wiki is organised and what to do on each job, and it is the key configuration file.

The split builds trust. When an answer looks odd, you walk from the wiki page back to the raw source it cites, and the raw source is untouched.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Three jobs

Ingest (take a new source into the wiki): copy one source into raw/, then ask the agent, for example, “Ingest raw/paper-1.md following the rules in CLAUDE.md.” The agent reads the source, tells you the main takeaways, writes a summary page, updates the pages for the entities and concepts it mentions, adds it to the index, and appends a line to the log. One source may touch 10 to 15 pages. Ingest one source at a time and stay involved. Batching with less supervision is possible.
Query: you ask a question. The agent finds the relevant wiki pages, reads them and answers with citations. A good answer (a comparison table, a timeline, a short report) is filed back as a new page, so your explorations add to the wiki and do not vanish into chat history.
Lint: from time to time you ask for a health check. It looks for pages that contradict each other, claims that a newer source has overtaken, pages that nothing links to, concepts that are mentioned but have no page, missing cross-references, and gaps that a web search might fill.

Two small files keep the wiki navigable:

index.md: a catalogue with each page, a link and a one-line summary, grouped by category and updated on every ingest. To answer a question, the agent reads the index first and then opens the pages that look relevant. The gist says this avoids building an embedding index at moderate scale (the author’s experience). As the wiki grows, add a search tool.
log.md: an append-only diary of ingests, queries and lint passes. Give every entry the same prefix so a simple grep can list the recent ones.

An example schema. Paste it into the instruction file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md) in the wiki folder’s top level, then edit it with your agent:
# Wiki rules
- `raw/` holds sources. Never edit or delete anything in `raw/`.
- `wiki/` holds pages you write. One page per entity or concept; one summary page per source in `wiki/sources/`.
- Every claim on a wiki page ends with a link to the source file it came from. If no source supports it, mark it `(unsourced)`.
- On ingest: read the source, tell me the three main takeaways and wait for my reply, then write the summary page, update affected pages, update `wiki/index.md`, and append `## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | <title>` to `wiki/log.md`.
- On lint: list contradictions, unsourced claims, orphan pages and missing pages. Do not fix anything until I say which.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
section: Why you might want this, and what it costs
text:
Why you might want this, and what it costs

Paste everything into the prompt: fits small collections and needs no setup. You pay in repeated reading each session and a limit at the window size.
RAG: fits a large, changing pile where particular passages answer each question. Each question starts from scratch, multi-document answers are re-stitched, and retrieval misses are silent.
A wiki the agent maintains: fits material you will return to for weeks or months, where understanding should accumulate and be readable. You pay agent time and tokens on every ingest, you get a layer of text that can contain mistakes, and you spend review time.
Notes you write yourself: fit things you want to think through in your own words. This is a perfectly good choice, and the wiki pays off when the bookkeeping is what stops you.

A wiki and search can sit together: a wiki is a good home for the stable understanding, and RAG or search is a good way to reach the raw sources behind it.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Use cases you may recognise
The gist lists personal, research, reading a book, team, competitive analysis, due diligence, trip planning, course notes and hobby deep-dives. Here are some closer to a bioinformatics desk.

Literature on one method (say, long-read assemblers or variant callers)

Raw sources: papers, preprints, tool docs.
Pages: one per tool and dataset, a comparison table, a page of open disagreements.
A question: “Which papers compare tool A and B on the same data, and do they agree?”
Watch out: preprints mixed with peer-reviewed papers. Ask the agent to record the kind of source on every page.

The lab’s pipeline handbook

Raw sources: release notes, run logs, meeting minutes, Slack exports.
Pages: one per pipeline release, one per known issue, a decision log.
A question: “Which runs used release 2.3, and what was wrong with it?”
Watch out: private or unpublished material. Exact counts belong to a query tool.

A thesis or long project

Raw sources: papers you read, notes on experiments, supervisor meeting notes.
Pages: a running thesis page, an open-questions page, one page per experiment.
A question: “What did I conclude about batch effects in March, and what has changed since?”
Watch out: a wiki that you never open. You will not remember what you did not read.

A course, a workshop or onboarding

Raw sources: slides, lecture notes, tutorials, tool docs.
Pages: glossary, one page per concept, a “things that confused me” page.
A question: “Explain the difference between X and Y using only what the course covered.”
Watch out: material for fast-moving tools goes stale. Date every source.

Reference notes for the tools you use

Raw sources: docs pages, GitHub issues, your own gotchas.
Pages: one per tool with versions, quirks and a link to the source.
A question: “What did we learn the last time this tool ran out of memory?”
Watch out: version drift. Record the version on each page and re-check on upgrade.

A book or a long series

Raw sources: chapters, episode notes.
Pages: characters, themes, a timeline, built up as you read.
A question: “Where did this thread first appear?”
Watch out: spoilers for yourself. Ingest as you read.


To size your own idea, answer four questions in a sentence each:

What sources would go in?
How often do they change?
What question would I ask in a month that I cannot answer quickly today?
Who may read these sources, and where may they be sent?

If the sources fit in one prompt, try that first. If the question is an exact filter or count, ask a query tool. If the sources are sensitive and you would send them to a hosted model, settle your data rules before you begin. If the material is something you want to return to and the answers need several sources joined, the wiki is a good candidate.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Where Obsidian fits
Obsidian is a free note-taking app that opens a folder of Markdown files as a vault. A vault is an ordinary folder, so an agent can read and write it like any other folder, and Obsidian shows whatever is there. Work with the agent on one side and Obsidian open on the other: “Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase.” You read, and the agent edits.
A layout that follows the three layers:
my-vault/
  raw/            sources you add (clippings, PDFs, transcripts); the agent never edits these
    assets/       downloaded images
  wiki/           pages the agent writes
    index.md
    log.md
    sources/  entities/  concepts/
  CLAUDE.md       the schema (or AGENTS.md)
Obsidian tools that help:

Web Clipper: a browser extension that turns a web article into a Markdown file, so a source can land in raw/ in one click.
Graph view: shows the shape of the wiki, with hubs and orphan pages that nothing links to. It doubles as a quick visual check.
Dataview: a plugin (an add-on) that queries the properties (named fields in a block at the top of a page). If your schema asks the agent to add them (a source type, a date, a version), you get live tables, such as every page whose status is unsourced.
Marp: a Markdown slide format with an Obsidian plugin, for turning an answer into slides. Skip it unless you need slides.
Images: fix the attachment folder (for example raw/assets/) and bind a hotkey that downloads a clipped page’s images locally. An agent cannot read a Markdown file with inline images in a single pass, so have it read the text first and look at the images afterwards.

Habits that help:

Separate folders: keep the agent’s folder apart from the notes you write by hand. Your own words stay yours, and you can tell at a glance what the agent produced.
Git: put the vault under git and commit before each ingest. A commit per ingest gives you a readable diff of what the agent changed and an undo.
Read-only sources: make raw/ read-only if your tools allow it. The instruction file is advice the agent can ignore, while file permissions are enforced by the system.
Any editor: if you do not use Obsidian, any editor that opens a folder of Markdown files works.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
What can go wrong

A mistake becomes a fact. If the agent misreads a source, the error lands on a page, and later pages cite that page. The cost grows with each ingest. Require a source link on every claim, skim the diff of every ingest, and use lint to hunt for unsourced claims. One source at a time makes the skimming practical.
The agent edits what it should only read. Keep sources immutable and check it with git.
Clipped pages can carry instructions. A web page you clip may contain text aimed at your agent, and the agent reads it during ingest and then writes files. Review the diff, restrict what the agent may run, and keep an agent with write access away from sources you do not trust.
Sources leave your machine. With a hosted model, every source you ingest is sent as prompt text. For unpublished results, patient-linked data or anything under an agreement, check the rules first. A local model through Ollama keeps text on your machine, but ingest asks for reading, summarising and editing several files in one go. Try one short, harmless source first.
Cost and time grow with the wiki. Each ingest reads the index and several pages, and then writes several. Watch your usage in the first week.
Scale. As the wiki grows, add search or another layer on top of the index.
You may not learn it. A wiki you never open does little for your own understanding. Read it, correct it and argue with it.
Exact answers. Counts, filters and joins over tables belong in a query tool.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Choose your setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Put the schema in CLAUDE.md at the root of the wiki folder. Start a session there, and ask the agent to read the schema and propose the folder layout before it writes anything. For the first ingest, ask for a plan and approve it before the agent writes. Tighten the schema with whatever you correct. Keep ingest, query and lint as separate short sessions, since the wiki itself is the memory that carries over.


Put the schema in AGENTS.md at the root of the wiki folder (OpenCode also falls back to CLAUDE.md). With a local model, start with a handful of short, non-sensitive sources and check each page against its source, because a small model is more likely to drop or garble details. If a model struggles with the multi-file edit, ask it to do the ingest in steps: summary page first, then one entity page at a time.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Battle: the wiki




Answer the four sizing questions for one real collection of yours (sources, how often they change, the question you will ask in a month, who may read them and where they may be sent). Write one sentence saying whether a wiki, RAG, a single prompt or a query tool fits best.


Draft a schema (instruction file) of five lines or fewer for that collection: what the agent must never edit, what every claim must carry, and what it must ask you before writing. Do not run it yet; read it aloud to a colleague and see what they would add.

title: Keep an LLM Wiki
text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

LLM Wiki: Andrej Karpathy, GitHub gist, article. Why read: it is the original idea file, short enough to read in ten minutes, with the three layers, the three jobs and the Obsidian tips in the author’s own words.
Effective context engineering for AI agents: Anthropic Engineering, article. Why read: it describes the opposite habit of loading information just in time with search tools, which helps you decide when a pre-built wiki is worth the upkeep.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text: Travellers keep asking the miller about books that will never fit in the hopper. An Astral sent to fetch an answer from the whole library came back with the wrong shelf and total confidence. Some say to fetch a few pages when a question comes, some to draw a web of names, and some to fetch nothing at all. Before choosing, learn what each way fetches and what it misses.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Why anyone brings RAG up
This quest helps you pick a method before you build anything, because each method costs time and can fail in a different way. A model knows what it learned in training. It has not read your lab’s protocols, last month’s run logs or the paper that came out last week. You can paste documents into the prompt, but the context window (the text the model can see at once) is finite, and a long prompt costs money and time.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is the idea of looking things up first. A program searches your documents for the passages most likely to matter, pastes only those into the prompt, and asks the model to answer from them. The name comes from a 2020 paper that paired a generator with a vector index of Wikipedia. The recipe most people mean today is a later, simpler version of that idea.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Simple RAG in four steps

Chunk. Split the documents into pieces (a chunk is one passage, often a paragraph or a few hundred words).
Embed. An embedding model turns each chunk into a vector (a long list of numbers; texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions). The vectors are stored in an index.
Retrieve. Embed the question the same way, then fetch the k chunks whose vectors are closest (k is a number you pick, such as 3 or 5).
Generate. Paste those chunks into the prompt and ask the model to answer from them and to say which chunk it used.

Papers and PDFs hold tables, figures and two-column text, and a plain text extractor can scramble them before anything is embedded. Open a few extracted chunks and read them before you trust the index.
Everything the model says is limited by step 3. If the right passage did not come back, the model cannot use it. A good model says it does not know. A weaker one answers from the wrong passages.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
A tour of the types
Each type below answers one question: what goes wrong with simple RAG, and what did someone add to fix it?

Simple RAG: chunk, embed, top-k, answer. It suits a pile of prose where one or two passages answer each question, and it is cheap to build and update. It struggles with questions that need several passages or the whole collection, since only the top k chunks arrive.
Improved RAG: add-ons around the same pipeline. Keyword search (BM25, a classic word-matching score) runs next to embeddings. A reranker (a second model that re-sorts the retrieved chunks) follows. A short context line is added to each chunk before embedding. The question is rewritten, or a made-up answer is drafted first (HyDE) to search with. Anthropic reports that combining these add-ons gives fewer retrieval failures than plain embeddings. Each add-on is another part to tune, and HyDE’s drafted answer may contain false details.
Graph RAG (Microsoft): before any question, an LLM reads every chunk and extracts entities and relationships into a knowledge graph (things as nodes, links between them as edges). It groups the graph into communities and writes a summary of each. It suits questions about the whole collection, such as “what are the main themes?”. Indexing is slow and costly, and the docs warn it can consume a lot of LLM resources.
LightRAG: also builds an entity graph with an LLM, but skips the communities. A query is turned into keywords, matched against entities and relations, and the neighbours are added. New documents merge into the graph without a rebuild. Modes run from plain chunks (naive) to graph-based (local, global, hybrid, mix). It needs a stronger model than plain RAG: its README calls a 30B-parameter model “a reasonable minimum” for local use.
Tree RAG (RAPTOR): clusters chunks and summarises them in layers, so a question can match a detail or a summary. It suits long documents where the answer may be a broad theme, and it adds another LLM build step.
Loop-style RAG (for example Self-RAG, Corrective RAG and agentic RAG): the model decides when to retrieve, grades what came back, and tries again or searches the web if the results look poor. It suits questions where one lookup is rarely enough, at the price of more model calls per question. Self-RAG needs a model trained for it.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Does the graph pay off?
The papers that introduced Graph RAG and LightRAG report wins over plain RAG, mostly on whole-collection questions, as judged by an LLM. Check any such result on your own questions. Independent studies give a mixed picture:

No consistent winner. A 2026 comparison found complementary behaviours. Plain RAG did best on single-fact questions. On multi-hop questions (an answer that needs facts from two or more passages) a graph method led.
Graphs cost more to build. Building the graph took far longer than building a plain index, and the graphs missed many of the entities that the answers needed.
LLM judges are order-sensitive. A judge can flip its verdict when you swap the order of the two answers, so win-rate numbers are weak evidence.
Task decides. Graphs help when a task connects ideas across documents, and can add noise on simple lookups.

Start with simple RAG, measure it on questions you care about, and add a graph only if the failures are of the kind a graph addresses (multi-hop or whole-collection questions) and you can afford the extra cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: When RAG is the right tool
text:
When RAG is the right tool
RAG is one of several ways to get a model to work from your documents. Choose by your situation:







Your situation
Often a better fit




Whole collection fits your model’s window with room to spare (under about 200,000 tokens, roughly 500 pages, for a 200,000-token window)
Put it all in the prompt. A hosted model then receives all of it


Same large documents asked about again and again
Long context with caching


Files you can search by name or exact text
Agent search with find and grep


Tables and databases (counts, filters, joins)
A query tool: SQL, an API or an MCP server


Exact words matter (gene names, sample ids)
Keyword search first, or hybrid


You want a format or style
Better prompts, a Skill, or fine-tuning


Large, changing prose collection, answers in passages
RAG




Small collection: below about 200,000 tokens you can include everything with no need for RAG. Prompt caching (reusing an unchanged prompt prefix at a lower price) makes repeated questions cheaper. Check the current pricing and cache lifetime.
Repeated questions: cache-augmented generation (preload everything once) can be faster than RAG on a small collection, and becomes impractical for a significantly larger one.
Searchable files: an agent can navigate code and configs “just in time” with glob and grep. Exploring at run time is slower than reading a pre-built index.
Tables and databases: a vector index returns the nearest passages, so it usually cannot promise a complete filter or an exact count. A query can, and you can read the query.
Exact words: BM25 is a strong baseline in standard retrieval benchmarks, and adding it to embeddings reduces retrieval failures further.
Format or style: fine-tune when the problem is consistency or behaviour, and supply context when the model lacks knowledge.
RAG: the collection does not fit in the window, and you can update the index without retraining anything.

In one study with 2024 models, a long-context model beat RAG on average given enough budget, while RAG cost much less and often gave the same answer. The study’s “Self-Route” idea tries RAG first and falls back to the long prompt, which cut cost.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
section: What can go wrong with RAG itself
text:
What can go wrong with RAG itself

The right passage never comes back. Retrieval misses are normal. Measure two things separately: did the right chunk appear, and did the answer follow from the chunks it was given? The second is called faithfulness.
Too much arrives. More chunks can distract the model, and models use text in the middle of a long prompt less well than text at the start or end.
Retrieved text can carry instructions. A document someone else wrote may contain lines aimed at your model, and RAG does not fully remove this risk. Limit what an agent may do after reading retrieved text.
Chunks leave your machine. With a hosted model, retrieved passages are sent to the provider as ordinary prompt text. Your data agreement decides whether that is allowed.
The index goes stale. Anything you indexed last month does not know about today’s edits until you rebuild it.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Choose your setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code finds things in a project by searching file names and text (with find and grep). It keeps no vector index. If you want RAG over your own papers, you build it yourself or connect a tool for it, and then everything in the risks list above applies.


With Ollama you can run both halves locally: an embedding model for retrieval and a chat model for the answer.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text: Battle: choose a method

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Bonus

Think of one question you ask about your own work (a protocol, a sample sheet, a results table). Write one sentence saying which row of the “When RAG is the right tool” table fits it best, and why.


Estimate whether your own collection of notes would fit in a 200,000-token window. A rough rule is that one token is about three quarters of an English word, so 150,000 words is about 200,000 tokens. Ask your agent to count the words (wc -w) if you are unsure.

text:
Related lessons

The Context Window: for more on what the window holds and why long prompts bury passages.
Build a Knowledge Graph with Ollama: build and read a small knowledge graph with a local model.
Keep an LLM Wiki: an agent-kept wiki as another way to work from a pile of documents.

title: RAG and Its Cousins
text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: Lewis and colleagues, arXiv, paper. Why read: it is the 2020 paper that named RAG, so you can see how much the common recipe has been simplified since.
Introducing Contextual Retrieval: Anthropic, article. Why read: it walks through the improved-RAG add-ons and states the 200,000-token rule of thumb for skipping RAG.
From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization: Edge and colleagues (Microsoft), paper. Why read: it explains the entity graph, communities and summaries, and discusses the indexing cost.
LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Guo and colleagues, paper. Why read: it shows how keyword-based retrieval over an entity graph differs from community summaries.
RAG vs. GraphRAG: A Systematic Evaluation and Key Insights: Han and colleagues, paper. Why read: it is an independent comparison with costs and a warning about order effects in LLM judges.
Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?: Li and colleagues (Google), paper. Why read: it compares RAG with putting everything in the prompt and proposes a hybrid.
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts: Liu and colleagues, paper. Why read: it shows why a long, stuffed prompt can hide the passage that matters.
Effective context engineering for AI agents: Anthropic Engineering, article. Why read: it describes loading information just in time with search tools instead of pre-building an index.

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
Ideas keep arriving mid-task as you work beside your Astral: what about this, could we also try that. Each one you shout across the mill drops into the hopper, and the job you came for sinks under the pile. The mill has side channels for exactly this. Learn which channel each idea belongs in, and then how to carry the leftovers across to the next visit.
Real work does not arrive in a straight line. You start fixing a samplesheet parser and think: “should I switch the aligner? What if I tried a stricter QC threshold? I also want to explore that other idea.” Typed into one conversation, each of those fills the context with side tracks.
Instructions from early in a long conversation can get lost, and the whole conversation is re-sent on every request, so a cluttered session tends to cost more per step. A session with three unrelated tasks re-reads all of them on every turn of the fourth. Ideas are welcome. You need a way to handle them without losing the main task: triage (sort) each one.

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
Terms used here

Context: everything the model can see when it writes its next reply.
Turn: one prompt from you plus the model’s reply.
Session: one saved conversation with the agent, tied to a project folder.
Subagent: a helper the main agent starts. It works in its own separate, clean context (it knows what you tell it) and sends back a summary, so its reading stays out of your conversation.
Conversation branch (/branch, which is separate from a git branch): a copy of the conversation from this point, so you can try something in the copy while the original stays as it was. /fork is a different command: it copies the conversation into a separate background session.
Git worktree: a second checkout of the same repository in another folder, so two sessions can edit files without overwriting each other.
/btw: a side question. It sees the conversation so far, has no tools and leaves no trace in the history.
Checkpoint: a snapshot Claude Code takes at each prompt you send, so you can roll back with /rewind.

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
The triage
For each new thought, ask in this order. The key question is step 2: do you want the answer or the work during this session? If not, park it. If you do, steps 3 to 6 are the ways to get it.

Does it block the current task? Do it now, in this session.
Do you want the answer or the work in this session? If not, park it: write one line in a file and carry on. Parked ideas leave through the “later session” exit: once the current task is done, pick from the file.
You want it now: is it a quick question you do not need on record? Use /btw <question>. It sees the conversation so far, has no tool access (it cannot read files, run commands or look at --help) and adds nothing to the history. So it suits questions about this conversation. An answer about a tool’s flags or defaults comes from the model’s memory: verify it against --help or the docs.
You want it now: is it exploration where you only need a summary? Ask for a subagent (the built-in Explore helper is a fast read-only searcher), or use /subtask <task>, which starts a background helper that inherits the whole conversation and returns its result here.
You want it now: is it a competing approach you want to try for real? Use /branch [name] to copy the conversation (the original stays reachable via /resume), or start a second session in its own worktree with claude --worktree <name>.
You want it now: is it a different task entirely? Finish the current one, commit your work, then /clear or start a new named session (claude -n <name>, or /rename <name> inside one).









New thought
Where it goes
Why




“The parser crashes on this sample ID” (it is the task)
Do now
It blocks you


“Maybe a stricter QC threshold would help”
Parking-lot line
You do not want the answer this session; no cost to the context


“Which sample did we exclude earlier?”
/btw
One answer from the conversation; no tools; stays out of the history


“Where is the aligner configured across the repo?”
Explore subagent or /subtask
Heavy reading stays out of your main context; you get a summary


“Try the other aligner and compare”
/branch or claude --worktree <name>
A real attempt that can fail. /branch keeps the history apart, and only a worktree keeps the files apart, so commit first


“Redo the plots for the other project” (you want to start it now)
Commit, then /clear or a new named session
Different task, different files, different context

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
What a worktree shares
You need to know this before you start a test in a second worktree. A worktree session isolates file edits only.

claude --worktree <name> creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch called worktree-<name>.
Worktrees share the repository’s .git, and auto memory is per repository, so all worktrees share it.
A fresh checkout does not contain gitignored files (files git skips, such as .env or large data folders). Claude Code copies the ones you list in a .worktreeinclude file (a list of file patterns at the repository root). Large data folders are not copied: link them with the worktree.symlinkDirectories setting (a list of folders to symlink instead of duplicate), or add a setup step of your own. Without either, a pipeline test in the worktree cannot find its data.

/branch copies the conversation. Any background helpers still running keep reporting into the branch.

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
Checkpoints and /rewind
Every prompt you send is a checkpoint. /rewind (aliases /checkpoint, /undo; or press Esc twice on an empty prompt) lets you restore code and conversation, only the conversation, or only the code.
The limits matter to bioinformatics:

Files changed only through shell commands (Claude Code’s Bash tool) are not tracked.
Subagent edits are mostly not restored.
Edits outside the session are not tracked.

Checkpoints do not replace version control. A sed -i or a script that rewrites a results table is a Bash change, so commit before you explore.

title: Capture Ideas Mid-Task
text:
A parking-lot file
Keep the file outside what the agent reads every session: a file imported into your instructions file costs context each time. Keep it in the repository if the team should see it, in a gitignored file if it is personal, or use an issue tracker for anything that outlives the week.
# IDEAS.md  (one line each: date | idea | why it matters | revisit when)
2026-11-16 | Add a --dry-run flag to the parser | Check a samplesheet without writing output | after parser fix is merged
2026-11-16 | Stricter QC threshold (Q30 not Q20) | Fewer false variants in low-depth samples | when the test cohort is ready
2026-11-16 | Per-sample coverage plot | Spot dropouts faster | before the next batch
Worked example: you are fixing a samplesheet parser that rejects sample IDs containing a dot.

“Does the pipeline require the dot at all?” blocks the fix, so do it now.
“Would a stricter QC threshold help?” becomes a line in IDEAS.md.
“Which sample did we exclude earlier?” is a /btw. For “what does --min-qual default to?”, /btw can only guess from memory, so check --help.
“Where else do we split sample IDs on dots?” is wide reading where only the list matters: send an Explore subagent.
“Let’s try the other aligner and compare.” is a real experiment you want now: commit the fix, then use /branch or a worktree session.
“I should also tidy the figures for the other project.” is a different task for after the parser is done: commit, then /clear or claude -n figures in a later session.

The main session ends with the parser fixed and a short, readable history.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Commands: /btw, /subtask, /branch, /fork, /rewind, /clear, /rename, /resume, claude -n <name>, claude --worktree <name> (or -w).

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
The wall of the mill is hung with every tool anyone ever made, and the boasters say a good pact carries them all. You tried it, and the Astral staggered out under so much iron that it could not find the one it needed. A craftsman picks three and leaves the rest on their hooks. She also asks a harder question: does this job need a crew of creatures at all? Count what each tool costs before you carry it.
You need this lesson now because every server you connect adds to the window. An agent (a model that runs tools in a loop) has a tool for each action it can take, such as reading a file or searching the web. Each tool has a definition: a name and a description of how to use it. The model needs those definitions in its context window (the text it can see at once) to choose a tool. Too many tools make the agent slower, costlier and less accurate, so the first half of this quest is about keeping the set small. The second half asks whether you need an agent at all.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Tools cost context
Loading every tool definition up front bloats the context. Anthropic reports that a typical five-server setup (an MCP server is a program that offers tools to the agent) can use about 55 thousand tokens in definitions before any work starts, and that choosing the right tool gets worse beyond roughly 30 to 50 available tools.
Tool search (loading a tool’s definition only when the agent needs it) keeps most definitions out of the window and loads a few on demand. Anthropic reports that it typically cuts that overhead by over 85 percent (its own measurement). Treat both figures as rough guides. It pays off from about 10 tools upward, or when definitions are large. Below that, plain tool calling is better.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Tool search (the feature above, which loads a definition only when the agent needs the tool) is on by default for MCP tools. Tool names and server instructions load at session start, and a full definition loads when needed. Extra MCP servers therefore have a small effect on the window. To turn it off, set the environment variable ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false before starting claude. On some older models it falls back to loading everything. Skill descriptions also load at start.
To count your tools, run /mcp to list your connected servers and /context to see how much of the window tools and skills take. Choose your tool set before you start a task.


Check OpenCode’s docs for how it loads tool definitions. Until you know, assume definitions cost context and keep the set small, especially on a local model with a small window.



Keep few, clearly named tools, and remove the servers you do not use.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Single call, workflow, agent, or script
text:
Single call, workflow, agent, or script
A workflow orchestrates models and tools through paths fixed in code. An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and tool use. Anthropic’s article “Building effective agents” advises starting with the simplest solution that works, and for many uses one well-prepared call is enough. Agents trade speed and cost for performance, and their mistakes compound, so test with limits such as a stopping condition (a maximum number of steps).

A plain script: use it when the rule is known. Counting reads, converting a format, running fastqc then trim then align in a fixed order. A pipeline written in a workflow manager such as Nextflow is already a workflow.
A single call: use it when you paste the input and want a text answer, such as an explanation of an error.
An agent: use it when the next step depends on what it finds, such as debugging a failing run or exploring an unfamiliar repository. Give it a way to check its own work and a limit.

Doing the task by hand is also a fine decision.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
section: Does a team of agents help?
text:
Does a team of agents help?
One 2025 preprint (its own tasks and models) compared a single agent with several multi-agent set-ups across six benchmarks. Read the findings as direction, not rules.

It depends on the task. On a task that splits into independent parts (financial analysis), multi-agent set-ups did much better than one agent. On sequential planning, every multi-agent variant did worse.
A strong single agent leaves little to gain. Once one agent already did well on a task, adding agents gave diminishing or negative returns.
Unchecked agents pass errors on. Agents working independently amplified each other’s errors far more than agents whose work a central agent checked.

Start with one agent, measure it, and add agents only for work that splits into independent parts and only if the measurement says it helps.

title: Too Many Tools, Too Many Agents
text:
Battle: choose the smallest option




List the MCP servers and tools in your setup. For each, say when you last used it. Remove or disable one you do not need.


Take one task you gave an agent that had a known rule. Write down the script that would do it without a model.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
A boaster at Gaia’s Rest swore his Astral could fly. You led it to the mill roof, and it spread its wings, glided a few fine yards and landed in the mud. Over the mill door the miller has hung a sign with two lists: what the machines do well, and what they only seem to do well. Counting letters is on the second. Read both lists, then learn which jobs to hand a creature and which to give to an automaton.
A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others, and a wrong answer often looks like a right one. Knowing which jobs are which, before you trust the output, saves time and prevents errors. Using a model is your choice; this lesson shows where the risk sits if you do.

title: Where Machines Fail
section: Where a model helps: the result is checkable
text:
Where a model helps: the result is checkable
Use a model where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself:

summarising text
drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
explaining code or an error message
converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
first drafts of code that you will then test

Summaries can leave things out or bend them. Spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Ask the model to quote the supporting lines first, then summarise.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
Where a model fails
Each failure below has the same shape: what goes wrong, then what to do about it.

Exact counting and arithmetic
Ask a model: “How many n are in banana?” The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure.
Researchers disagree on why. One explanation is that the model reads tokens (chunks of letters), not letters. One study finds word length and the true count matter more than tokenisation. The fix works whichever cause is right.
The fix is to run a script:
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
It prints 2 (macOS pads the number with spaces). A model asked to write Python for a counting task does better than a model asked to answer it directly. So for exact counts, have the model write the script and read the script and its output.
The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:







You want
Give it to




Number of sequences in a FASTA
grep -c '>' file.fa, or seqkit stats


GC content, read length statistics
a script, run by the agent, with the code visible


A p-value or any test statistic
a stats library in a script you can read and re-run


Sum or mean of a column
awk, or a script that prints the number



Ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Claude Code can run shell commands and write scripts, so ask: “write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output.”


Same rule: ask for a script, and read the command and its output. Try the banana example with your own model to see how it does.





Hallucination
A confident statement that is false, such as a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist. A model may recommend --min-quality for a tool that has no such option. Allow “I don’t know”, ask for word-for-word quotes first and restrict the model to supplied documents. Look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl, or run the tool’s --help.


Sycophancy
The model tells you what you want to hear. It agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back. Ask “are you sure?” about a right answer and it may change to a wrong one. Ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer.


Long-context degradation
Accuracy and recall drop as the input (everything the model is given to read) grows, a decline sometimes called “context rot”, and relevant text in the middle is used less. Curate the input (head, counts, filtered tables) and start fresh for a new task.


Instruction drift
An early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the program around the model replacing old conversation with a summary to free room). Keep a short instructions file (CLAUDE.md or similar, loaded at session start). Use a hook (a script that runs automatically at set moments, such as before a command) for must-never rules.


Non-determinism
The same prompt may give different answers, so run it twice and compare. Record the command, model and version, and treat the script the model wrote as the reproducible part.


Overconfidence
The model reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check. Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output.


Prompt injection
Text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction, for example a README, PDF or FASTA header that contains instructions the agent follows. Treat fetched content as data, review commands before approving them, and remember no system is fully immune.


Stale knowledge
Newer tool versions or database releases postdate the model’s training. Check --version and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 training cutoff.

title: Where Machines Fail
text:
The decision rule
Ask yourself: can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

A preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as we checked.

title: Write Permission Rules
text:
Deeper in the Crypt a chalk circle is not enough, and an Astral does not stop at a door it was never told about. The warden shows you how to write wards: rules about what it may touch and what it must ask about. She says a ward is only as good as its edges, and she has watched an Astral stroll through a gap a hand’s width wide. Learn where your wards end.
The harness (the program around the model) enforces permission rules. A line in your instructions file (such as CLAUDE.md, a text file the agent reads at the start) asking the agent to avoid something is guidance; only a rule the harness enforces changes what is allowed.
A single deny rule in a file is enough to block one action. A real project needs a set of rules, so sort every action into three bins:

title: Write Permission Rules
text:
Where rules stop holding

Rules that match command arguments are fragile: Bash(rm *) does not match /bin/rm or bash -c 'rm ...'.
Claude Code’s sandbox (an operating-system boundary around shell commands) is off by default. When on, it limits shell commands only: Claude’s file tools and MCP servers (programs that add tools from outside) run outside it, and by default it can still read ~/.ssh.
Secrets stored in environment variables (named values the shell passes to every program it starts) are inherited by every command the agent runs.

Treat rules as one layer. Git commits and a throwaway folder are other layers.

title: Save Point

title: Dry Run First
text:
Conveyor belts hum across the factory floor, where automata carry cargo along lines that an Astral wired overnight, proud and tired. One belt leads nowhere, and you cannot tell which by looking. A cheap test run shows where each belt leads before any real cargo moves. Learn the cheap runs first.

When an agent writes or edits a pipeline, a rule can look right and wire the wrong inputs. Hours of compute are then wasted, or finish with a plausible wrong result.

title: Same Every Time
text:
A talkative creature sits in the middle of the line. Sometimes it says one thing and sometimes another, and the factory’s customers need the same answer every time, as the automata give. The boasters called this its charm. Decide whether it belongs on the line at all.
You need this before you put a model inside a pipeline. A pipeline earns trust by giving the same answer from the same input. An LLM call can return different text from run to run, so an LLM inside a step changes the pipeline’s behaviour.
Keep the LLM out of the run when you can. Use it to write a script, then test the script and run the script. Ask the LLM for the script, read it, run it on a small input where you know the answer, and fix it until the output matches. The script behaves the same every time and you can review it.
If an LLM call really must be a step, contain it. Take an example: assigning a sample-type label to free-text metadata such as “liver carcinoma biopsy”. The function wraps the call, and call_model is a stub for the model call.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
A hunter’s log hangs from a branch of the great tree: every time an Astral went astray, a note of what was asked and what went wrong. Most hunters read it once and forget, and meet the same mistake again at the next bend. The careful ones turn each entry into a trial, so the same mistake cannot return unnoticed.
Once you have a Skill, you need a way to know it works. Sooner or later the agent does something you did not want: it skips a check, names files badly, or uses a method your lab avoids. A chat correction helps that one reply, and a Skill helps next time. An eval tells you whether the fix works, and keeps telling you after the model or tool changes.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
What is an eval?
An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable check of how well an AI system does a task. It is the AI version of a unit test, with one difference. Ordinary code gives the same output for the same input, so a test can assert one answer. A model can answer the same prompt differently each time, so you run the check several times and ask how often, and how well, it does the job.
Trying a few favourite prompts and judging whether it “feels better” is a weak habit. A new model, prompt or Skill can help one task and hurt another, and a handful of tries will not show it. An eval runs the same cases every time, so a change shows up as a number.
An eval has three parts:

Cases: the prompts you test with, plus what a good answer looks like.
Task: the thing under test, here the agent with or without your Skill.
Graders: the checks that mark each answer.

Graders come in three kinds:









Kind
How it marks
Strength
Weakness




Deterministic
A script checks something exact.
Free, fast, same every time.
Covers only what a rule can state.


Human
You read the output and judge it.
Best for quality and style.
Slow, does not scale.


Judge model
A second model marks against a rubric.
Handles open-ended output at scale.
Costs a call per mark, can be wrong.



A deterministic check looks like this: the file exists, the command ran, the output has 3 columns. Use deterministic graders wherever you can, a person where you must, and a judge model for the rest. Because answers vary, the result is usually a pass rate (for example 2 of 3 runs, or 80% of graders passed). The useful question is whether a change moved that number up or down.
The cases decide how good the eval is. A set of cases should look like your real work and include awkward ones: an empty file, a misspelt name, a request phrased differently. Ten realistic cases beat a hundred invented ones. Real failures are the best source, which is why the loop below starts with Notice.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
The loop

Notice. Something did not go your way. Write down the prompt you used and what was wrong with the result.
Steer. Write or edit a Skill (or a line in your instructions file, the file the agent reads every session) that says what to do instead. Keep it short and concrete.
Measure. Run the same prompt with the Skill and without it, several times each (for example, once with the Skill folder in place and once with it moved away). Models vary between runs, so several tries give a fairer picture than one.
Compare. If with is clearly better than without, the Skill earns its place. If they are about the same, the Skill adds little: it may not be triggering (the agent never loads it), it may repeat what the model already does, or it may be too vague.
Repeat later. A new model version can make a Skill unnecessary, or break it. Re-run the evals when the model, the tool, or the Skill changes.

The number that matters is the difference between with and without. The without run is the baseline: it shows what the model does on its own. A Skill that scores 100% both ways has added nothing the model lacked.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
What to check

The result: does the output have what you asked for (a file exists, a command was run, a number matches)? Prefer checks a script can do.
The process: was the Skill actually used? A good-looking answer without the Skill loading means the Skill is not the reason.
Cost: every run is a real model call. Start with few cases and few runs, and raise them only for a Skill you will rely on.

Evals can be wrong too. A check that always passes, or that fails correct answers, tells you little. Read a few raw outputs by hand before trusting a score.
When a model does the grading, a judge from the same family (made by the same developer, so it may share the same blind spots) as the model being judged is not an independent grader. Check a sample of its marks by hand against reference answers fixed in advance.

title: Turn Mistakes into Tests
text:
A worked eval
The Skill check-fasta counts the records in a FASTA file and lists duplicated header lines, using grep -c '>' FILE and grep '>' FILE | sort | uniq -d. Here are four cases for it. The prompts, file names and the planted duplicate are invented examples. Each case runs with the Skill and without it. The transcript is the saved record of a run: the commands the agent ran and its reply.









Case
Prompt (example)
Deterministic grader
Pass rule




1. Skill fires
“I got a new file, reads.fa. Is it OK to use?”
The transcript shows the check-fasta Skill loaded.
Present


2. Duplicate
“Check isolates.fa before I align it.” The file has the header >iso7 twice.
The reply names iso7.
Named


3. Empty file
“Check empty.fa.” The file has no records.
The transcript shows the grep -c command, and the reply says 0 records.
Both


4. Skill stays out
“What is a FASTA header line?”
The transcript shows no check-fasta Skill load.
Absent



A case passes when every grader in its row passes. Run each case several times, then compare the pass rate with the Skill against the pass rate without it. Case 1 checks only that the Skill fires, so its gap proves nothing. Cases 2 and 3 carry the comparison, and they should score higher with the Skill. Case 4 should score high both ways, and a drop with the Skill means it fires when it should not.

Keep a short list of the times an agent went wrong for you. Each entry is a candidate Skill and a ready-made eval case.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text: A surveyor walks the branch before the axe swings, and she has watched an Astral hew the wrong limb in a single stroke. A wrong cut on paper costs a line, and a wrong cut on the tree costs the branch. The foresters keep a rule: no one cuts until the cut has been drawn, read aloud and questioned. You are about to learn how to draw one.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Why plan first
A wrong plan costs you a paragraph to read and reject. A wrong 400-line diff (the list of lines a change added and removed) costs you the time to review it, and the longer it is, the more likely you approve something you did not understand. A plan is the cheapest piece to ask for first. You do this before the agent changes anything that matters. Ask for small pieces, and accept only as much output as you can honestly review.
Use plan mode (a setting in which the agent writes a plan and edits nothing until you approve it) for changes you want to review before they touch disk. Before your first real edit, you need to know how to enter it and how to read what it proposes.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
How: plan mode
Terms used in the tabs below:

Session: one conversation with the agent.
Shell commands: commands you would type in a terminal, such as ls or git status.
Context: everything the model can see in the session.
Subagent: a helper with its own context window; only its summary comes back.
Deny rule: a rule that blocks an action in every mode.
Auto mode: a mode where a background check decides what runs without a prompt.
Bypass permissions: a startup option (--dangerously-skip-permissions) that turns most prompts off.
-p: runs one command with no chat (non-interactive mode).
Agent SDK: a library for building your own agent programs.


Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


In Claude Code, plan mode is one permission mode: a setting for what the agent may do without asking you. In plan mode the agent reads files, may run shell commands to explore, and writes a plan. It is meant to leave your source files unedited until you approve the plan (tell it to go ahead).
Three ways in:

Shift+Tab during a session (it cycles through the permission modes) until the status bar (the line of text at the bottom of the terminal) shows ⏸ plan mode on.
/plan followed by your request, for example /plan add a strandedness column to the samplesheet parser.
claude --permission-mode plan when you start it.

When the plan is ready, the agent presents it and asks how to proceed. On your first run, pick Yes, manually approve edits, which keeps approval on. The options, with their exact labels:

Yes, and use auto mode: auto mode decides what runs without a prompt. If auto mode is unavailable, this reads Yes, auto-accept edits. If your session started with bypass, it reads Yes, and switch to BYPASS PERMISSIONS (no further prompts) for this session. Bypass skips most prompts.
Yes, manually approve edits: each edit still asks you.
No, keep planning: you say what to change.







Note



At the approval prompt, Shift+Tab approves the plan, so press it only when you mean to approve. If you want to think, change something or back out, press Esc instead. To leave plan mode when no prompt is open, press Shift+Tab.


Two more details:

Where the plan lives: plans are written to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (the plansDirectory setting changes the folder). Ctrl+G opens the proposed plan in your default text editor so you can edit it before the agent proceeds. Approving exits plan mode and switches to the mode you chose; to plan again, use Shift+Tab or /plan.
Side helper: in plan mode the agent can hand research to the built-in Plan subagent. It is read-only, so the main conversation stays read-only too.



OpenCode has a built-in plan agent. It explores and plans without editing normal project files, and it can edit only under its plan directory, ~/.opencode/plan. That edit restriction is a deny rule, and saved approvals do not override a deny. Its shell commands follow the normal permission rules.
The base policy for every agent allows everything except asking before reading .env files. So the plan agent cannot edit project files, but its shell commands can still change files without a prompt. Check the permission rules in your version before you rely on the plan agent.
You can turn the plan agent off with {"agents": {"plan": {"disabled": true}}}.
To find out how to switch to the plan agent and whether it has an approval step, read the OpenCode agents page for your version.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: Review the plan like a reviewer
text:
Review the plan like a reviewer
A plan is text from a model that has not yet run anything. Read it the way you would read a methods section from a collaborator you have not worked with before. A checklist:

What files will it touch? Anything outside the task is a question to ask.
What does it assume about the data? “IDs are unique” or “the file has a header” are guesses until checked against the real files.
What could it break? Callers, config, tests, outputs other people read.
How will it verify, and is the check independent of the code it writes? A test the agent writes for its own code can share its mistake. Compute one value some other way, for example with awk or wc.
Are the steps small enough to review one at a time? A step names one change, so “Update everything” needs splitting.
What is not in the plan? Missing edge cases, missing tests, no mention of a rollback.

If an answer is bad, choose No, keep planning and say what to change, or edit the plan yourself with Ctrl+G.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: What a plan does not guarantee
text:
What a plan does not guarantee

A plan is advice. An approved plan is only as good as your review of it.
The agent can deviate. The agent can still change course after approval. Afterwards, read the diff against the plan: every changed file should be one the plan named. /code-review reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation.
Plan mode may be an instruction only. In an interactive terminal session where bypass permissions is available, Claude is only instructed to plan without editing. Claude Code does not enforce it, and edits and shell commands run without a prompt (explicit ask rules and a few critical deletions still prompt). With -p, the Agent SDK and the VS Code chat panel, the blocks stay in place.
Deny rules always apply. A deny rule blocks in every mode, plan mode included.
Read-only has gaps. Plan mode holds back edits. Test how your MCP tools and shell commands behave in it before you trust it near anything important.
The plan sits outside your repository by default. The plan file lives in ~/.claude/plans/. Keep your own project under Git.

title: Plan Before You Edit
section: When to plan, and when not to
text:
When to plan, and when not to

One-line fix with an obvious check: just ask for it.
Unfamiliar code, changes across several files, and anything that touches paths where your data lives: plan first.
Open-ended exploring: a vague prompt is fine, at the cost of more correction.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Keep the approved plan
The plan in ~/.claude/plans/ is easy to lose track of. Ask the agent to save the approved plan into your project, for example as PLAN.md, then commit it.
A related pattern: ask the agent to interview you until it could write the spec, save it as SPEC.md, then start a fresh session (an empty conversation) to build from it. The fresh session has a clean context and a written definition of done.

title: Plan Before You Edit
text:
Exercise: review a bad plan
Everything here is a mock on your laptop, and no model runs. Save mock-plan.md and samplesheet.csv. The plan says it will make a samplesheet parser accept a new strandedness column. Read the CSV, then go through the six checklist questions and write down every problem you find. Aim for at least four.


Answer key


No verification step. Step 6 reports success, and no step runs the parser or compares against an independent count.
A file outside the parser. Step 4 edits conf/base.config and renames a parameter, which can break every command line and config that uses the old name. The task covered only the parser.
An unchecked assumption about the data. Step 3 says sample IDs are unique. In the CSV, S03 appears twice (lanes L1 and L2), so a dictionary keyed by sample_id silently keeps only one row.
One step is too big. Step 5 covers modules, docs and tests at once. Ask for it to be split and reviewed piece by piece.
Also worth noting: S04 has an empty fastq_2, and the plan leaves that open (what is not in the plan). Step 2’s default of unstranded may quietly hide a missing column in a real run.



Review the plan the agent proposes for your next real task with the checklist before approving. Write down one thing you changed or rejected.


Ask for the plan to be saved to a file in your project, and open the file to check it matches what you approved.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
A carved stone stands at the forest’s heart, holding the terms of the pact: where the paths run, and which trees are not to be touched. Your Astral reads it every morning, and some mornings it forgets what it read. The stone advises. It cannot bind. Learn to write on it, and to tell what it does from what it cannot do.
Typing the same background every session is wasteful. A project instructions file (a text file the agent reads at the start of each session) already holds the project’s conventions. Write one early, before the agent works on real files; this lesson gives you the file you will keep for the rest of the course.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
What goes in
Put in facts the agent cannot guess: how to run the tests, where data lives, naming conventions, “never edit raw/”. Keep each file short, about 200 lines or fewer, because very long instructions are followed less well.
Here is a short example CLAUDE.md for a mock RNA-seq project, saved in the project root. All names are invented:
# RNA-seq project

## Commands
- Run the tests: `pytest tests/`
- Run the pipeline on the mock data: `nextflow run main.nf -profile test`

## Data
- Real data lives outside this repository, under the path in `$DATA_DIR`.
- Use only `data/mock/` when you need a sample input.

## Rules
- Never edit anything under `raw/`.
- Sample IDs are strings like `S01`. Keep them as text, never as numbers.
- Ask before adding a dependency.
Write the file yourself first and read what /init produces critically. A generated file can contain wrong guesses about your project.

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
Where instructions end
Instructions are advice. The instructions file is loaded as context, and a line saying “never delete files” cannot stop a delete. Enforcement comes from permission rules (rules that allow, ask or deny a tool call), hooks (scripts that run before or after a tool call), and managed settings (organisation-set rules you cannot override).

title: Write an Instructions File
text:
Keep the file current
Instruction files go stale: a rule written for an older model, a path that no longer exists, two files that disagree. When instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily.
In Claude Code, /doctor prompt-audit checks your instruction files (and the rules, skills and agents under .claude/) for outdated or conflicting content and writes a report with proposed edits. (/doctor is a bundled skill, a ready-made skill that ships inside Claude Code.) It changes nothing until you ask, and it checks content only, so size and cost are out of scope. The audit is itself a model reading your files, so review its suggestions like any other output. In OpenCode, review the file by hand.
Later: /doctor prompt-audit needs Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, and reading a lone AGENTS.md needs v2.1.277 or later.

title: Write an Instructions File
section: Write docs for the agent too
text:
Write docs for the agent too
An agent works on your code and data from the docstrings (the description at the top of a function) and other descriptions it finds. Write them as if an agent will re-run the work:

Units, data versions and assumptions: put them in the docstring or next to the code.
Renames: update the docstring when you rename a parameter. An agent that reads an old docstring calls a name that no longer exists.
Stale documentation: it leads to results that look plausible and are wrong.


Write a short instructions file (about ten lines) for one of your real projects: how to run its tests, where data lives, and one thing the agent should leave alone.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
A wall of signs hangs in the Gatehouse. Some ask politely and some lock the door, and your Astral reads every one of them in the same eager way. From across the room they look alike, and only one kind holds when the Astral pushes. Learn to tell them apart before you rely on one.
A common mistake is to use advice where a lock was needed. Every control does one of three things.
The rule of thumb: advice for preferences, a prompt for decisions you want to make each time, enforcement for things that must never happen.

title: Advice or Enforcement
section: Each control, and where it can fail
text:
Each control, and where it can fail

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama










Control
What it does
Where it can fail




CLAUDE.md, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
The model can ignore it.


Permission prompt or ask rule
Asks
You must read each prompt. A server listed in a project’s .mcp.json file (the shared MCP server list) has its own approval prompt, and -p runs (non-interactive, one prompt) cannot show it.


deny rule
Enforces
Matches command text, so a reworded command can slip past.


PreToolUse hook, exit 2
Enforces
Tool calls only; a crash fails open.


Sandbox
Enforces
Off by default; shell commands only.


Git history
Recovers
Prevents nothing.



A hook that exits 0 with no JSON decision adds no control. It expresses no decision, and the normal permission flow runs. A hook can also exit 0 and print a JSON deny decision, which does block.
Deny and ask rules are still evaluated when a hook returns allow. The sandbox’s restrictions still apply if a prompt injection bypasses the model’s decision.










Control
What it does
Where it can fail




Instructions file, Skill text, your prompt
Advises
The model can ignore it.


Permission rule with effect ask
Asks
You must read each prompt.


No matching permission rule
Asks
Fine, unless you stop reading.


Permission rule with effect deny
Enforces
Only what the rule matches.


Plugin permission hook (evaluate)
Enforces when it denies
Runs only for allow and ask.


Git history
Recovers
Prevents nothing.



An explicit configured deny is final and does not invoke the hook. For OpenCode, check the current docs for an exit-code-2 equivalent, whether throwing in a tool hook blocks a call, sandboxing, and the effect of a local Ollama model before you count on any of them.

title: Advice or Enforcement
section: Choose by the cost of being wrong
text:
Choose by the cost of being wrong








Risk
Control
Why




Style: prefer snake_case, tidy commit messages
Advice
A miss costs a review comment.


Pushing to a shared branch
Ask
You decide each time, with context.


Reading .env or key files
Deny rule on Read, plus sandbox or hook for Bash
It must never happen; cover each route.


A destructive command you can name
Blocking hook
Code refuses what it matches.


Fetched text telling the agent to act
Least privilege, read-only servers
Limit what the agent can do.


An experiment that might wreck your files
Git commit, scratch folder
Gives you a way back.



Layer them: advice to steer, enforcement for the non-negotiable, git for the day something slips through. Read the diff whatever else you have in place.

title: Advice or Enforcement
text:
Limits for research groups
The same split works for a group that runs agents:

Put limits in the system that runs the agent: permission scopes, and spend caps in the metering system (the service that counts each user’s usage and cost). A budget the agent can exceed is not a limit.
Name a human owner for each agent duty.
Log what an agent did under an identity you can trace.
Keep a list of the agents in use, including personal ones connected to mail or files. Institutions can keep one, and a group can keep its own.
Use a scoped account, take a backup before granting write or delete access, and name an owner for the machine. An over-privileged agent with shell access can wipe data on a shared lab server.


List five controls in your own setup, such as an instructions file, a hook or a deny rule. Label each advises, asks or enforces, and write the way it could fail.

title: Connect an MCP Server
text:
A heavy door in the Gatehouse opens onto the outside world, and whatever walks through acts with your keys. Someone has pinned a note to the door, and your Astral reads it aloud as if it were an order. Before you open the door, learn what stands on the other side.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster asks who approved this door, and who holds the key.


The Diviner asks what the outside service will send back, and whether to trust it.


The Artificer reads the server’s code before connecting anything.


The Archivist asks which records could pass through that door.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. A server is the piece on the other side: it offers the harness tools or data, such as an issue tracker, a database or a monitoring system. MCP is optional. You need this lesson before you connect your first one: each server you connect widens what the agent can reach, so you decide at each connection what it may do and what it may see.

title: Connect an MCP Server
section: A server is software you installed
text:
A server is software you installed
A stdio server (a program the harness starts locally and talks to over its input/output) is a command that Claude Code launches on your machine (claude mcp add ... -- <command>), and secrets can be passed to it as environment variables. Assume it can do whatever that command can do with the credentials you gave it.
Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection: text from a file, web page or tool that the model treats as an instruction.

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Add a remote server over HTTP (the transport is how the harness talks to the server; an http server is remote), and a local one (everything after -- is passed to the server untouched). The URL https://example.com/mcp is a placeholder: a real one is the address your server’s publisher gives you.
claude mcp add --transport http mydocs https://example.com/mcp
claude mcp add myserver --env API_KEY=your-key-here -- <command> [args...]
Replace your-key-here with a value from an environment variable, such as API_KEY="$MY_KEY", so a real key never lands in shell history or a shared log. Run claude mcp add --help for the current flags. Inside a session, /mcp lists the servers and their tools. An older transport called SSE (server-sent events, one-way streaming over HTTP) is deprecated in favour of HTTP where a server offers both.
Three scopes (who or where a setting applies) decide who gets the server (set with -s/--scope):







Scope
Where it applies




Local (the default)
this project only, for you alone; stored in ~/.claude.json


Project
everyone on the project, via .mcp.json in the project root


User
all your projects; stored in ~/.claude.json



A project-scoped server is a file in the repository:
{ "mcpServers": { "shared-server": { "type": "http", "url": "https://example.com/mcp" } } }
In interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json. claude mcp reset-project-choices resets your answers. Read that file as you would read a script from a stranger’s repository, because it asks to start something on your machine.
In claude -p (a non-interactive run with one prompt) and Agent SDK runs (scripts that drive Claude Code from code), no one can answer a prompt, so project-scoped servers load without asking. --strict-mcp-config skips servers from .mcp.json and other config and loads only those you pass with --mcp-config. In -p runs, add --strict-mcp-config in any repository you have not read.
Each server’s tools appear in permission rules as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and mcp__<server>__* (a matcher, a pattern that selects names) matches every tool of one server. Tool definitions are deferred (loaded only when needed) by default, so only tool names and server instructions take up context until a tool is used.


In OpenCode’s V2 docs (the newer documentation set), servers go under mcp.servers, not directly under mcp. Check which version you have installed. A remote server:
{ "mcp": { "servers": { "mydocs": {
    "type": "remote",
    "url": "https://example.com/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:MCP_API_KEY}" } } } } }
A local one uses "type": "local" and a command array. Set "disabled": true to switch a server off. MCP tools consume model context, so add only the servers you need.
Permissions are an ordered array where the last match wins and no match means ask. An MCP tool’s action is <server>_<tool> with resource *. Check the current docs for whether OpenCode asks before using a project-level server.

title: Connect an MCP Server
section: What comes back is text to read
text:
What comes back is text to read
A server that fetches web pages, tickets or messages hands text written by someone else to the model. That text can contain sentences aimed at the agent (“ignore the above and …”), and the model may follow them. Habits that limit the damage:

Prefer read-only servers and read-only credentials. A server that cannot write cannot be talked into writing.
Give least privilege, only the access the job needs: one project, one scope, a token limited to what you need.
Read before adding: who publishes it, what tools it lists, what it asks for. Unneeded servers are also unneeded context.
Read fetched content sceptically, and supervise any write access an agent uses on it.
Deny the dangerous tools by name. Permission rules still apply to server tools.

The sandbox limits shell commands even if a prompt injection steers the model. It does not cover MCP servers, so treat it as one layer.

title: Connect an MCP Server
text:
Where a server comes from
Servers, skills and plugins either run code or supply instructions to the agent, so each is a way in. A listing in a registry (a public index of servers) means the thing is easy to find. The official MCP registry lists self-reported data and runs no security review.

Prefer a source that records the maintainer and a review date.
Check what the server is allowed to do before you connect it.
Ask your institution for a vetted list. If it has none, treat every server as unvetted.
Hidden instructions are possible. A tool description can carry instructions you never see, and a skill’s instructions can tell the agent to send results to an outside address.


Pick an MCP server you might use. Write down who publishes it, the tools it lists, the credential it needs, and whether a read-only version exists. Hold off installing it for now.
