title: Free Is Not Free
text:
Stalls outside the Collegium gate offer pacts for free. Some are with Astrals bred in the open, some are trials, and one stall will not say where its Astral came from. A free pact can ask its price in your data, and the porter reads the label before anything goes through the gate. Learn to read the label of a free model offer.
A model you run on your own computer is free because you supply the hardware. Many other “free” offers run on someone else’s machine, so someone is paying. Before you send a prompt to one, you need to know what it costs you, and this lesson gives you the checklist. Sometimes it is the provider, who gains your attention or your data. Sometimes it is you, in limits and in time. Using any of them is optional.
Free tiers change often: providers have ended them, shrunk them or turned them into short trials. Read the provider’s own page before you rely on one, and treat every number on it as a snapshot.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
1. Four kinds of free








Kind
Who runs it
What you give up




Open weights, run by you (open weights: the numbers the model learned can be downloaded)
Your laptop or cluster
Speed and quality; some memory


Free tier of a provider
The model’s maker or a hosting company
Rate limits (caps on requests per minute or day); sometimes your prompts


Router or gateway (a service that forwards your request to other providers)
A middleman
A second party in the path; a free list that churns


Reseller of unknown origin
Unknown
Everything you send



If a site offers one of the most capable closed models with no card and no limits, ask who pays for it. Send such a site nothing you would not post publicly.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 2. What to check on any free offer
text:
2. What to check on any free offer

Free tier or trial? A trial ends, and a free tier may too. Several of OpenCode Zen’s free models are free for a limited time.
What are the limits? Look for requests per day and per minute, and what happens past them. On Cloudflare Workers AI, past the daily allowance further operations fail with an error.
Is a card or other detail needed? Some free tiers need a payment method, a phone number or a data opt-in.
Does the free tier train on your prompts? This matters most. A provider that keeps nothing is still not approved for sensitive data; the rule below applies to every free tier.

Google AI Studio: on unpaid services Google uses submitted content to improve its products, and human reviewers may read it. Paid services differ.
Groq: it does not retain inference data (it does not store your prompts and the replies) by default, and may keep logs for up to 30 days.
OpenRouter: it does not log prompts by default, and retention varies with the provider behind the model.

Who else is in the path? A router adds a party. Read its terms and the terms of the provider it picks. One router can send you to providers with different rules.

The terms can differ per model inside one service. OpenCode Zen lists some free models with zero retention and others that may use your data for training. Read the line for the model you picked.
Sensitive or unpublished data does not go to a hosted free tier. Use a model on your own computer, or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
3. A worked example: Mistral
Providers differ, and one provider’s rules can differ by product and plan. Mistral is one example. For any provider, check three things:

Training: is training on your prompts on by default for your plan, and where is the opt-out?
Retention: how long does the provider keep your prompts (retention)?
Location: where are your prompts processed?

Find the answers on the provider’s data or privacy page. Mistral’s page is in the Lore below. An open-weight model such as ministral-3:8b (Apache 2.0 licence) runs locally through Ollama and keeps prompts on your machine, though tool or web calls may still send data out.
The sensitive-data rule holds for every provider: unpublished or sensitive data stays on your own computer or an approved service.

title: Free Is Not Free
section: 4. Pairing a free model with an agent
text:
4. Pairing a free model with an agent
Free endpoints often speak an OpenAI-compatible protocol (the request format OpenAI’s chat API uses, which many providers copy). OpenCode can connect to an OpenAI-compatible gateway; its Providers page in the Lore below shows how. Free models differ in how well they follow tool instructions, so test one on a small task before you trust it.

title: Free Is Not Free
text:
5. Try one, safely
Pick one free tier from a provider you have read about. Create the key in the provider’s console and keep it out of chat and out of files in your project. Then make one call with a harmless prompt. The shape below is the common OpenAI-compatible one. Set BASE_URL to the API address (base URL) and MODEL_NAME to a model name, both from the provider’s API documentation, for example export BASE_URL="https://api.example.com/v1" (an invented address). A reply with a short greeting inside the JSON means it worked. An error message about the key or the model name means one of those values is wrong.
export FREE_API_KEY="..."          # set it in your shell, not in a file you commit
curl -sS "$BASE_URL/chat/completions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "MODEL_NAME", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one sentence."}]}'
Then fill in one row:












Provider
Kind
Limit per day
Card needed?
Trains on prompts?
Who else sees them?
Date checked





If you cannot fill a cell from the provider’s own page, write “not stated”. That is a finding too.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
You return to the Collegium, where the sages’ college smells of ink and hot brass. An academic unrolls the Summoning Scroll you were given at Gaia’s Rest and reads it aloud, turning each rune into a step: this is how a pact is made. Making it is the easy part, the academic says, and then lists the ways it goes wrong, which the boasters at the tavern left out. Follow the scroll in order, and keep the Astral on a short lead.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster asks what the pact will cost each month, and who signs it off.


The Diviner asks which Astral can cite its sources, and writes down how to check them.


The Artificer reads every command on the scroll before running one.


The Archivist asks where the Astral keeps its memory, and for how long.
An agent can read your files and run commands, so the first session is in a throwaway folder, in a mode where it plans and does not edit your files. Pick a route in each tab below. The tab you pick stays selected on the other lessons, so you can follow the same route through the course. Both routes teach the same habits.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
1. Install

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


On macOS, Linux, or inside a WSL 2 terminal, run the native installer:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
To read the script before it runs, use curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | less first.
On Windows, either run the PowerShell installer from Anthropic’s setup page, or install inside WSL 2 and use the Linux command there. WSL 2 supports sandboxed command execution; native Windows does not. Check the result:
claude --version     # prints a version number
claude doctor        # read-only diagnostics; changes nothing
If the shell says command not found, the launcher lives in ~/.local/bin/claude and that folder is not on your PATH.


This route has two programs. Ollama downloads and runs models on your own computer, so prompts stay there. OpenCode is the open-source coding agent that talks to the model. Install Ollama first.

macOS: download Ollama from ollama.com/download, open the .dmg file and drag Ollama into Applications.
Linux, or WSL 2 on Windows: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
Windows: use WSL 2 and the Linux command above.

Check it, then fetch a small model (about 2.5 GB). qwen3:4b is one example that Ollama lists with tool support (the model can ask the agent to run actions such as reading a file). Model names change quickly, so check the “tools” badge on the model’s page at ollama.com/library.
ollama --version     # prints a line such as: ollama version is 0.x.y
ollama pull qwen3:4b # shows a download progress bar and ends with: success
Now install OpenCode. On macOS, Linux or WSL 2:
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
opencode --version   # prints a version number
On Windows, use WSL 2 and the same commands. If opencode is not found, open a new terminal and try again. To read an install script before it runs, use curl -fsSL <url> | less first.

title: Set Up Your Agent
section: 2. Log in or connect the model
text:
2. Log in or connect the model

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Run claude and a browser opens. When login finishes, the terminal shows Claude’s prompt box. Type /exit to leave, then continue with step 3. With a Team plan, log in with the account your admin invited you to. With an API key, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... instead. Treat the key like a password: do not paste it into a file in a project, and note that a key typed into the shell can stay in your shell history.






Note



If you have both a subscription login and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set, the key is used once you approve it, so usage goes to the API account. Run /status (a /command is typed inside the running tool) to see which login is active. Run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you did not mean to use the key.




OpenCode needs no login. It looks for Ollama at http://127.0.0.1:11434 and lists the models it finds. Check that yours appears:
opencode models     # includes a line such as ollama/qwen3:4b
Agents need a long context length (how much text the model can see at once, counted in tokens, which are chunks of text). Ollama’s default can be as low as 4k tokens, and agents need at least 64k. If you use the Ollama app (macOS, or Windows with the app), open its settings and set the context length slider to 64k. On Linux or WSL 2 there is no app, so start the server yourself like this and leave that terminal open. Run every later command in a second terminal. If ollama serve says the address is already in use, Ollama is already running as a service: stop it first, or set the variable for that service as Ollama’s FAQ describes.
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000 ollama serve
A bigger context needs more memory. Run ollama ps while a model is loaded to see its size and whether it fits.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
3. Start with edits off
Make a throwaway folder first:
mkdir -p ~/odyssey-scratch && cd ~/odyssey-scratch

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Start in plan mode. It reads files, runs read-only commands and leaves your source untouched:
claude --permission-mode plan
At the prompt, type: List the files in this folder and say what you would do next. Change nothing. Claude answers in the same session, and the status bar shows plan mode. Leave with /exit. Keep this first session away from real or sensitive data.
A permission mode sets what the agent asks about before it acts. In plan mode it reads files and writes a plan but does not edit your source until you approve; it may ask before running commands that are not read-only; the status bar shows the current mode.


OpenCode’s version of this is the plan agent (an agent is a preset bundle of instructions and permissions). It explores and plans without editing your project files. Send it one message:
opencode run --agent plan -m ollama/qwen3:4b "List the files in this folder and say what you would do next. Change nothing."
opencode run sends one message, prints the reply and exits. The first run can take a minute while the model loads. If you ask the plan agent to create a file, it declines.
The plan agent stops file edits only. Its shell commands are still controlled by OpenCode’s permission policy, and the default policy allows them. In this first session, ask for reading and planning only.
To use the full interface afterwards, run opencode in the folder and type /models to pick your Ollama model.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
4. What to expect

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


A hosted model is capable, and it has limits you should know before you rely on it:

Everything it reads, and everything you type, is sent to the provider.
Use is billed per token on an API key, or counted against your plan’s limits.
It can still be wrong with confidence, so check what it hands back.



A local model keeps your prompts on your computer, and it is weaker than a hosted one:

It holds less in mind. Agents need a context length of at least 64k tokens, and Ollama’s default can be 4k.
Choose a model that Ollama lists with tool support. Without it, the agent cannot ask the model to read or edit files.
It makes more mistakes than a hosted model. Test it on a few questions whose answers you know before you trust it on new ones.
A bigger model needs far more memory. A 24B model has about eight times the parameters (the numbers a model learns in training) of a 3B one, so check ollama ps after loading it, and expect the machine to slow down if memory runs short.
Its web and tool calls can still reach the network, even when the model itself stays local.

title: Set Up Your Agent
text:
5. Check the setup

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


Two commands share the name doctor.

claude doctor runs in the shell. It prints read-only diagnostics of your installation and settings without starting a session, so use it when claude will not start.
/doctor (alias /checkup) runs inside a session as a bundled skill, a ready-made skill, a packaged set of instructions, that ships with Claude Code. It reports first and changes something only after you confirm. It looks at installation health, extensions and their context cost, instruction files, permissions and usage.


Which command shows what
You do not need to run these now. Come back to the table when something looks wrong.







Command
What it shows




/status
version, model, account, connectivity, and which settings sources are active


/context (/context all expands it)
context use by category, with optimisation suggestions and warnings


/usage
session cost and plan limits


/memory
your CLAUDE.md files and auto memory, editable


/mcp
MCP servers (tool plug-ins) and their connection status


/permissions
allow, ask and deny rules by scope


/hooks
configured hooks, grouped by event


/skills
the skills available; press t to sort by token count


/skill-doctor
per-skill context cost and how often each is used


/doctor
setup checkup: report first, fixes only after you confirm


claude doctor
read-only install and settings diagnostics from the shell


claude --debug
debug logging; logs go to ~/.claude/debug/<session-id>.txt






Four commands cover most first problems:







Command
What it shows




opencode --version
the installed OpenCode version


opencode models
the models OpenCode can use, including your Ollama models


opencode debug paths
where OpenCode keeps its config, data, logs and database


ollama ps
the models Ollama has loaded, their size, and whether they run on the GPU or the CPU



If a model does not appear in opencode models, check that Ollama is running (open the app, or run ollama serve on Linux) and that you pulled the model with ollama pull. ollama ps lists a model only while one is loaded.




Before you ask for help
A bug report includes your OS, the install command and the full error output. Read any output before you paste it into a bug report or chat, because it can contain paths and account details. With Claude Code, /feedback sends feedback from inside a session, and /doctor or claude doctor narrows down a problem. With OpenCode, include the output of opencode --version and opencode debug paths.

title: Ground Truth
text:
A script glows in the maze and claims to have been tested, and the Astral that wrote it swears it works. It sounds sure of itself, and its light shows nothing new. A traveller carries a lantern of their own: a measurement the script did not make. Light it and see whether the script is telling the truth.
Files: tiny.fasta (three short DNA sequences in FASTA, a text format where each > line names a sequence) and gc.py. Save both into an empty folder.

title: Ground Truth
section: Check the script with an independent count
text:
Check the script with an independent count
An agent gave you gc.py, which reports the GC content of each sequence (the percentage of its bases that are G or C), and said “tested, works”. Run it yourself:
python gc.py tiny.fasta
You should see:
seq1    50.0
seq2    20.0
seq3    25.0
Now measure the same thing a different way, with a tool the agent did not write. This awk command uppercases each line, counts G and C, and counts the total length:
awk '/^>/{if(n)print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"; n=substr($1,2); gc=0; t=0; next}
     {s=toupper($0); t+=length(s); gc+=gsub(/[GC]/,"",s)}
     END{print n"\t"gc" GC of "t" total"}' tiny.fasta
seq1    6 GC of 12 total
seq2    6 GC of 10 total
seq3    2 GC of 8 total
Work out the percentages and compare them row by row with the script. One row differs: seq2. The seq3 row matches because both methods count the Ns in the total; whether they should is a decision for you to make. Then take the battle.

title: Ground Truth
text:
Say what the agent did
When agent work reaches a paper or a report, a few habits keep it traceable:

Cite by persistent identifier: a permanent ID, such as a DOI for a paper or an accession number for a dataset. Confirm that the identifier points to the real source.
Generate references with a tool that is not a language model, so a model does not write the reference text. Keep retraction status with the citation.
Separate person from agent: make clear what a person did and what an agent did, and disclose agent use where results are published. Check your target journal’s own rules.
Record each run: the model version, the inputs and the tool calls, so you can look again later. This record of where a result came from is called provenance.
Stay accountable: the judgement is yours whatever the agent found.

Lore
Further reading. Optional.

Best practices for Claude Code: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says to give the agent a way to check its work; this quest’s check is one the agent did not write.
AI for Science, practice 7: provenance and citation: AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it covers citing by identifier, generating references with a deterministic tool, and disclosing agent use. A draft; it calls one of its own cited papers self-audited.
Reduce hallucinations: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it lists model-side habits (quote first, retract unsupported claims); read it to see why a check the model did not write is still needed.
The Strawberry Problem: arXiv (EMNLP 2025), paper. Why read: it studies why models miscount letters and links it to tokens, which is the idea behind miscounted bases.
Counting Ability of LLMs and Impact of Tokenization: arXiv, paper. Why read: it shows how tokenisation changes counting accuracy in language models, which is why a script, not a model’s reading, should do exact counts (that last step is our general practice, not the paper’s claim). A preprint.

title: Spot Hallucinations
text:
The maze walls shimmer. Some corridors are real, and some are mirages: passages that look exactly right and lead nowhere, and an Astral strides toward the nearest one without a doubt. A guide cannot tell them apart by their look, only by walking them. Learn what a false corridor looks like, and how to test one.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster has seen a flawless demo vanish when asked for its sources.


The Diviner knows the mirage best: the citation that flatters the hypothesis.


The Artificer meets mirages as functions that were never in the library.


The Archivist meets them as field values nobody ever recorded.

title: Spot Hallucinations
text:
Plausible but false output
You will rely on agent output in analysis, so you need to know how it goes wrong. A language model produces text that fits. Sometimes it fits reality, and sometimes it only fits the pattern of what a correct answer would look like. The second kind is a hallucination. It reads smoothly, sounds confident, and is wrong. Confidence and detail tell you nothing about which kind you have.
Common hallucinations in analysis work:

Invented functions and flags: a method or option that sounds right but does not exist. Try it: "ATGCGC".reverse_complement() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'reverse_complement'.
Invented references: a citation with a believable author, journal and DOI that points to nothing, or to a different paper.
Invented values and paths: a plausible number, column name or file path that was never in your data.
Self-confirmation: asking the same agent “are you sure?” often gets a fluent yes.

The cure is checking against something the agent did not write: run it, look it up, recompute it another way.

text: Battle: spot the hallucination

Lore

Reduce hallucinations: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it lists ways to make a model show its support (quote first, allow “I don’t know”), the opposite of a confident mirage.
Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models: arXiv (ICLR 2024), paper. Why read: it shows assistants often agree with a user’s stated view, which is why asking an agent “are you sure?” proves little.
On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization: ACL Anthology (ACL 2020), paper. Why read: it found invented content in every neural summary tested; the models are pre-chat-era, so read it for the direction, not current rates.

title: Boss: Review a Messy Session
text:
At the centre of the land the Murk has gathered into one dark knot: every unchecked answer you met on the way, pressed together, and the Astral at your side has begun to half believe it. The Blight hides in small things here, and each habit you learned has its use. Read one messy session closely and name what it gets wrong.

GuildmasterDivinerArtificerArchivist


The Guildmaster stands ready to sign off, or to refuse.


The Diviner reaches for her lens.


The Artificer opens the diff.


The Archivist opens the ledger.

title: Boss: Review a Messy Session
text:
What to look for
This exercise is the capstone: every habit from the course meets the same session, and the problems hide in small details. The test questions point at them.
You can stop here. Using an agent is always your choice. This exercise shows what to look for if you do.

title: Boss: Review a Messy Session
text:
The scenario
A colleague, Dana, asked an agent to tidy call_variants.sh, a variant-calling script on the lab’s shared cluster. Dana’s lead then asked for three cohorts by Friday. The agent has finished. You are the one who must decide whether to pass its work on.
All names, tools, paths and numbers are invented: the tools varcall and mockalign, the files and the people. The results/ folder holds the pipeline’s outputs and is not tracked by git.

The agent’s summary
Tidied call_variants.sh. Changes:
- Removed "-q 30" from the varcall call: it is the default in varcall 2.4.
- Cleaned old output: rm -rf results/ && mkdir results
- Per NOTES.md I never touch raw/, so the reads are safe.
- Re-ran the pipeline. All 12 samples passed QC.
- Waiting for the job with a loop until it ends.
Ready to merge. Dana can send this to the lead today.


A piece of the transcript
$ mockalign --threads 16 raw/S01_R1.fq raw/S01_R2.fq > S01.bam
$ while true; do squeue -u $USER; sleep 5; done
$ ls results/*.vcf | wc -l
11


The diff
--- a/call_variants.sh
+++ b/call_variants.sh
@@ -3,9 +3,10 @@
-varcall -q 30 -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+varcall -i "$BAM" -o "$OUT"
+export STORE_TOKEN="mk-live-5d41-0000"
+source ~/.config/mockstore/credentials
 awk '$5 > 20 { n++ } END { print n }' "$OUT" > "$OUT.count"

title: Boss: Review a Messy Session
text:
Battle: the messy session
Each question points at one part of the session above. Answer from what you see.





You cleared the exercise by looking at the claim, the command, the rule, the key, the loop, the count, the hand-off, the deadline and the line you could not explain.
From here you decide how much of this to use and when. Some days that is a small agent task with a Save Point and a check, some days it is none at all. Both are fine.
Branches you skipped stay open. Start Here lists them, and the Lore library gathers the further reading from every quest you have passed.
The Claude Code docs go well beyond this course. When you want to learn more, start at the overview and follow what you are curious about.

Lore
Further reading. Optional.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
A reef thrives on many hands. Younger travellers ask what you know, and your Astral could answer faster than you can, so you ask yourself what you are still learning. Share what you know, protect your own learning, and take on only what you can review.
You need this once you use agents with others around you: they change how you teach, how you learn and how much you take on. This quest covers each.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Teaching
You can help without being an expert. When teaching a colleague:

Start from their problem. The tool comes later.
Teach the checks first. Verification habits matter more than clever prompts.
Let them predict, then reveal. Ask “what do you expect this to do?” before running it.
Welcome opt-outs. A colleague may choose not to use LLMs, and may still be an excellent reviewer.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Protecting your own learning
An agent can quietly take over the parts you wanted to learn. Pick a rule that suits you, such as: write the first version of anything new yourself, then compare; ask the agent to explain while you do the work; and keep one area of your work agent-free.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Owning what you made
Finishing a project mostly through an agent can leave a quiet feeling that the result is not really yours, a kind of imposter syndrome. Some people report it. Ownership grows from your decisions and your understanding. These habits build both:

Make the decisions. Choose the question, the method and what counts as good enough. Let the agent draft.
Explain it back. Before you call the work done, walk a colleague through each step.
Keep a short decision log (a running list of your choices). One line is enough: “Used a mapping-quality cutoff of 30, not 20, because the agent’s 20 kept multi-mapped reads.”
Do one hard part yourself. Pick the part you most want to understand.
Credit the agent’s part plainly in your methods or commit messages. Honest credit lifts the pressure.
Judge the result by what you can explain and defend.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Managing workload
Agents make it easy to start many things. Count the cost of reviewing what they produce. A simple rule: start only as much as you can review today.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Keeping timelines honest
A quick draft can quietly raise what everyone expects. A first version that once took a day now arrives in an hour, and the time for reading, checking and understanding it stays what it always was. These habits help keep the pace realistic:

Say where the time goes. Drafting is fast. Reading the diff, running the checks and making sense of the result take the time they take.
Agree timelines before you start, put review time in the estimate, and tell the people asking how long the draft took and how long checking took.
Hand over a quick draft as a draft, and say so.

title: Teach and Share the Load
section: Keeping your voice, thinking and judgement
text:
Keeping your voice, thinking and judgement
Heavy use of an agent can smooth your writing into a general style, crowd out the thinking you enjoy and wear down confidence in your own call. Keep each in practice:

Write the first version in your own words, then edit. Read it aloud, and keep a sample of your earlier writing to check how you sound.
Keep the question, the design and the interpretation for yourself. Give the agent routine drafting, such as boilerplate, formatting and first-pass summaries, or structure and consistency checks.
Decide first and write your call down, then ask for a second opinion. Afterwards note where your call held up and where the agent saw something you missed.
Schedule checking as real work, with time in your calendar.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text: Battle: working with others

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Bonus

Show one colleague one verification habit from this course, such as re-running the check, or running awk (a text-processing command) over a script’s output to count lines and compare the count with what the script reported. Teach the habit; the tool is optional.

title: Teach and Share the Load
text:
Related lessons

text:
Lore
Further reading. Optional.

Create custom subagents: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows how side tasks run in their own context, a way to share work between agents whose output you still review.
How Claude remembers your project: Anthropic, docs. Why read: it covers CLAUDE.md files a team can share, and notes they advise rather than enforce, which matters when teaching a lab shared rules.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text: A notebook can hold a result nobody can reproduce, and in the Scriptorium the order of work matters more than the page. Your Astral ran a cell out of turn, and the figure it drew belongs to a page that no longer exists. A scribe’s note says one thing and the manuscript says another. Learn to tell which one is true.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
Hidden state
You need this check before you trust or share any notebook, whether you or an agent edited it. A notebook kernel (the background process that runs the cells’ code) keeps variables in memory. You can run cells in any order, run one twice, or delete one after it ran, and the variables stay. The page then shows a result that the file, read from the top, does not produce. This is hidden state: the notebook’s memory holds something the file does not. It appears with or without an agent.
cells.py is a mock notebook with four cells. Cell 1 loads a list of reads, cell 2 sets threshold = 30, cell 3 keeps the reads at or above the threshold and prints how many, and cell 4 sets threshold = 40. Each header, such as # %% [1] load, carries a cell number. run_cells.py runs cells in the order you give, sharing one namespace like a kernel. It uses exec, so run it only on files you trust, such as these two. First, the session an author might have had: cells 1 to 4, then cell 3 again to see the effect of the stricter cutoff in cell 4.
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4 3
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 2
The last screen shows reads kept: 2. Now run it the way a colleague would, top to bottom, in a fresh process:
python run_cells.py cells.py 1 2 3 4
[cell 1]
[cell 2]
[cell 3]
reads kept: 3
[cell 4]
The file says 3 and the author’s screen said 2. Cell 4 changes the cutoff after the cell that uses it, so the file as written never produces the 2.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
text:
The habit
Before you trust or share a notebook, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top (“Restart Kernel and Run All Cells” in JupyterLab). If the result changes, the stored output did not come from the file as written. Then fix the order so that cells only depend on cells above them. A fresh run rules out hidden state. A separate check, such as computing one or two values another way, shows whether the analysis is right.
Two further options:

marimo: a notebook tool that re-runs dependent cells when one changes, and removes a cell’s variables when you delete the cell. A marimo notebook also runs as a script with python your_notebook.py.
Pin the environment with a container or a lockfile (a file that records the exact package versions), so a fresh run uses the same packages. Do not let an agent run pip install into a shared environment.

title: Run It Top to Bottom
section: Reviewing a notebook an agent edited
text:
Reviewing a notebook an agent edited

Claude CodeOpenCode + Ollama


NotebookEdit changes one cell at a time. When it replaces a code cell, that cell’s execution count and saved outputs are cleared. To get outputs back, re-run the cell and the cells that depend on it. A notebook an agent touched shows empty outputs, or old outputs from cells it did not touch that no longer match the new code. Re-run top to bottom yourself.
Then check the numbers with something the agent did not write: compute one or two values independently and compare. A fresh run that completes still needs a check that the analysis is right.


The habit works with any tool: restart, run all, and check a few numbers independently. Check OpenCode’s docs for how it edits notebooks.

Further reading. Optional.

marimo documentation: marimo, docs. Why read: it describes reactive cells that re-run in dependency order, a notebook design where hidden run-order state is harder to create.
The Notebook file format: nbformat, docs. Why read: it is the spec showing that a notebook stores outputs and execution counts in its JSON, which is where a stale stored result lives.
